Brian Mast (R-Fla.), the chairperson of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, has said that he will issue a subpoena to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang if he does not respond to the committee’s request to meet with them on November 18 by Wednesday, November 11, according to ABC News . The House invited him to a “joint, closed-door briefing” with the heads of the House committees on China, Foreign Affairs, and Intelligence, and that they will focus on his company’s “ security protocols against foreign adversary espionage.”

Congress first called the embattled CEO on November 7, a few days after rumors started circulating about Huang’s “closeness” to a particular Chinese executive suspected of passing information to Chinese intelligence. The following day, Nvidia released a statement from Jensen admitting to an affair with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, apologizing for his unfaithfulness, while the company’s board of directors confirmed it will launch an independent investigation regarding the allegations that the CEO has been specifically targeted by China’s Ministry of State Security (MSS). Aside from having to face Congress, Jensen Huang is also reportedly being looked into by the FBI.

It remains unclear whether Jensen Huang was targeted by intelligence agencies, but he came into prominence with the AI boom that was arguably fueled by Nvidia’s AI chips. This led to the AI race as we know it today, with the U.S. taking steps to delay China’s advancement for fears that it will use the technology for military purposes. We also don’t know if Huang Le or Alice Huang is actually a Chinese spy or an “innocent” bystander caught in a web of accusations. And, even if she did work with the MSS, the question remains as to whether she specifically targeted the Nvidia CEO or whether Chinese intelligence discovered their indiscretion and used that as a convenient tool for blackmail to extract information from her.

However, former CIA agent Darrel Blocker told ABC News that the authorities should just focus on Jensen. “I think that the biggest concern is that the focus or overfocus on just Jensen Huang and Nvidia risks losing sight of the fact that other people have been targeted by the Chinese. Are they talking to the engineers? Are they talking to other people who might have even more access than even the CEO has? So, this focus should not be singular; it should include everyone in the company, and quite frankly, every tech company out there should be looking at all the contacts that their officers and employees have.”

“It’s definitely not a one-time thing. When you run a trillion-dollar company, you know that you have a bullseye on your back; whether it’s from competition or rather from nation-states, so this is absolutely not a one-off. Jensen Huang is not the only person at Nvidia that has access to the crown jewels, so I would be looking at the other people in terms of the access that they enjoy and their proximity to Chinese nationals.”

Brian Mast, told ABC News on Tuesday that he's prepared to subpoena Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang if he does not respond by Wednesday to a request from several House Republicans for a closed-door briefing on Huang's reported relationship with an alleged Chinese spy. Last week, Mast as well as Rick Crawford, the chair of the House Intelligence Committee, and John Moolenaar, the chair of the House China Committee, sent Huang a letter requesting he appear for a "joint, closed-door briefing." The focus of the briefing would be on Nvidia's "security protocols against foreign adversary espionage" after the tech giant on Sunday announced an investigation into its CEO following New York Times' reporting that he had an affair with an alleged Chinese government agent, identified as Alice Huang, a top executive at Singapore-based data company Megaspeed. Jensen Huang has not yet responded to the Republicans' request that he appear for a briefing. Asked by ABC News if he would consider issuing a subpoena to Huang should he not respond, Mast said "absolutely." It's unclear how a potential subpoena of Huang would play out. House Republicans lose control of their committees in January when the chamber turns over to Democrats. The subpoena would likely expire and Democrats would need to issue a new one. ABC News reached out to Nvidia for comment from Huang for this story. Congressional Republicans on the Select Committee on China also sent a letter to Huang requesting that he appear for a closed-door briefing Nov. 18 concerning his relationship with Alice Huang. It is not known if Huang will appear before that committee; Nvidia hasn't publicly responded to the request. Mast said there is a "lengthy" list of things he wants to hear from the Nvidia CEO including what correspondence he had with the Chinese government. Mast added that he is "100%" worried about the national security implications of Huang's reported relationship given that he runs the world's largest computer chip manufacturer. "They're American chips. You know. So we thank God that Jensen is an American entrepreneur. You know, it's an American tech company because they're the best chips anywhere in the globe," Mast said. "But that being said, we don't want China to access them, to use them, to produce them like that." Nvidia's board said they have "no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised" by Huang's affair. Huang "fully supports the review" and will cooperate with it, the Nvidia statement further said. Several Democrats have expressed concerns about national security after the report, with House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries telling ABC News that there are "real concerns" that need to be addressed. "We're going to need a full briefing, specifically as it relates to the Nvidia issue, so we can all get to the bottom of what has happened and what the implications are in terms of America's national security," Jeffries said. On Monday, President Donald Trump said the FBI is investigating the matter. Trump said he spoke with Huang in a phone call on Monday, during which the CEO said that he "didn't know" he was involved with an alleged Chinese spy. "He said he had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy," the president told reporters during a press briefing on Monday. It's unclear when -- if ever -- the Trump administration alerted Nvidia that its CEO was the target of an alleged Chinese espionage plot. extraction.body: Nvidia’s board announced that Jensen Huang — its longtime co-founder, president, and CEO — has resigned after reports of two extramarital affairs, one with an alleged Chinese spy and one with an Nvidia executive who reported to Huang. A press release published Thursday following a late Wednesday night board meeting announced Huang’s resignation as CEO, president, and board member, effective immediately, with current CFO Colette Kress appointed interim CEO. Kress has been with Nvidia since 2013, with previous stops at Cisco and Microsoft. Nvidia is also changing its corporate structure in Huang’s absence, appointing former Synopsys CEO Harvey C. The statement does not include a quote from Huang, while Kress is quoted as saying, “NVIDIA’s strength has always come from its people, and together with our leadership team, I am committed to building on the extraordinary foundation Jensen created over the last 33 years. We will continue advancing the work that has made NVIDIA a leader in accelerated computing and AI, and execute on the opportunities ahead. Our focus remains on serving our customers, partners, developers and shareholders.” Now Nvidia says, “The Board is initiating a search for a permanent Chief Executive Officer and will consider internal and external candidates,” and reports about who that might be have already surfaced, putting Kress, Apple hardware chief Johny Srouji, Nvidia VP Ian Buck, AMD CEO (and cousin of Jensen Huang) Lisa Su, and Arm CEO Rene Haas at the top of the list. Huang had been at the helm of what’s now known as the most powerful company in AI since its founding in 1993. In the years since, it’s become the main purveyor of the chips fueling AI advancement and deployment in the US, and it has enjoyed near-unbridled power and influence — demand for Nvidia’s chips constantly outpaces supply, and AI CEOs are constantly putting in requests to buy more, sometimes to no avail. Nvidia’s investment portfolio — worth about $99 billion and spanning AI companies from frontier labs to neoclouds — has also granted it a lot of sway in the AI space. And in recent years, Huang himself has enjoyed a close relationship with President Donald Trump. Over the past week, that influence has been a double-edged sword for Huang, after news broke that he had been involved in a romantic relationship with Alice Huang (no relation), an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based cloud provider and big customer of Nvidia itself. The Megaspeed executive was also allegedly a surveillance operative passing information along to China’s Ministry of State Security. She was focused on gaining information about advanced AI chips in the US and trying to influence the technology being made available to China, The New York Times reported. Huang admitted he had been “unfaithful” to his wife and apologized to his family and shareholders in a memo to Nvidia employees over the weekend. As The Verge wrote earlier this week, “questions are swirling around how the affair may have influenced Huang’s reported push to sell advanced chips to China — and potentially even influenced President Trump’s own decisions surrounding AI export controls.” As of Monday, analysts, venture capitalists and even Trump had expected Huang would come out the other side of the scandal with his chief executive status intact. But on Wednesday, news broke that Huang had had a second extramarital affair — this time with an executive reporting directly to him. The New York Times, citing five people who worked at Nvidia, identified the relationship as being with Nvidia’s VP of healthcare, Kimberly Powell. Soon after the news broke, The Wall Street Journal reported, citing people familiar with the matter, that Nvidia’s board was meeting as soon as Wednesday evening in order to decide Huang’s future at the company and potentially oust him from his role.

The married American-Taiwanese businessman, who was the president, chief executive officer, and member of the board for the AI behemoth he founded 30 years ago, has stepped down after admitting to cheating on his wife. 'Jensen’s contributions to Nvidia are profound,' the company wrote in a press release announcing his resignation. 'Nvidia is one of the most consequential technology companies in the world. The Board and the company thank Jensen for his immeasurable contributions to the company and the industry.' Chief financial officer Colette Kress, who has worked at Nvidia since 2013, will take the reins on an interim basis as it looks to appoint a permanent successor. It comes after a New York Times investigation revealed that Huang, 63, had been the target of an espionage plot by the Chinese government. He admitted to having an extramarital affair with Alex Huang, a Chinese executive at a company base din Singapore, who had allegedly been recruited by the CCP. It has also since been claimed that the billionaire also had an extramarital relationship with his colleague – Kimberly Powell, 48, Nvidia's vice president of healthcare. Nvidia boss Jensen Huang with suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang, who is no relation Nvidia vice president of healthcare Kimberly Powell Huang's alleged affair would have violated the company's code of conduct, under which employees are told to 'avoid situations where our actions conflict' including 'personal relationships'. The news sent shockwaves through the stock market. Nvidia shares fell nearly 10 per cent in pre-market trading in New York on Thursday, wiping another $420 billion off its value. That takes losses this week to $730 billion, or 16 per cent. The company has shed around $2 trillion of value since its peak on October 6. Chris Weston, head of research at Pepperstone brokerage, described the news that Huang was stepping down as a 'bombshell'. 'It appears the board has heard enough to make what can only be described as a groundbreaking decision, one with potentially profound implications for Nvidia and the broader AI ecosystem,' he said. The crisis at Nvidia follows weeks of turmoil for AI stocks as investors fretted over whether huge spending on infrastructure such as data centers would ever yield acceptable returns. Democrat’s sweeping victories in the US midterm elections last week fueled anxiety amid fears it would result in a clampdown on data centers and put the brakes on the AI revolution. Nvidia ( NVDA ) CEO Jensen Huang is stepping down as CEO following reports that he had an affair with a fellow executive at the AI giant and after he admitted to having a separate affair with a woman whom US intelligence officials believe is a Chinese spy. CFO Colette Kress will succeed Huang as interim CEO until the company names either a permanent CEO. The chip giant is looking both internally and externally for candidates. The Board has full confidence in Colette and the leadership team, and we expect the company's operations, customer commitments and product roadmap to continue without interruption." Kress, in a statement, said that she is committed to building on the work Jensen has to turn Nvidia into the company it has become. "We will continue advancing the work that has made Nvidia a leader in accelerated computing and AI, and execute on the opportunities ahead. According to The New York Times , Huang engaged in a relationship with Nvidia executive Kimberly Powell, who heads the company's healthcare efforts. Nvidia's board has said it has launched an independent investigation into the matter, but added it has no reason to believe Nvidia trade secrets or national security were compromised. Huang co-founded Nvidia in 1993 alongside Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem, with a vision to bring 3D graphics to the gaming industry. The company primarily focused on the space for years before releasing its CUDA technology in 2006, allowing users to take advantage of Nvidia's graphics chips for general-purpose computing. The company took that a step further in 2013 with the release of its first AI server, the DGX-1. Both CUDA and the DGX-1 gave Nvidia an early lead in the AI hardware race when OpenAI launched its ChatGPT in late 2022. That helped catapult Nvidia's market capitalization into the stratosphere and turned Huang into an overnight celebrity in the US and abroad. As the company became more important to the AI trade and US economy, Huang's profile rocketed higher, becoming one of the most powerful CEOs in the world. He has been a regular presence in Washington, D.C., making numerous appearances alongside President Trump. The usually leather jacket-clad Huang drove Nvidia's product strategy for years behind the scenes and, as its public face, hosted packed keynotes across the world. He has also lobbied Washington to ease export restrictions on the company's chips for export to China, a key AI market. The Biden administration initially banned the sale of Nvidia chips to China over fears that the country's government would use them to supplant the US as the world's AI leader and develop powerful AI models for military purposes. President Trump, however, has eased some of those restrictions, allowing the sale of less-than-state-of-the-art chips to the country.

A press release published Thursday following a late Wednesday night board meeting announced Huang’s resignation as CEO, president, and board member, effective immediately, with current CFO Colette Kress appointed interim CEO. Kress has been with Nvidia since 2013, with previous stops at Cisco and Microsoft. Nvidia is also changing its corporate structure in Huang’s absence, appointing former Synopsys CEO Harvey C. The statement does not include a quote from Huang, while Kress is quoted as saying, “NVIDIA’s strength has always come from its people, and together with our leadership team, I am committed to building on the extraordinary foundation Jensen created over the last 33 years. We will continue advancing the work that has made NVIDIA a leader in accelerated computing and AI, and execute on the opportunities ahead. Our focus remains on serving our customers, partners, developers and shareholders.” Now Nvidia says, “The Board is initiating a search for a permanent Chief Executive Officer and will consider internal and external candidates,” and reports about who that might be have already surfaced, putting Kress, Apple hardware chief Johny Srouji, Nvidia VP Ian Buck, AMD CEO (and cousin of Jensen Huang) Lisa Su, and Arm CEO Rene Haas at the top of the list. Huang had been at the helm of what’s now known as the most powerful company in AI since its founding in 1993. In the years since, it’s become the main purveyor of the chips fueling AI advancement and deployment in the US, and it has enjoyed near-unbridled power and influence — demand for Nvidia’s chips constantly outpaces supply, and AI CEOs are constantly putting in requests to buy more, sometimes to no avail. Nvidia’s investment portfolio — worth about $99 billion and spanning AI companies from frontier labs to neoclouds — has also granted it a lot of sway in the AI space. And in recent years, Huang himself has enjoyed a close relationship with President Donald Trump. Over the past week, that influence has been a double-edged sword for Huang, after news broke that he had been involved in a romantic relationship with Alice Huang (no relation), an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based cloud provider and big customer of Nvidia itself. She was focused on gaining information about advanced AI chips in the US and trying to influence the technology being made available to China, The New York Times reported. Huang admitted he had been “unfaithful” to his wife and apologized to his family and shareholders in a memo to Nvidia employees over the weekend. But on Wednesday, news broke that Huang had had a second extramarital affair — this time with an executive reporting directly to him. The New York Times, citing five people who worked at Nvidia, identified the relationship as being with Nvidia’s VP of healthcare, Kimberly Powell. Soon after the news broke, The Wall Street Journal reported, citing people familiar with the matter, that Nvidia’s board was meeting as soon as Wednesday evening in order to decide Huang’s future at the company and potentially oust him from his role.

extraction.body: Nvidia founder Jensen Huang has resigned in the wake of an investigation into his affairs with an alleged Chinese spy and one of his underlings at the company. The married American-Taiwanese businessman, who was the president, chief executive officer, and member of the board for the AI behemoth he founded 30 years ago, has stepped down after admitting to cheating on his wife. 'Jensen’s contributions to Nvidia are profound,' the company wrote in a press release announcing his resignation. 'Nvidia is one of the most consequential technology companies in the world. The Board and the company thank Jensen for his immeasurable contributions to the company and the industry.' Chief financial officer Colette Kress, who has worked at Nvidia since 2013, will take the reins on an interim basis as it looks to appoint a permanent successor. It comes after a New York Times investigation revealed that Huang, 63, had been the target of an espionage plot by the Chinese government. He admitted to having an extramarital affair with Alex Huang, a Chinese executive at a company base din Singapore, who had allegedly been recruited by the CCP. It has also since been claimed that the billionaire also had an extramarital relationship with his colleague – Kimberly Powell, 48, Nvidia's vice president of healthcare. Nvidia boss Jensen Huang with suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang, who is no relation Nvidia vice president of healthcare Kimberly Powell Huang's alleged affair would have violated the company's code of conduct, under which employees are told to 'avoid situations where our actions conflict' including 'personal relationships'. The news sent shockwaves through the stock market. Nvidia shares fell nearly 10 per cent in pre-market trading in New York on Thursday, wiping another $420 billion off its value. That takes losses this week to $730 billion, or 16 per cent. The company has shed around $2 trillion of value since its peak on October 6. Chris Weston, head of research at Pepperstone brokerage, described the news that Huang was stepping down as a 'bombshell'. 'It appears the board has heard enough to make what can only be described as a groundbreaking decision, one with potentially profound implications for Nvidia and the broader AI ecosystem,' he said. The crisis at Nvidia follows weeks of turmoil for AI stocks as investors fretted over whether huge spending on infrastructure such as data centers would ever yield acceptable returns. Democrat’s sweeping victories in the US midterm elections last week fueled anxiety amid fears it would result in a clampdown on data centers and put the brakes on the AI revolution. This is a breaking news story with updates to follow.

sources.title: Apple HomeView Review: A Versatile Smart Display And Siri-Powered Home Hub - Engadget
passages: Apple's entry into the smart display category was rumored for years.
Now that the HomeView ($299) is here, Apple is hoping the iPhone faithful will like its mix of elevated design and newly expanded Siri capabilities .
Unlike smart displays from Amazon and Google, Apple's approach relies on a companion device.
As you'd imagine, that means the HomeView's usefulness, like CarPlay's, is directly tied to how much you use Apple's core apps — things like Messages, Calendar, Photos, Reminders and others.

If all of that is OK to you, and if you're willing to give Siri access to personal data inside some of those apps, the HomeView can quickly become a very versatile device with something for your whole family.
The ability to automatically distinguish between different family members, and for Siri to pull in personalized context for each person, makes this a useful home hub.
The company explained that this enables the HomeView to recognize your face and voice, or that of other users in your home, without exposing any of the data to the operating system.
With the Home app and devices compatible with HomeKit and Matter, this display becomes the command center for your cameras, thermostat, lighting and more.
At times, Siri showed text answers on the HomeView in addition to reciting the info.
But it's important to remember that HomeView is just a conduit for Siri AI and its newly expanded abilities.
These same things can be done on an iPhone or other compatible Apple devices, meaning you don't really have to spend $300 on a dedicated display for these tools.
Apple is years behind the competition when it comes to smart displays.
The Home Modular face puts your favorite smart home devices on the same screen thanks to customizable widgets.
The HomeView may look like an enlarged Apple Watch's screen, but the two devices also overlap in another area: faces.
If it's in direct sunlight, you can expect the maximum 500 nits, but at night, it can dial things down to just 0.3 nits — the lowest brightness ever on an Apple display.
Apple ships the standard version of the device with a USB-C to USB-C cable and a 30-watt power adapter.
The HomeView essentially consists of two parts: a cylindrical, domed base and a 7-inch Liquid Retina display.
Lastly, Live Activities displays real-time info for a variety of tasks on HomeView.
Google's current slate of smart displays is much more modest, with only the aging second-generation Nest Hub and Nest Hub Max as the available options.
That's OK though, because right now, the only video app that's available on HomeView is Apple TV.

And unless you like watching your shows within a thin band that sits in the middle of a square display, flanked by thick black bars on the top and bottom, you, too, will find the video experience on HomeView underwhelming.
I would love to see Apple bring F1 multiview to this display though, putting two small alternate feeds below the main broadcast.
I've been reviewing the tabletop HomeView with a base, so I've enjoyed the added woofer and passive radiators, which balance out full-range drivers with extra bass.
It also works with the iPhone, iPad and Apple Watch, plus you can send and receive intercom messages from anywhere — not just inside your home.
I'm just pointing this all out to say Apple is advertising the ideal scenario, which is honestly an excellent experience, but you may not encounter it every time you cook with HomeView.

I would love to see Apple bring F1 multiview to this display though, putting two small alternate feeds below the main broadcast. Yes, they'd be tiny, but at least that's a better use of the space and eliminates the awkward black bars. Apple says third-party developers are welcome to enable their apps for use on the HomeView, but doing so would also mean optimizing them for CarPlay. Only time will tell if developers are going to go through the extra steps of making that happen. When it comes to audio-only content though, the HomeView is great. I'd classify the sound quality here as the midpoint between the HomePod mini and the larger HomePod. I've been reviewing the tabletop HomeView with a base, so I've enjoyed the added woofer and passive radiators, which balance out full-range drivers with extra bass. Across a variety of genres, bass is tight and punchy, and vocals cut through the mix clearly. The system never loses other instruments either, as you can easily pick up the guitars in Anberlin's "Gravity." Switch to something more chill, like Sam Barber's "If I May," and the acoustic instruments lay a base for the singer's unique vocals. Drums are more subdued here, and the HomeView does well to keep them from overpowering the mix. I should also note the HomeView can get pretty darn loud. I measured 87dB with my Apple Watch standing right in front of the device. But I should also warn you that it's not a comfortable listening volume if you're standing close to the display. However, given the compact stature of the device and its limited sonic prowess, you're more likely to notice the excellent overall clarity and even-handed tuning more than any dimensional effects. While watching an episode of Masters of the Air, for example, I found the sound perfectly fine, but wouldn't classify it as very immersive. Apple included a few more entertainment-related conveniences on the HomeView that add utility. For one, it works with the HomePod, HomePod mini and AirPlay-compatible speakers for multiroom audio, which allows you to play the same thing everywhere or pick specific songs for each room. When listening to songs from Apple Music, you'll see animated album artwork if an artist has it, and lyrics are available with a single tap. And just like you can with your iPhone and HomePod speakers, you can handoff content from your phone to the HomeView just by placing your handset in front of the display. The HomeView may look like an enlarged Apple Watch's screen, but the two devices also overlap in another area: faces. These screens are what you see when the HomeView is in what I like to call rest mode, when it's just sitting there not being actively used. You can have it just be a clock, as there are three faces just for that purpose, or display your calendar or the weather. There's also an animated Snoopy face that updates based on the time of day, weather, holidays and sporting events. Then there are the two Home faces that work with smart home devices that I already mentioned. Those all have their purpose, but my two favorites are the Photos and Modular faces. The former makes the HomeView a digital picture frame and you can get specific about what shows up there. You can opt for it to cycle through photos of specific events (Memories), people, pets or cities, for example, but you can also set up Shared Albums that it will source from. If you do that last one, new photos will automatically appear every time they're added to the collection. The Modular face is what I've used most, as its customizable collection of widgets puts the calendar, date, time and weather in one spot. Of course, you can pick and choose what shows up here based on your needs or preferences, you're not forced to use the same combination I do. The best thing about faces is that you can easily switch between them by swiping horizontally on one. A long press brings up the face customization interface where you're free to fine-tune things like color and widgets (where available) to your heart's content. One feature that Apple has spent a lot of time showing off on the HomeView is FaceTime. The smart display has a 12-megapixel Center Stage camera in its top bezel, which means you can conduct video chats without reaching for your iPhone. Of course, the Center Stage software will keep you centered in the frame as you move around, which will be handy if you need to take a call from the kitchen while you're cooking, for example. You can start FaceTime calls on the HomeView, or you can hand them off from your iPhone. I'll also note that you can take voice calls from the HomeView, and in general, the device works well for both types of chats. Find My is also available on the HomeView, allowing you to locate everything from your iPhone to your AirPods, or anything that has an AirTag attached to it. Of course, you can also use this to find family and friends who are sharing their location with you. The intercom feature from HomePods is on the HomeView as well, which comes in handy if you have multiple Apple speakers spread throughout your house. It also works with the iPhone, iPad and Apple Watch, plus you can send and receive intercom messages from anywhere — not just inside your home. Lastly, Live Activities displays real-time info for a variety of tasks on HomeView. Like it does on your iPhone, the feature puts your progress at the top of the display on a floating, tappable button. Live Activities on the HomeView are a bit limited though, only capable of showing active timers/alarms, FaceTime calls, Safari media playback and Now Playing controls for Apple Music or Apple TV. I found it also surfaced audio controls for my go-to podcast app Pocket Casts as well. One thing that doesn't show up there that I wish it did is Live Activities from the Sports app. It would be great if the live scores for my favorite teams or an update on who's leading the F1 grand prix were available at a glance. Apple is years behind the competition when it comes to smart displays. The company's two main rivals in this category, Amazon and Google, have been honing their products since 2017 and 2018 respectively. The premise has always been similar to Apple's: a combination display and speaker that's a conduit for each company's virtual assistant — or in 2026 terms, each company's AI. Amazon's current Echo Show lineup has six options, ranging from 5 inches up to 21 inches, with the largest models ditching the speaker base for a wall mount or stand. The most affordable, the Echo Show 5 , is $100. Google's current slate of smart displays is much more modest, with only the aging second-generation Nest Hub and Nest Hub Max as the available options. Those are going for $100 and $229 respectively, and only the pricier of the two has a built-in camera for video calls. Apple may have lagged behind the competition on introducing a smart display, but the HomeView checks a lot of boxes that make it a very powerful option for iPhone users. It's also more elegantly designed than all of its main competitors. The ability to automatically distinguish between different family members, and for Siri to pull in personalized context for each person, makes this a useful home hub. When you factor in the cooking assistance, smart home compatibility and FaceTime chops, the HomeView can easily become the command center for any household. Just be sure to keep your iPhone (or iPad) handy if you want to make the most of it.

It also works with the iPhone, iPad and Apple Watch, plus you can send and receive intercom messages from anywhere — not just inside your home.

Lastly, Live Activities displays real-time info for a variety of tasks on HomeView. Like it does on your iPhone, the feature puts your progress at the top of the display on a floating, tappable button. Live Activities on the HomeView are a bit limited though, only capable of showing active timers/alarms, FaceTime calls, Safari media playback and Now Playing controls for Apple Music or Apple TV. I found it also surfaced audio controls for my go-to podcast app Pocket Casts as well. One thing that doesn't show up there that I wish it did is Live Activities from the Sports app. It would be great if the live scores for my favorite teams or an update on who's leading the F1 grand prix were available at a glance.

Apple is years behind the competition when it comes to smart displays. The company's two main rivals in this category, Amazon and Google, have been honing their products since 2017 and 2018 respectively. The premise has always been similar to Apple's: a combination display and speaker that's a conduit for each company's virtual assistant — or in 2026 terms, each company's AI.

Amazon's current Echo Show lineup has six options, ranging from 5 inches up to 21 inches, with the largest models ditching the speaker base for a wall mount or stand. The most affordable, the Echo Show 5 , is $100. Google's current slate of smart displays is much more modest, with only the aging second-generation Nest Hub and Nest Hub Max as the available options. Those are going for $100 and $229 respectively, and only the pricier of the two has a built-in camera for video calls.

Apple may have lagged behind the competition on introducing a smart display, but the HomeView checks a lot of boxes that make it a very powerful option for iPhone users. It's also more elegantly designed than all of its main competitors. The ability to automatically distinguish between different family members, and for Siri to pull in personalized context for each person, makes this a useful home hub. When you factor in the cooking assistance, smart home compatibility and FaceTime chops, the HomeView can easily become the command center for any household. Just be sure to keep your iPhone (or iPad) handy if you want to make the most of it.

passages: The new Apple HomeView asks a BIG question: If your household is already filled with iPhones, iPads, and smart speakers, does Apple's first dedicated smart display justify a permanent spot on your kitchen counter?

Front-on view of the 1:1 square display canvas, balancing glanceable widgets and quick-launch icons for shared household spaces | Image: Ben McKimm / Man of Many 30-Second Apple HomeView Verdict Pros: Distance-adaptive UI scales text and widgets automatically depending on how far away you stand.
But before we dive into the full Apple HomeView review, let's look at what we're dealing with here.
If you typically mount things in your hallways, entryways, or dedicated smart home control points, Apple also offers HomeView (Wall Mounted) in Space Grey and Silver.
When viewed at night, HomeView can dial its backlight down to just 0.3 nits, the lowest display brightness Apple has ever offered.
Now that I've spent the past week living with the Apple HomeView in my kitchen, I have an answer.
Does it bridge the gap between a shared family noticeboard, an entertainment player, and a deeply personalised smart home controller?
I needed a screen to glance at information quickly, but Apple's home strategy was entirely screenless.
Placed on a bedside table, it eliminates the harsh backlight glow that plagues conventional smart displays in pitch-black bedrooms.

extraction.body: The new Apple HomeView asks a BIG question: If your household is already filled with iPhones, iPads, and smart speakers, does Apple's first dedicated smart display justify a permanent spot on your kitchen counter? Now that I've spent the past week living with the Apple HomeView in my kitchen, I have an answer. My Google Nest Hub (2nd Gen) died two weeks before the HomeView was announced. I needed a screen to glance at information quickly, but Apple's home strategy was entirely screenless. It pairs a square 7-inch Liquid Retina display with an A18 chip, a Spatial Audio acoustic system, and the new Siri AI. Does it bridge the gap between a shared family noticeboard, an entertainment player, and a deeply personalised smart home controller? I've spent the past week living with the new device as the central command hub in my kitchen and living space, putting it through its paces across busy morning routines, cooking sessions, and smart home automations. But before we dive into the full Apple HomeView review, let's look at what we're dealing with here. You can get your HomeView in both a tabletop model (featuring a machined aluminium domed base and an adjustable stainless steel hinge) and a sleek wall-mounted variant (that loses a little sound quality). It packs a 1088 x 1088 Liquid Retina display that dims down to just 0.3 nits for bedside use, alongside four beamforming microphones and a 12MP Center Stage camera. However, taking full advantage of the experience requires accepting a few deliberate ecosystem dependencies: neither model has an internal battery (both require wired power), personal context features rely on having a paired Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone or iPad on your network, and the wall-mounted model sells its mounts and power cables separately. Front-on view of the 1:1 square display canvas, balancing glanceable widgets and quick-launch icons for shared household spaces | Image: Ben McKimm / Man of Many 30-Second Apple HomeView Verdict Pros: Distance-adaptive UI scales text and widgets automatically depending on how far away you stand. 7-inch Liquid Retina display drops to a record-low 0.3 nits for distraction-free nightstand use. Recognises up to six household members via face and voice to surface apps, etc., privately. Tabletop model pairs dual full-range drivers with a down-firing woofer and passive radiators. Streams up to nine live HomeKit and Matter camera feeds simultaneously on the Home Camera. Cons: Requires permanent wired power via USB-C, with no built-in battery for cordless portability. Personal context Siri AI and expressive voices require an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone or iPad. Wall-mounted model omits the base woofer and sells mounts, cable, and power adapter separately. No-brainer if you're deeply invested in the Apple ecosystem and want a dedicated, privacy-first kitchen companion, bedside clock, or smart home control panel that everyone in the house can share. Table of contents30-Second Apple HomeView VerdictShould You Buy the Apple HomeView?Apple HomeView Technical SpecificationsDesign, Hardware, and Wall-Mounting OptionsLiquid Retina Display and Distance-Adaptive UISound Quality and Multiroom EntertainmentA18 Performance, Siri AI, and Multi-User ControlsEveryday Utility: Cooking, FaceTime, and Smart Home HubMan of Many's Verdict on the Apple HomeViewFAQsWhy Trust Man of Many? Measuring just 5.73 inches (14.55 cm) wide and adjusting between 5.38 (13.67 cm) and 6.83 inches (17.35 cm) tall depending on tilt, the tabletop model anchors its screen to a hefty, 100 per cent recycled aluminium domed base via a stainless steel hinge. You can get the tabletop HomeView in four finishes (Silver, Starlight, Rose Pink, and Space Grey), and it includes a colour-matched 1.5-metre USB-C cable and power adapter in the box. Neither variant includes a battery, meaning permanent wired power is mandatory. If you typically mount things in your hallways, entryways, or dedicated smart home control points, Apple also offers HomeView (Wall Mounted) in Space Grey and Silver. Rather than sitting on a domed base, it pairs with a trio of purpose-built mounts from Schneider Home (sold separately alongside the required cable and power adapter): Power Mount USB-C Wall Connector: Self-installed option with an attached cable. Power Mount AC Wired: Hardwired mount for a flush installation with no visible cords. Front view of the 1088 x 1088 square display canvas, highlighting the active user profile badge in the top corner powered by A18 Secure Exclaves | Image: Ben McKimm / Man of Many Liquid Retina Display and Distance-Adaptive UI While 7 inches (6.98 inches diagonally, accounting for rounded corners) may sound modest on paper, the 1:1 square aspect ratio gives HomeView a generous canvas. The LED-backlit IPS panel runs at a crisp 1088 x 1088 resolution (220 ppi) with an oleophobic coating that does a decent job of shrugging off kitchen smudges. The real standout is the display's dynamic range. I have my review unit placed in a sunlit kitchen, where the True Tone and auto-brightness features regularly push the panel up to its peak 500 nits so recipes and camera feeds remain legible. When viewed at night, HomeView can dial its backlight down to just 0.3 nits, the lowest display brightness Apple has ever offered. Placed on a bedside table, it eliminates the harsh backlight glow that plagues conventional smart displays in pitch-black bedrooms. To make that 7-inch screen legible from across a room without cluttering the interface, Apple built a clever distance-adaptive UI. When you're standing across the living room, HomeView presents clean, large-scale typography, such as today's high and low temperatures or basic Live Activities. Walk closer to the display, and the interface transitions to reveal richer, more granular details such as hourly weather breakdowns, interactive controls, and expanded Siri responses.

Apple announced HomeView on Tuesday, October 13, 2026, as part of its "Welcome home" launch.
HomeView has a compact, square display mounted above a rounded aluminum speaker base, with a design that recalls Apple's classic iMac G4.

Powered by Apple's A18 chip and Apple Intelligence, HomeView offers a much more capable version of Siri that can answer questions conversationally, help with everyday tasks, and access personal information from a compatible iPhone or iPad.
HomeView introduces a range of capabilities that aren't available on Apple's traditional HomePod speakers.

extraction.body: Apple HomeView is Apple's first dedicated smart-home display, combining a 7-inch touchscreen, powerful speakers, a camera, and Siri AI in a device designed to sit at the center of the connected home. Announced on October 13, 2026 and on sale from November 13, it brings together smart-home controls, entertainment, video calling, calendars, reminders, and other everyday information. Powered by Apple's A18 chip and Apple Intelligence, HomeView offers a much more capable version of Siri that can answer questions conversationally, help with everyday tasks, and access personal information from a compatible iPhone or iPad. HomeView is designed to work alongside Apple's existing HomePod speakers, Apple TV, iPhone, and iPad. It integrates with the Apple Home app, supporting compatible HomeKit and Matter accessories, including lights, locks, thermostats, and security cameras. It can also serve as a central smart-home hub, making it easier to manage devices and automations throughout the house. Unlike a HomePod with a screen added, HomeView is designed around visual interaction as well as voice control. Its touchscreen, customizable widgets, FaceTime camera, personalized Home Screens, and dedicated smart-home dashboards make it more like a shared household computer than a conventional smart speaker. HomeView introduces a range of capabilities that aren't available on Apple's traditional HomePod speakers. While HomePod focuses primarily on music, Siri, and voice-controlled smart-home functions, HomeView adds a touchscreen, camera, personalized interface, and much deeper integration with Apple apps and services. HomeView also supports Handoff from iPhone, Live Activities, Find My, and multiroom audio with compatible AirPlay speakers. How does HomeView compare with HomePod and iPad? The biggest difference between HomeView and HomePod is the display. While a HomePod can control smart-home devices and play music using Siri, HomeView provides an interactive dashboard and visual feedback, making it more useful for managing a busy household. HomeView also offers capabilities that make it a potential alternative to an iPad in certain situations. It can display recipes, calendars, photos, and video calls without needing someone to pick it up or unlock it. However, HomeView isn't intended to replace an iPad. HomeView is designed to stay in one place and provide convenient access to household information, entertainment, and smart-home controls. Apple HomeView release date: When will it go on sale? Apple announced HomeView on Tuesday, October 13, 2026, as part of its "Welcome home" launch. HomeView is initially available in the United States, United Kingdom, Canada, Australia, India, New Zealand, Singapore, and South Africa. Apple says it is working toward resolving the situation, but hasn't announced a European release date. HomeView can be ordered from the Apple website, Apple Store app, and selected retailers. Apple hasn't announced any general shipping delays beyond the roughly one-month gap between its announcement and retail availability, although individual delivery estimates may vary. The November 13 date confirms the mid-November launch timeframe reported before the announcement. Earlier speculation about an October 30 launch is now superseded by Apple's official schedule. Apple HomeView design: What does it look like? HomeView has a compact, square display mounted above a rounded aluminum speaker base, with a design that recalls Apple's classic iMac G4. A stainless steel hinge allows the screen to tilt, making it easy to adjust the viewing angle when HomeView is positioned on a kitchen counter, desk, or bedside table. The tabletop model is available in four colors: Silver, Starlight, Rose Pink, and Space Gray. The base incorporates the speakers, including a downward-firing woofer, while the display contains two additional full-range drivers. Apple uses 100 percent recycled aluminum in the base and includes a color-matched USB-C power cable. The wall-mounted HomeView has a different design, with a slim square enclosure that's just 0.39 inch thick. Unlike the tabletop model, it doesn't include a separate woofer and requires a compatible wall mount, sold separately. Apple hasn't listed conventional volume or power buttons in the published specifications, with touch and Siri providing the primary controls. coreStoryFacts.text: Apple's entry into the smart display category was rumored for years.
Now that the HomeView ($299) is here, Apple is hoping the iPhone faithful will like its mix of elevated design and newly expanded Siri capabilities .
Unlike smart displays from Amazon and Google, Apple's approach relies on a companion device.
As you'd imagine, that means the HomeView's usefulness, like CarPlay's, is directly tied to how much you use Apple's core apps — things like Messages, Calendar, Photos, Reminders and others.

If all of that is OK to you, and if you're willing to give Siri access to personal data inside some of those apps, the HomeView can quickly become a very versatile device with something for your whole family.
The ability to automatically distinguish between different family members, and for Siri to pull in personalized context for each person, makes this a useful home hub.
The company explained that this enables the HomeView to recognize your face and voice, or that of other users in your home, without exposing any of the data to the operating system.
With the Home app and devices compatible with HomeKit and Matter, this display becomes the command center for your cameras, thermostat, lighting and more.
At times, Siri showed text answers on the HomeView in addition to reciting the info.
But it's important to remember that HomeView is just a conduit for Siri AI and its newly expanded abilities.
These same things can be done on an iPhone or other compatible Apple devices, meaning you don't really have to spend $300 on a dedicated display for these tools.
Apple is years behind the competition when it comes to smart displays.
The Home Modular face puts your favorite smart home devices on the same screen thanks to customizable widgets.
The HomeView may look like an enlarged Apple Watch's screen, but the two devices also overlap in another area: faces.
If it's in direct sunlight, you can expect the maximum 500 nits, but at night, it can dial things down to just 0.3 nits — the lowest brightness ever on an Apple display.
Apple ships the standard version of the device with a USB-C to USB-C cable and a 30-watt power adapter.
The HomeView essentially consists of two parts: a cylindrical, domed base and a 7-inch Liquid Retina display.
Lastly, Live Activities displays real-time info for a variety of tasks on HomeView.
Google's current slate of smart displays is much more modest, with only the aging second-generation Nest Hub and Nest Hub Max as the available options.
That's OK though, because right now, the only video app that's available on HomeView is Apple TV.

And unless you like watching your shows within a thin band that sits in the middle of a square display, flanked by thick black bars on the top and bottom, you, too, will find the video experience on HomeView underwhelming.
I would love to see Apple bring F1 multiview to this display though, putting two small alternate feeds below the main broadcast.
I've been reviewing the tabletop HomeView with a base, so I've enjoyed the added woofer and passive radiators, which balance out full-range drivers with extra bass.
It also works with the iPhone, iPad and Apple Watch, plus you can send and receive intercom messages from anywhere — not just inside your home.

extraction.body: The company’s smart screen debut heavily relies on an iPhone or iPad — for better and for worse. Apple's entry into the smart display category was rumored for years. By the time its debut home hub device arrives this week, the company will be nearly a decade behind its main rivals in the space. In true Apple fashion, it refused to rush new products just because most of the competition was doing it. Now that the HomeView ($299) is here, Apple is hoping the iPhone faithful will like its mix of elevated design and newly expanded Siri capabilities . Unlike smart displays from Amazon and Google, Apple's approach relies on a companion device. That means you'll need either an iPhone or an iPad to mirror apps using technology similar to CarPlay. As you'd imagine, that means the HomeView's usefulness, like CarPlay's, is directly tied to how much you use Apple's core apps — things like Messages, Calendar, Photos, Reminders and others. You'll also need to have some smart home devices to make the most of the smart display and be willing to use Safari as your recipe box. If all of that is OK to you, and if you're willing to give Siri access to personal data inside some of those apps, the HomeView can quickly become a very versatile device with something for your whole family. I have fond memories of the iMac G4 . It was the first computer I used in a design lab in college, and I loved how I could reposition the display to suit the task at hand. The first time I saw the HomeView, those memories flooded back. Apple's smart home display doesn't exactly replicate the G4 styling, but it's close enough for a decent nostalgia hit for me. The HomeView essentially consists of two parts: a cylindrical, domed base and a 7-inch Liquid Retina display. At least, that's if you get the tabletop version. The wall-mounted option is just the screen, and you'll have to pay at least $59.95 for a mount. Every version of the HomeView has two full-range drivers in the display itself. The base houses additional components, like a down-firing woofer and a pair of force-canceling passive radiators for fuller sound with more bass than the wall-mounted models. That display has an LED-backlit multi-touch IPS panel that offers a 1,088 x 1,088 resolution at 200 pixels per inch. Apple says it also added an oleophobic fingerprint-resistant coating to cut down on grime from everyday use. There's an ambient light sensor that enables the HomeView to adjust both brightness and warmth as needed. If it's in direct sunlight, you can expect the maximum 500 nits, but at night, it can dial things down to just 0.3 nits — the lowest brightness ever on an Apple display. The company believes this makes it perfect for a nightstand, if you're willing to have a camera pointed at or near your bed. The HomeView's display has bezels like an iPad and the shape of a large Apple Watch. Unlike either of those devices, though, it has no physical buttons for controls. All of the interaction is done via swipes and taps on the touchscreen itself, or, as I'll elaborate on in a bit, with your voice. And unlike that iMac I'm nostalgic for, you can only tilt the display — you can't adjust its height. While that will suit most of your needs, I'm sure there are a lot of people who would've liked the ability to change the height or rotate the screen as well. Once you do adjust the way it tilts, a built-in accelerometer detects the new angle and alters the audio performance of the display's two drivers to match it. Another item to discuss in terms of design is the HomeView's lone port. Around back, there's a single USB-C jack for power. Apple ships the standard version of the device with a USB-C to USB-C cable and a 30-watt power adapter. If you opt for the USB-C wall mount, which already costs $59.99, you'll need to purchase the power adapter separately. The company offers a 40W dynamic power adapter (up to 60W max) for $39 while the minimum required power supply ( 20W ) will cost you $19. Obviously, the AC wired and PoE (power over Ethernet) wired mounts won't need a power adapter. And lastly, there's the matter of color. For the standard (table or countertop) version of HomeView, you can choose from Silver, Starlight, Rose Pink or Space Gray options. On those, the sides and back of the display match the base. For the wall-mounted version, you can only pick between Silver and Space Gray. And, just in case you need the reminder, both HomeView models are the same price ($299). One of the HomeView's most helpful traits is its ability to put Siri AI front and center in your home. The smart device runs on Apple's A18 chip, the processor that debuted with the iPhone 16 line in 2024. The company is using it here for its Secure Exclaves which give it the ability to process camera and microphone feeds on-device in a manner that can't be accessed by Apple. The company explained that this enables the HomeView to recognize your face and voice, or that of other users in your home, without exposing any of the data to the operating system. That's important, because Siri AI now has access to more of your personal data, like your conversations in Messages, info from your Calendar invites and other bits of "personal context" from various apps. Of course, you have to opt-in to all of this by enabling Apple Intelligence on your iPhone or iPad, and you can limit which apps Siri can index data from. If you do decide to use the system, I can attest that it works well on the HomeView, though it's merely another vessel for the larger AI system. During a lengthy conversation about lighthouses in North Carolina, Siri gave me information about visiting a variety of locations in the state. It provided information that I didn't specifically ask for, like which ones were still active, and got more comprehensive when my follow-up query was a bit vague. For example, when I asked "Which lighthouse is the easiest to get to?" Siri responded with both a list of ones you can park close to and highlighted the one that requires the least amount of climbing. Siri was able to check my calendar to see if I was free to take the trip on a certain date and provided travel time from my house (including follow-up questions about the cities I'd pass through). I was finally able to stump the AI when I asked about "good hotels" near the Currituck Beach Lighthouse in Corolla, but even still, things felt more natural and conversational than interactions I've had with Siri in the past. At times, Siri showed text answers on the HomeView in addition to reciting the info. When I asked about driving time or my schedule, a preview of the best route and the specific day on my calendar popped up respectively. What's more, I got a notification on my phone from the Home app letting me know Siri responded to a request for personal content. But it's important to remember that HomeView is just a conduit for Siri AI and its newly expanded abilities. These same things can be done on an iPhone or other compatible Apple devices, meaning you don't really have to spend $300 on a dedicated display for these tools. One final note on security: Since the HomeView is heavily reliant on an iPhone or iPad, those devices must be nearby and recently unlocked (and enrolled in the shared home) for Siri to access personal data. The HomeView uses facial and voice recognition to know who's speaking, and to know when they walk away, so prying eyes can't see your texts if they rush over after you've been looking at Messages or other potentially sensitive apps. Guests or family members who don't have an iPhone or iPad can still use basic functions (control smart home devices, check weather, play music, etc), including asking Siri rudimentary questions. When I first spent time with the HomeView last month, the feature I was most excited about was the recipe integration in Safari. I'm happy to report that feeling remains, for the most part, but there's one caveat that does impact the overall experience. Going back means you'll get all of the steps on a single slide, requiring you to scroll instead of swipe. This is a long block of text, which can be overwhelming, especially compared to the short, easy-to-follow slides that alleviate some of the stress from following complicated instructions. And if you ever need to peek back at that ingredients list, the properly formatted versions have an always-present shortcut in the bottom right corner. To be clear, the formatting isn't an Apple problem; it's entirely up to the creator or publisher to present their recipes a certain way. I'm just pointing this all out to say Apple is advertising the ideal scenario, which is honestly an excellent experience, but you may not encounter it every time you cook with HomeView. Another big piece of the HomeView puzzle is its ability to act as a smart home hub. With the Home app and devices compatible with HomeKit and Matter, this display becomes the command center for your cameras, thermostat, lighting and more. There's a Home dashboard that shows everything you've connected to the system. You can then create scenes and automations, or ask Siri to handle those for you. We'll get to HomeView customization in a bit, but it's important to mention two Home faces here. The Home Modular face puts your favorite smart home devices on the same screen thanks to customizable widgets. These give you control over each connected gadget, including the ability to check a camera feed, without opening any apps on your phone. Of course, you can always ask Siri to do things for you by summoning the assistant on the HomeView. I'm sure Apple's AI is tired of adjusting my thermostat at this point, as that's what I've primarily been doing during my testing. There's also a Home Camera face that's all video, all the time. Here, you can livestream up to nine feeds at once, giving you the ability to keep tabs on things wherever you have cameras positioned. If a visitor is detected, you can just tap on the HomeView to unlock a smart door lock (provided you have one of those, of course). We are a Blink household, though, and those aren't yet compatible with HomeKit, so I wasn't able to test any of Apple's camera features. If you have an iCloud+ subscription, HomeView works with compatible security cameras (again, HomeKit and Matter) to detect people, pets, packages and vehicles. When any of those are seen, you'll get a notification and a live feed on the display. HomeView can also detect smoke or carbon monoxide alarms and send alerts to your iPhone, iPad or Apple Watch — even when you're away from home. That feature, known as Sound Recognition, is also available on the HomePod and HomePod mini. The HomeView's speakers make it a solid option for music, podcasts and other audio entertainment. But, despite its crisp, vivid display, the device is not well-suited for watching videos. That's OK though, because right now, the only video app that's available on HomeView is Apple TV. And unless you like watching your shows within a thin band that sits in the middle of a square display, flanked by thick black bars on the top and bottom, you, too, will find the video experience on HomeView underwhelming. I would love to see Apple bring F1 multiview to this display though, putting two small alternate feeds below the main broadcast. Yes, they'd be tiny, but at least that's a better use of the space and eliminates the awkward black bars. The HomeView runs on the same platform as CarPlay , which is why the various video streaming apps you have on your iPhone don't show up on this device. Apple says third-party developers are welcome to enable their apps for use on the HomeView, but doing so would also mean optimizing them for CarPlay. Only time will tell if developers are going to go through the extra steps of making that happen. When it comes to audio-only content though, the HomeView is great. I'd classify the sound quality here as the midpoint between the HomePod mini and the larger HomePod. I've been reviewing the tabletop HomeView with a base, so I've enjoyed the added woofer and passive radiators, which balance out full-range drivers with extra bass. Across a variety of genres, bass is tight and punchy, and vocals cut through the mix clearly. The system never loses other instruments either, as you can easily pick up the guitars in Anberlin's "Gravity." Switch to something more chill, like Sam Barber's "If I May," and the acoustic instruments lay a base for the singer's unique vocals. Drums are more subdued here, and the HomeView does well to keep them from overpowering the mix. I should also note the HomeView can get pretty darn loud. I measured 87dB with my Apple Watch standing right in front of the device. But I should also warn you that it's not a comfortable listening volume if you're standing close to the display. It might be nice for a party, but you'll likely stay around 50 percent or less for the most part. Spatial Audio with Dolby Atmos is available on the HomeView for compatible music, movies and shows. However, given the compact stature of the device and its limited sonic prowess, you're more likely to notice the excellent overall clarity and even-handed tuning more than any dimensional effects. While watching an episode of Masters of the Air, for example, I found the sound perfectly fine, but wouldn't classify it as very immersive. Apple included a few more entertainment-related conveniences on the HomeView that add utility. For one, it works with the HomePod, HomePod mini and AirPlay-compatible speakers for multiroom audio, which allows you to play the same thing everywhere or pick specific songs for each room. When listening to songs from Apple Music, you'll see animated album artwork if an artist has it, and lyrics are available with a single tap. And just like you can with your iPhone and HomePod speakers, you can handoff content from your phone to the HomeView just by placing your handset in front of the display. The HomeView may look like an enlarged Apple Watch's screen, but the two devices also overlap in another area: faces. These screens are what you see when the HomeView is in what I like to call rest mode, when it's just sitting there not being actively used. You can have it just be a clock, as there are three faces just for that purpose, or display your calendar or the weather. There's also an animated Snoopy face that updates based on the time of day, weather, holidays and sporting events. Then there are the two Home faces that work with smart home devices that I already mentioned. Those all have their purpose, but my two favorites are the Photos and Modular faces. The former makes the HomeView a digital picture frame and you can get specific about what shows up there. You can opt for it to cycle through photos of specific events (Memories), people, pets or cities, for example, but you can also set up Shared Albums that it will source from. If you do that last one, new photos will automatically appear every time they're added to the collection. The Modular face is what I've used most, as its customizable collection of widgets puts the calendar, date, time and weather in one spot. Of course, you can pick and choose what shows up here based on your needs or preferences, you're not forced to use the same combination I do. The best thing about faces is that you can easily switch between them by swiping horizontally on one. A long press brings up the face customization interface where you're free to fine-tune things like color and widgets (where available) to your heart's content. One feature that Apple has spent a lot of time showing off on the HomeView is FaceTime. The smart display has a 12-megapixel Center Stage camera in its top bezel, which means you can conduct video chats without reaching for your iPhone. Of course, the Center Stage software will keep you centered in the frame as you move around, which will be handy if you need to take a call from the kitchen while you're cooking, for example. You can start FaceTime calls on the HomeView, or you can hand them off from your iPhone. I'll also note that you can take voice calls from the HomeView, and in general, the device works well for both types of chats. Find My is also available on the HomeView, allowing you to locate everything from your iPhone to your AirPods, or anything that has an AirTag attached to it. Of course, you can also use this to find family and friends who are sharing their location with you. The intercom feature from HomePods is on the HomeView as well, which comes in handy if you have multiple Apple speakers spread throughout your house. It also works with the iPhone, iPad and Apple Watch, plus you can send and receive intercom messages from anywhere — not just inside your home. Lastly, Live Activities displays real-time info for a variety of tasks on HomeView. Like it does on your iPhone, the feature puts your progress at the top of the display on a floating, tappable button. Live Activities on the HomeView are a bit limited though, only capable of showing active timers/alarms, FaceTime calls, Safari media playback and Now Playing controls for Apple Music or Apple TV. I found it also surfaced audio controls for my go-to podcast app Pocket Casts as well. One thing that doesn't show up there that I wish it did is Live Activities from the Sports app. It would be great if the live scores for my favorite teams or an update on who's leading the F1 grand prix were available at a glance. Apple is years behind the competition when it comes to smart displays. The company's two main rivals in this category, Amazon and Google, have been honing their products since 2017 and 2018 respectively. The premise has always been similar to Apple's: a combination display and speaker that's a conduit for each company's virtual assistant — or in 2026 terms, each company's AI. Amazon's current Echo Show lineup has six options, ranging from 5 inches up to 21 inches, with the largest models ditching the speaker base for a wall mount or stand. The most affordable, the Echo Show 5 , is $100. Google's current slate of smart displays is much more modest, with only the aging second-generation Nest Hub and Nest Hub Max as the available options. Those are going for $100 and $229 respectively, and only the pricier of the two has a built-in camera for video calls. Apple may have lagged behind the competition on introducing a smart display, but the HomeView checks a lot of boxes that make it a very powerful option for iPhone users. It's also more elegantly designed than all of its main competitors. The ability to automatically distinguish between different family members, and for Siri to pull in personalized context for each person, makes this a useful home hub. When you factor in the cooking assistance, smart home compatibility and FaceTime chops, the HomeView can easily become the command center for any household. Just be sure to keep your iPhone (or iPad) handy if you want to make the most of it.

If you have an iCloud+ subscription, HomeView works with compatible security cameras (again, HomeKit and Matter) to detect people, pets, packages and vehicles. When any of those are seen, you'll get a notification and a live feed on the display. HomeView can also detect smoke or carbon monoxide alarms and send alerts to your iPhone, iPad or Apple Watch — even when you're away from home. That feature, known as Sound Recognition, is also available on the HomePod and HomePod mini.

The HomeView's speakers make it a solid option for music, podcasts and other audio entertainment. But, despite its crisp, vivid display, the device is not well-suited for watching videos. That's OK though, because right now, the only video app that's available on HomeView is Apple TV. And unless you like watching your shows within a thin band that sits in the middle of a square display, flanked by thick black bars on the top and bottom, you, too, will find the video experience on HomeView underwhelming. I would love to see Apple bring F1 multiview to this display though, putting two small alternate feeds below the main broadcast. Yes, they'd be tiny, but at least that's a better use of the space and eliminates the awkward black bars.

The HomeView runs on the same platform as CarPlay , which is why the various video streaming apps you have on your iPhone don't show up on this device. Apple says third-party developers are welcome to enable their apps for use on the HomeView, but doing so would also mean optimizing them for CarPlay. Only time will tell if developers are going to go through the extra steps of making that happen.

When it comes to audio-only content though, the HomeView is great. I'd classify the sound quality here as the midpoint between the HomePod mini and the larger HomePod. I've been reviewing the tabletop HomeView with a base, so I've enjoyed the added woofer and passive radiators, which balance out full-range drivers with extra bass. Across a variety of genres, bass is tight and punchy, and vocals cut through the mix clearly. The system never loses other instruments either, as you can easily pick up the guitars in Anberlin's "Gravity." Switch to something more chill, like Sam Barber's "If I May," and the acoustic instruments lay a base for the singer's unique vocals. Drums are more subdued here, and the HomeView does well to keep them from overpowering the mix.

I should also note the HomeView can get pretty darn loud. I measured 87dB with my Apple Watch standing right in front of the device. But I should also warn you that it's not a comfortable listening volume if you're standing close to the display. It might be nice for a party, but you'll likely stay around 50 percent or less for the most part.

Spatial Audio with Dolby Atmos is available on the HomeView for compatible music, movies and shows. However, given the compact stature of the device and its limited sonic prowess, you're more likely to notice the excellent overall clarity and even-handed tuning more than any dimensional effects. While watching an episode of Masters of the Air, for example, I found the sound perfectly fine, but wouldn't classify it as very immersive.

Apple included a few more entertainment-related conveniences on the HomeView that add utility. For one, it works with the HomePod, HomePod mini and AirPlay-compatible speakers for multiroom audio, which allows you to play the same thing everywhere or pick specific songs for each room. When listening to songs from Apple Music, you'll see animated album artwork if an artist has it, and lyrics are available with a single tap. And just like you can with your iPhone and HomePod speakers, you can handoff content from your phone to the HomeView just by placing your handset in front of the display.

The HomeView may look like an enlarged Apple Watch's screen, but the two devices also overlap in another area: faces. These screens are what you see when the HomeView is in what I like to call rest mode, when it's just sitting there not being actively used. You can have it just be a clock, as there are three faces just for that purpose, or display your calendar or the weather. There's also an animated Snoopy face that updates based on the time of day, weather, holidays and sporting events. Then there are the two Home faces that work with smart home devices that I already mentioned.

Those all have their purpose, but my two favorites are the Photos and Modular faces. The former makes the HomeView a digital picture frame and you can get specific about what shows up there. You can opt for it to cycle through photos of specific events (Memories), people, pets or cities, for example, but you can also set up Shared Albums that it will source from. If you do that last one, new photos will automatically appear every time they're added to the collection. The Modular face is what I've used most, as its customizable collection of widgets puts the calendar, date, time and weather in one spot. Of course, you can pick and choose what shows up here based on your needs or preferences, you're not forced to use the same combination I do.

The best thing about faces is that you can easily switch between them by swiping horizontally on one. A long press brings up the face customization interface where you're free to fine-tune things like color and widgets (where available) to your heart's content.

One feature that Apple has spent a lot of time showing off on the HomeView is FaceTime. The smart display has a 12-megapixel Center Stage camera in its top bezel, which means you can conduct video chats without reaching for your iPhone. Of course, the Center Stage software will keep you centered in the frame as you move around, which will be handy if you need to take a call from the kitchen while you're cooking, for example. You can start FaceTime calls on the HomeView, or you can hand them off from your iPhone. I'll also note that you can take voice calls from the HomeView, and in general, the device works well for both types of chats.

Find My is also available on the HomeView, allowing you to locate everything from your iPhone to your AirPods, or anything that has an AirTag attached to it. Of course, you can also use this to find family and friends who are sharing their location with you. The intercom feature from HomePods is on the HomeView as well, which comes in handy if you have multiple Apple speakers spread throughout your house. It also works with the iPhone, iPad and Apple Watch, plus you can send and receive intercom messages from anywhere — not just inside your home.

Lastly, Live Activities displays real-time info for a variety of tasks on HomeView. Like it does on your iPhone, the feature puts your progress at the top of the display on a floating, tappable button. Live Activities on the HomeView are a bit limited though, only capable of showing active timers/alarms, FaceTime calls, Safari media playback and Now Playing controls for Apple Music or Apple TV. I found it also surfaced audio controls for my go-to podcast app Pocket Casts as well. One thing that doesn't show up there that I wish it did is Live Activities from the Sports app. It would be great if the live scores for my favorite teams or an update on who's leading the F1 grand prix were available at a glance.

Apple is years behind the competition when it comes to smart displays. The company's two main rivals in this category, Amazon and Google, have been honing their products since 2017 and 2018 respectively. The premise has always been similar to Apple's: a combination display and speaker that's a conduit for each company's virtual assistant — or in 2026 terms, each company's AI.

Amazon's current Echo Show lineup has six options, ranging from 5 inches up to 21 inches, with the largest models ditching the speaker base for a wall mount or stand. The most affordable, the Echo Show 5 , is $100. Google's current slate of smart displays is much more modest, with only the aging second-generation Nest Hub and Nest Hub Max as the available options. Those are going for $100 and $229 respectively, and only the pricier of the two has a built-in camera for video calls.

Apple may have lagged behind the competition on introducing a smart display, but the HomeView checks a lot of boxes that make it a very powerful option for iPhone users. It's also more elegantly designed than all of its main competitors. The ability to automatically distinguish between different family members, and for Siri to pull in personalized context for each person, makes this a useful home hub. When you factor in the cooking assistance, smart home compatibility and FaceTime chops, the HomeView can easily become the command center for any household. Just be sure to keep your iPhone (or iPad) handy if you want to make the most of it.

passages: The new Apple HomeView asks a BIG question: If your household is already filled with iPhones, iPads, and smart speakers, does Apple's first dedicated smart display justify a permanent spot on your kitchen counter?

Front-on view of the 1:1 square display canvas, balancing glanceable widgets and quick-launch icons for shared household spaces | Image: Ben McKimm / Man of Many 30-Second Apple HomeView Verdict Pros: Distance-adaptive UI scales text and widgets automatically depending on how far away you stand.
But before we dive into the full Apple HomeView review, let's look at what we're dealing with here.
If you typically mount things in your hallways, entryways, or dedicated smart home control points, Apple also offers HomeView (Wall Mounted) in Space Grey and Silver.
When viewed at night, HomeView can dial its backlight down to just 0.3 nits, the lowest display brightness Apple has ever offered.
Now that I've spent the past week living with the Apple HomeView in my kitchen, I have an answer.
Does it bridge the gap between a shared family noticeboard, an entertainment player, and a deeply personalised smart home controller?
I needed a screen to glance at information quickly, but Apple's home strategy was entirely screenless.
Placed on a bedside table, it eliminates the harsh backlight glow that plagues conventional smart displays in pitch-black bedrooms.
