extraction.body: The new Apple HomeView asks a BIG question: If your household is already filled with iPhones, iPads, and smart speakers, does Apple's first dedicated smart display justify a permanent spot on your kitchen counter? Now that I've spent the past week living with the Apple HomeView in my kitchen, I have an answer. My Google Nest Hub (2nd Gen) died two weeks before the HomeView was announced. I needed a screen to glance at information quickly, but Apple's home strategy was entirely screenless. It pairs a square 7-inch Liquid Retina display with an A18 chip, a Spatial Audio acoustic system, and the new Siri AI. Does it bridge the gap between a shared family noticeboard, an entertainment player, and a deeply personalised smart home controller? I've spent the past week living with the new device as the central command hub in my kitchen and living space, putting it through its paces across busy morning routines, cooking sessions, and smart home automations. But before we dive into the full Apple HomeView review, let's look at what we're dealing with here. You can get your HomeView in both a tabletop model (featuring a machined aluminium domed base and an adjustable stainless steel hinge) and a sleek wall-mounted variant (that loses a little sound quality). It packs a 1088 x 1088 Liquid Retina display that dims down to just 0.3 nits for bedside use, alongside four beamforming microphones and a 12MP Center Stage camera. However, taking full advantage of the experience requires accepting a few deliberate ecosystem dependencies: neither model has an internal battery (both require wired power), personal context features rely on having a paired Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone or iPad on your network, and the wall-mounted model sells its mounts and power cables separately. Front-on view of the 1:1 square display canvas, balancing glanceable widgets and quick-launch icons for shared household spaces | Image: Ben McKimm / Man of Many 30-Second Apple HomeView Verdict Pros: Distance-adaptive UI scales text and widgets automatically depending on how far away you stand. 7-inch Liquid Retina display drops to a record-low 0.3 nits for distraction-free nightstand use. Recognises up to six household members via face and voice to surface apps, etc., privately. Tabletop model pairs dual full-range drivers with a down-firing woofer and passive radiators. Streams up to nine live HomeKit and Matter camera feeds simultaneously on the Home Camera. Cons: Requires permanent wired power via USB-C, with no built-in battery for cordless portability. Personal context Siri AI and expressive voices require an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone or iPad. Wall-mounted model omits the base woofer and sells mounts, cable, and power adapter separately. No-brainer if you're deeply invested in the Apple ecosystem and want a dedicated, privacy-first kitchen companion, bedside clock, or smart home control panel that everyone in the house can share. Table of contents30-Second Apple HomeView VerdictShould You Buy the Apple HomeView?Apple HomeView Technical SpecificationsDesign, Hardware, and Wall-Mounting OptionsLiquid Retina Display and Distance-Adaptive UISound Quality and Multiroom EntertainmentA18 Performance, Siri AI, and Multi-User ControlsEveryday Utility: Cooking, FaceTime, and Smart Home HubMan of Many's Verdict on the Apple HomeViewFAQsWhy Trust Man of Many? Measuring just 5.73 inches (14.55 cm) wide and adjusting between 5.38 (13.67 cm) and 6.83 inches (17.35 cm) tall depending on tilt, the tabletop model anchors its screen to a hefty, 100 per cent recycled aluminium domed base via a stainless steel hinge. You can get the tabletop HomeView in four finishes (Silver, Starlight, Rose Pink, and Space Grey), and it includes a colour-matched 1.5-metre USB-C cable and power adapter in the box. Neither variant includes a battery, meaning permanent wired power is mandatory. If you typically mount things in your hallways, entryways, or dedicated smart home control points, Apple also offers HomeView (Wall Mounted) in Space Grey and Silver. Rather than sitting on a domed base, it pairs with a trio of purpose-built mounts from Schneider Home (sold separately alongside the required cable and power adapter): Power Mount USB-C Wall Connector: Self-installed option with an attached cable. Power Mount AC Wired: Hardwired mount for a flush installation with no visible cords. Front view of the 1088 x 1088 square display canvas, highlighting the active user profile badge in the top corner powered by A18 Secure Exclaves | Image: Ben McKimm / Man of Many Liquid Retina Display and Distance-Adaptive UI While 7 inches (6.98 inches diagonally, accounting for rounded corners) may sound modest on paper, the 1:1 square aspect ratio gives HomeView a generous canvas. The LED-backlit IPS panel runs at a crisp 1088 x 1088 resolution (220 ppi) with an oleophobic coating that does a decent job of shrugging off kitchen smudges. The real standout is the display's dynamic range. I have my review unit placed in a sunlit kitchen, where the True Tone and auto-brightness features regularly push the panel up to its peak 500 nits so recipes and camera feeds remain legible. When viewed at night, HomeView can dial its backlight down to just 0.3 nits, the lowest display brightness Apple has ever offered. Placed on a bedside table, it eliminates the harsh backlight glow that plagues conventional smart displays in pitch-black bedrooms. To make that 7-inch screen legible from across a room without cluttering the interface, Apple built a clever distance-adaptive UI. When you're standing across the living room, HomeView presents clean, large-scale typography, such as today's high and low temperatures or basic Live Activities. Walk closer to the display, and the interface transitions to reveal richer, more granular details such as hourly weather breakdowns, interactive controls, and expanded Siri responses.

passages: Apple HomeView is Apple's first dedicated smart-home display, combining a 7-inch touchscreen, powerful speakers, a camera, and Siri AI in a device designed to sit at the center of the connected home.

While HomePod focuses primarily on music, Siri, and voice-controlled smart-home functions, HomeView adds a touchscreen, camera, personalized interface, and much deeper integration with Apple apps and services.
Apple announced HomeView on Tuesday, October 13, 2026, as part of its "Welcome home" launch.
HomeView has a compact, square display mounted above a rounded aluminum speaker base, with a design that recalls Apple's classic iMac G4.

Powered by Apple's A18 chip and Apple Intelligence, HomeView offers a much more capable version of Siri that can answer questions conversationally, help with everyday tasks, and access personal information from a compatible iPhone or iPad.
HomeView introduces a range of capabilities that aren't available on Apple's traditional HomePod speakers.
Apple HomeView release date: When will it go on sale?
Apple HomeView design: What does it look like?
While a HomePod can control smart-home devices and play music using Siri, HomeView provides an interactive dashboard and visual feedback, making it more useful for managing a busy household.
HomeView can be ordered from the Apple website, Apple Store app, and selected retailers.
Apple uses 100 percent recycled aluminum in the base and includes a color-matched USB-C power cable.
Apple says it is working toward resolving the situation, but hasn't announced a European release date.
It integrates with the Apple Home app, supporting compatible HomeKit and Matter accessories, including lights, locks, thermostats, and security cameras.
Apple hasn't listed conventional volume or power buttons in the published specifications, with touch and Siri providing the primary controls.
The biggest difference between HomeView and HomePod is the display.
It can display recipes, calendars, photos, and video calls without needing someone to pick it up or unlock it.

extraction.body: Apple HomeView is Apple's first dedicated smart-home display, combining a 7-inch touchscreen, powerful speakers, a camera, and Siri AI in a device designed to sit at the center of the connected home. Announced on October 13, 2026 and on sale from November 13, it brings together smart-home controls, entertainment, video calling, calendars, reminders, and other everyday information. Powered by Apple's A18 chip and Apple Intelligence, HomeView offers a much more capable version of Siri that can answer questions conversationally, help with everyday tasks, and access personal information from a compatible iPhone or iPad. HomeView is designed to work alongside Apple's existing HomePod speakers, Apple TV, iPhone, and iPad. It integrates with the Apple Home app, supporting compatible HomeKit and Matter accessories, including lights, locks, thermostats, and security cameras. It can also serve as a central smart-home hub, making it easier to manage devices and automations throughout the house. Unlike a HomePod with a screen added, HomeView is designed around visual interaction as well as voice control. Its touchscreen, customizable widgets, FaceTime camera, personalized Home Screens, and dedicated smart-home dashboards make it more like a shared household computer than a conventional smart speaker. HomeView introduces a range of capabilities that aren't available on Apple's traditional HomePod speakers. While HomePod focuses primarily on music, Siri, and voice-controlled smart-home functions, HomeView adds a touchscreen, camera, personalized interface, and much deeper integration with Apple apps and services. HomeView also supports Handoff from iPhone, Live Activities, Find My, and multiroom audio with compatible AirPlay speakers. How does HomeView compare with HomePod and iPad? The biggest difference between HomeView and HomePod is the display. While a HomePod can control smart-home devices and play music using Siri, HomeView provides an interactive dashboard and visual feedback, making it more useful for managing a busy household. HomeView also offers capabilities that make it a potential alternative to an iPad in certain situations. It can display recipes, calendars, photos, and video calls without needing someone to pick it up or unlock it. However, HomeView isn't intended to replace an iPad. HomeView is designed to stay in one place and provide convenient access to household information, entertainment, and smart-home controls. Apple HomeView release date: When will it go on sale? Apple announced HomeView on Tuesday, October 13, 2026, as part of its "Welcome home" launch. HomeView is initially available in the United States, United Kingdom, Canada, Australia, India, New Zealand, Singapore, and South Africa. Apple says it is working toward resolving the situation, but hasn't announced a European release date. HomeView can be ordered from the Apple website, Apple Store app, and selected retailers. Apple hasn't announced any general shipping delays beyond the roughly one-month gap between its announcement and retail availability, although individual delivery estimates may vary. The November 13 date confirms the mid-November launch timeframe reported before the announcement. Earlier speculation about an October 30 launch is now superseded by Apple's official schedule. Apple HomeView design: What does it look like? HomeView has a compact, square display mounted above a rounded aluminum speaker base, with a design that recalls Apple's classic iMac G4. A stainless steel hinge allows the screen to tilt, making it easy to adjust the viewing angle when HomeView is positioned on a kitchen counter, desk, or bedside table. The tabletop model is available in four colors: Silver, Starlight, Rose Pink, and Space Gray. The base incorporates the speakers, including a downward-firing woofer, while the display contains two additional full-range drivers. Apple uses 100 percent recycled aluminum in the base and includes a color-matched USB-C power cable. The wall-mounted HomeView has a different design, with a slim square enclosure that's just 0.39 inch thick. Unlike the tabletop model, it doesn't include a separate woofer and requires a compatible wall mount, sold separately. Apple hasn't listed conventional volume or power buttons in the published specifications, with touch and Siri providing the primary controls. HomeView dimensions and weight Does Apple HomeView have a camera?

extraction.body: Thom Dunn is a writer focusing on home heating and cooling. He once blew up a power strip with a space heater and a Marshall half-stack. We have added the Google TV Streamer (4K) to replace the discontinued Chromecast with Google TV . Google’s Nest Audio and Nest Mini react to voice commands to retrieve news, music, entertainment, and answers to easy questions, and to control lights and appliances throughout the house. With their context-aware search capabilities, ever-growing Actions library, ability to synchronize with multiple Google accounts, and wide support for various smart-home devices, these Google Home speakers bring voice-controlled convenience to (almost) every corner of your life. This is a great choice for anyone looking for an inexpensive multiroom audio system or a way to use their Google accounts to make a voice-controlled smart home even smarter. All of the major smart-speaker platforms (Google Home, Alexa, and Siri) allow you to control a mix of smart-home devices with your voice, adding an extra layer of convenience and accessibility to your smart-home system. We mostly prefer Alexa because it works with a greater number of devices, but if you want a deeper integration with all things Google, or if you already have a Google Home speaker, there’s no reason to switch platforms. (We do have Alexa device and HomeKit device guides for owners of those systems.) One of the advantages of the Nest Audio over other smart-home speakers is that it uses Google for search results, and Google usually provides more-satisfying answers than other search engines. In addition, it can tie in with multiple Google accounts, distinguishing between them by the sound of each different voice. That voice-control expertise means the Nest Audio is great at providing information from your calendars, reminders, Maps data, and more. Or, with the Nest Mini , you can add these capabilities for just $50. And, of course, you can set up your Nest Audio to control your lights as well as Internet of Things–enabled air conditioners , sprinklers , robot vacuums , and more. Below we’ve selected the best Google Home–compatible devices from all of our smart-home reviews. This model has useful Scenes (presets of color and dimness) and emits bold colors, yet it’s cheaper than most smart bulbs. The WiZ 60W A19 Color LED is our top smart LED light bulb pick because it produces bold colors, has useful preset Scenes, is easy to use, can connect to other smart devices without needing a hub, and is still budget-friendly. Note, however, that this Philips bulbs line isn’t directly compatible with Philips Hue bulbs. This reliable, affordable dimmer switch uses Wi-Fi so it doesn’t need a hub, and it works with Google Home and other platforms. TP-Link’s Kasa Smart Wi-Fi Light Switch Dimmer KS220 is our top in-wall smart light-switch pick for a reason—it’s reliable, easy to use, and affordable enough that you can reasonably add a bunch of them around the house. This dimmer switch connects directly to your Wi-Fi network and has three buttons to control lighting (on/off and dim), and the easy-to-navigate app allows you to customize the controls, create automated schedules, and control grouped switches simultaneously. Since the KS220 integrates with Google Home, you can tie lights to voice commands and make specific requests like “Hey Google, dim the living room to 25%.” This easy-to-install, sharp-looking deadbolt works flawlessly, is intuitive to use, and provides robust security. The Schlage Encode Smart WiFi Deadbolt provides fast, easy keyless entry to your home using a straightforward keypad (though there is a keyway as a failsafe). The Google Home app allows you to unlock the door remotely, though it does require inputting a PIN code. And to program new codes for guests and visitors, you’ll still need to rely on the free Schlage app. Google’s newest streamer makes it easier to find, organize and revisit your favorite media than any other player. In addition to Google Home it supports Matter smart home connectivity. The Google TV Streamer (4K) , which replaced the discontinued Chromecast with Google TV , is our favorite media streamer —though it does cost twice as much. It excels at making it intuitive and easy to access video content, which is the most important of its jobs. It doesn’t take much time to notice it’s far faster, and even more responsive than competing models, thanks in part to the addition of 10 times as much internal storage as the Chromecast. The Google TV Streamer supports 4K HDR video streaming with Dolby Vision and Dolby Atmos and also supports Matter, which means you can opt to integrate it with other Google Home devices, but also interact with smart platforms like Apple Home or Amazon Alexa. Included is a Bluetooth remote control which supports voice search and works splendidly, though it doesn’t have a hands-free option. The Tailwind iQ3 Smart WiFi Garage Door Opener is the most responsive and reliable smart garage-door controller we tested. Tailwind solved the common issues of false alerts and unreliable geofencing for opening and closing, thanks to a hardwired door sensor and a unique Bluetooth/GPS technology that lets you control the door hands-free. The downside is that it is slightly more complicated to install than other options. The TP-Link Tapo Wire-Free Magnetic Security Camera is the best cordless outdoor Wi-Fi home security camera we’ve found so far. It can accurately distinguish between people, animals, vehicles, and general motion. And in testing it delivers clear images day and night. It’s also inexpensive and can run up to 300 days on a single charge (we averaged three to four months of use during testing). As cool as it is to have a little robot helper that zips around your house and cleans your floors and carpets, it’s even better when you can just sit back and tell your automated vacuum cleaner what to do, without even having to push a button. The Roborock Q5+ works with Google Home, so you can make it start, stop, pause, resume, and go home using voice commands . Our reviewer did note that pronunciation is important when using voice commands with any smart-home platform, but it appears to be a common complaint among Roborock users. The TP-Link Kasa Smart Wi-Fi Plug Slim (EP25) works reliably, has an app that’s easy to use, and can track usage of lamps, fans, or whatever else you plug into it. You can also schedule the plug to go on and off based on the time of day and the day of the week, as well as local sunrise and sunset. And you can turn those same devices on and off on the fly using the app or voice controls when paired with the Google Home app. If you want to take that convenience outside, the TP-Link Tapo TP25 Outdoor Plug is built to weather the outdoors, with an operating-temperature range of -4 to 122 degrees Fahrenheit. It supports Matter, and it features two outlets that you can control independently using the sound of your voice. One of the smallest and most powerful sous vide options available, this model adds your Google smart speaker to the cooking process to tweak temperatures and provide extra help in the kitchen. Sous vide is French for “under vacuum,” and it’s a method of cooking that lets you make restaurant-quality dishes at home by submerging your food in a vacuum-sealed bag in a heated water bath. Home versions of the sous vide have been available for a while but have only recently become more affordable. Although it’s not our top-pick sous vide appliance, the Breville Joule Turbo is impressively high-tech, letting you check on your steak or tweak temperatures through Google Assistant—integrated voice commands. And, of course, you can ask Google Assistant for help with recipes, measurements, and timers. Nest’s smart thermostat features a large, crisp, and useful display and wide compatibility with HVAC systems. Nothing warms up a cold day better than telling your thermostat to turn up the heat instead of having to crawl out from under the blankets to do it manually. Our Runner-up smart thermostat , the Google Nest Learning Thermostat (3rd generation) , lets you raise or lower the temperature or switch to a preprogrammed Away or Home setting, with just a few words. If you’re willing to take a leap of faith, you can allow the Nest to learn your habits and then create a schedule that should match your preferences (you can always tweak it as you like manually or using app or voice commands). I’m a writer with a focus on heating, cooling, and humidification devices, as well as gadgets such as Christmas lights and karaoke machines. extraction.body: Nabu Casa — the commercial side of the Open Home Foundation, which runs Home Assistant — just launched the Home Assistant Connect Aux-2, a multi-function box designed to help you bring more non-smart devices into your smart home. It’s part of Home Assistant’s ongoing efforts to become more user-friendly. I’ve been testing the Aux-2 for a couple days and I’ve found it unsurprisingly useful and surprisingly easy to set up. The Aux-2 is a $69 box about the size of a deck of cards. Its USB port lets you plug in a Nabu Casa Z-Wave or Zigbee antenna in case your Home Assistant hub isn’t in a good spot. And you can connect an amplifier or powered speakers to its audio jack to stream music to older audio equipment. All of these things leverage Home Assistant’s capabilities as an open-source platform. The Aux-2 is based on ESPHome, an open platform for making DIY smart home devices from cheap, flexible ESP boards, and it uses existing Home Assistant/ESPHome integrations for all its features. The serial integration was developed earlier this year; Music Assistant and SendSpin, which power the audio-out feature, are in active development. I have a Home Assistant install, but even after several years it is not my primary smart home platform simply because of friction and time constraints. Instead, I have a hodgepodge of Google Home, Apple Home, and a few devices that are only in Home Assistant. But the Aux-2’s capabilities perfectly intersect with two things I’d been meaning to do anyway, one of which I’m already using Home Assistant for. First, I have a garage fridge, because I live in Texas. I also have children, which means sometimes the fridge or freezer door gets left open. A couple years ago, I set up a few Aqara temperature sensors, connected to Home Assistant via a now-discontinued Zigbee dongle, and set up an automation to alert me if the fridge or freezer get too warm. But they frequently drop connection (probably because they’re inside a fridge in the garage), they chew through coin cell batteries, and they have no displays, which means I also have a cheap Acu-rite hygrometer in the fridge so I can see the temperature without pulling out my phone. Someone tipped me off to Govee’s Bluetooth hygrometers, but I’d need a Bluetooth proxy to get them into Home Assistant. I also have a set of in-wall speakers in my living room that I’ve never used. Do I try to get them to work with my four Sonos speakers? Setting up the Aux-2 was much easier than I expected. Mercifully, they maintained their Bluetooth connection through three walls and a fridge, and now my fridge monitoring setup works again. The audio capability took a little longer, but most of that was spent hooking the speakers up to the amp I ended up buying and setting up Music Assistant, which I didn’t have installed. Music Assistant lives on your Home Assistant hardware and can play from many different services — from Spotify to YouTube Music to local files and more — and to many different outputs, like Sonos, Wiim, AirPlay, Google Cast, and others, but they all need to be configured, and that took a beat. I can now play music to the in-wall speakers using Music Assistant. Sendspin, the whole-home audio standard (also developed by the Open Home Foundation) is supposed to be able to let you group speakers from different protocols under certain conditions, but I haven’t gotten that working yet. The Aux-2 doesn’t do anything you couldn’t do already with an ESP32 board and various accessories, or even other ESP-based devices. The Apollo Automations Cast-1, for example, costs $35 and supports the same music-casting and Bluetooth proxy features I’m actually using from the Aux-2 at the moment. You could bodge together something even cheaper with DIY parts. Both Nabu Casa and Apollo fund the Open Home Foundation, which develops Home Assistant and ESPHome (and Sendspin and Music Assistant), and both provide hardware that’s a little easier to use than DIY options. I bought a three-pack of ESP32 boards for $16 three years ago. But now that I’ve used the Aux-2 and dipped my toe into the ESPHome waters, maybe I will.

extraction.body: Home Assistant works with a huge number of smart home devices, but it doesn't work with everything. If you have smart home tech that you've not been able to connect to Home Assistant in the past, it's worth checking again. Command a vast range of devices, with or without an internet connection. Home Assistant releases updates on a monthly cycle, with smaller patch releases during the month. Each monthly update adds new features to Home Assistant, and these always include new integrations that have been officially added to Home Assistant. There are usually a significant number of integrations added each month. For example, the 2026.4 release included 14 new integrations, including Infrared, UniFi Access, WiiM, and Autoskope. Over the past 12 months, there have been no fewer than four new integrations in any release, with some months adding as many as 17. This doesn't include custom components that you can install via HACS that are not officially supported integrations. Many of these custom components allow you to connect smart home devices that aren't supported by Home Assistant integrations, and some custom components go on to become official integrations. Home Assistant Green is a pre-built hub directly from the Home Assistant team. It's a plug-and-play solution that comes with everything you need to set up Home Assistant in your home without needing to install the software yourself. Some new Home Assistant integrations only allow you to connect a limited number of smart devices from a specific brand. There are some, however, that open up access to a whole swathe of smart home devices. One such example is the Infrared integration, which was added in Home Assistant 2026.4. The Infrared integration adds native support for controlling IR devices such as TVs or AC units using Home Assistant. In the past, to do so, you needed to use manual workarounds or custom integrations, but Home Assistant now has a dedicated native platform for infrared control. It means that you can turn cheap ESP32 devices into infrared proxies that can send and receive IR signals and control them directly from Home Assistant. For example, you can send commands to your TV as if you were pressing the buttons on your remote, and use them to turn on the TV, change the channels, turn up the volume, and more. Currently, there's only an LG Infrared integration that will let you control an LG straight out of the box, but for other IR devices, you can use the remote.learn_command action to learn the commands that your remote sends out, and the remote.send_command action to send these commands from your IR proxy. It means that in theory, you can add almost any IR device that uses a remote to Home Assistant. Infrared devices aren't the only devices that you can add to Home Assistant. There's support for all the major protocols, including those that you might not expect. For example, if you have Bluetooth smart devices around your home, you may assume that you can't hook these up to Home Assistant due to the limited range of Bluetooth. However, you can also use ESP32 devices as Bluetooth proxies and place them near your Bluetooth devices. These proxies can receive commands over Wi-Fi from Home Assistant and send out the relevant Bluetooth signals to your Bluetooth devices, controlling them as if they were already within Bluetooth range of your Home Assistant server. Home Assistant also has mature support for Matter, and continues to add new Matter features. Home Assistant 2026.4 included an update that allows you to manage users and PIN codes for Matter-compatible smart locks directly from within Home Assistant. If you have Matter devices, Home Assistant is a great way to connect and control them. If you want to see if a smart home device you own will work with Home Assistant, there are a few things you can do. The first is to see if the device is automatically discovered. Power the device on and ensure it's connected, and you may find that it appears in Home Assistant's list of discovered devices. If it isn't, the next step is to search for an official integration. On the Integrations page, click the Add Integration button and type the brand of your device to see if any results appear. If they do, install the integration and follow the setup instructions to connect your device. If there's no official integration, you can try HACS. This is a store of community-created custom components, many of which allow you to connect specific brands of smart home devices. If you can't find a custom component in the HACS store, try searching online, as some require manual installation. If nothing works, you can try the Home Assistant community forums . You may find that someone is working on a solution. Home Assistant supports a huge range of smart home devices, and the list continues to grow. Before replacing old gear or assuming a device won't work, it's worth checking Home Assistant again. Support may have arrived since the last time you checked. We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful. The best of How-To Geek, directly in your inbox.

sources.title: The Best Smart Home Devices We've Tested for 2026 - PCMag
passages: Editors' Note, June 17, 2026: With this update, we made several changes to our list of recommended smart home devices.
All of our picks have been vetted for currency and availability.

I'm PCMag's managing editor for consumer electronics, overseeing an experienced team of analysts covering smart home, home entertainment, wearables, fitness and health tech, and various other product categories.
I have been with PCMag for more than 10 years, and in that time have written more than 6,000 articles and reviews for the site.
I previously served as an analyst focused on smart home and wearable devices, and before that I was a reporter covering consumer tech news.
I'm also a yoga instructor, and have been actively teaching group and private classes for nearly a decade.
These days, there's a smart version of pretty much every home device you can think of.
What follows is a rundown of the best smart devices we've tested for every area of the house.
Our tour of the ultimate smart home wouldn't be complete without a visit to the backyard.
The first step in choosing one is deciding which voice assistance platform is the right fit for your home: Alexa, Google Assistant, or Siri.
All three support most major smart home device brands.
Similarly, a smart display offers all the benefits of a smart speaker and organizes your smart home controls on a single screen, conveniently located on your bedside table.

Arguably the most important part of a truly connected home, these devices offer both security and convenience, allowing you to come and go as you please, while also monitoring who enters and leaves your home when you're away.
If you want privacy but still like to let the sun in, the Feather River Doors Smart Glass offers the best of both worlds.

Whether you're lucky enough to have a dedicated workout room or just an empty corner with enough space for a yoga mat, the smart home gym equipment market offers a wealth of options for improving your fitness.
Smart fitness devices, such as the Peloton Cross Training Bike+ , allow for a level of interactivity far beyond their more affordable, non-connected counterparts.
It also offers hands-free voice control with Alexa or the first-party Sonos assistant.

extraction.body: Trained exclusively on our massive library of expert buying advice, finding the right tech to fit your life has never been easier. We've tested hundreds of smart home products in more than 20 categories to help determine which ones are best for every room in (and out of) the house. I’m PCMag’s senior writer covering smart home and wearable devices. I’ve been reporting on tech professionally for nearly a decade and have been obsessing about it for much longer than that. Prior to joining PCMag, I made educational videos for an electronics store called Abt Electronics in Illinois, and before that, I spent eight years covering the smart home market for CNET. I'm PCMag's managing editor for consumer electronics, overseeing an experienced team of analysts covering smart home, home entertainment, wearables, fitness and health tech, and various other product categories. I have been with PCMag for more than 10 years, and in that time have written more than 6,000 articles and reviews for the site. I previously served as an analyst focused on smart home and wearable devices, and before that I was a reporter covering consumer tech news. I'm also a yoga instructor, and have been actively teaching group and private classes for nearly a decade. These days, there's a smart version of pretty much every home device you can think of. These products (usually) connect to the internet, so you can control them from your phone through a companion app. Most also work with various forms of voice control. What follows is a rundown of the best smart devices we've tested for every area of the house. We have arranged our products by room to help keep things organized, but that doesn't mean you can't use most of these gadgets just about anywhere. Make sure to check back soon, as we regularly test new products and update this guide accordingly. Editors' Note, June 17, 2026: With this update, we made several changes to our list of recommended smart home devices. All of our picks have been vetted for currency and availability. At the ultimate smart home, you're met with technology before you even step through the front door. Some of the most useful connected home gadgets reside in the front yard, starting with outdoor security cameras . Our top pick overall for keeping tabs on your home from your phone is the Aqara Camera Hub G5 Pro . This high-resolution, weather-resistant security camera provides sharp video, color night vision, and AI-powered motion detection and alerts. Better yet, it acts as a hub for other smart home devices with built-in support for the Matter , Thread , and Zigbee protocols. For those times you want to check whether it's a delivery person or an unwanted solicitor knocking on your door, a video doorbell will let you see who's there without getting up from the couch. Beyond this convenience, video doorbells can serve as the first line of defense against property theft, home invasion, and porch pirates. They not only let you see and speak with the person outside, but they also record footage of visitors approaching your door while you're away or unable to answer. Our favorite model, the Arlo Video Doorbell , delivers clear HD or 2K video with a wide 180-degree diagonal field of view, allowing for either a wired or wireless setup. It works with many third-party devices and supports voice control. Another piece of technology you might want on your front door is a smart lock . Arguably the most important part of a truly connected home, these devices offer both security and convenience, allowing you to come and go as you please, while also monitoring who enters and leaves your home when you're away. Our current top pick is the Ultraloq Bolt Fingerprint , which adds HomeKit support to our previous favorite while remaining a dependable and versatile smart lock that lets you gain entry or lock up with your voice and fingerprint, as well as via keypad, mobile app, or traditional keys. If you want privacy but still like to let the sun in, the Feather River Doors Smart Glass offers the best of both worlds. This smart entry door switches between opaque and transparent glass at the push of a button or a voice command. When it comes to living room technology, televisions and soundbars are the obvious stars of the show. However, many other gadgets aim to enhance the ambiance, convenience, and security of your primary living space. For starters, a smart speaker is a must for the living room. Beyond playing music, our favorite models serve as a central command center, letting you control nearly any other connected home gadget by voice. The first step in choosing one is deciding which voice assistance platform is the right fit for your home: Alexa, Google Assistant, or Siri. All three support most major smart home device brands. If Alexa is your voice assistant of choice, we suggest the Amazon Echo Dot Max as an affordable option with impressive sound quality. If you prefer Google, we recommend waiting to see how the upcoming Google Home Speaker fares. And if you prefer Siri, you can get a HomePod or a HomePod mini . If you choose this route, make sure that any other smart home devices you purchase are compatible with Apple HomeKit or Matter . Meanwhile, the Sonos Era 300 and 100 support Alexa but not Google Assistant or Siri. As an alternative or in addition to a smart speaker, you might want a smart display . They offer the same hands-free voice assistant features as a smart speaker, but with a useful touch screen on which you can view live feeds from your smart doorbell or security camera, make video calls, and control your connected gadgets with a few taps. When not in use, your living room smart display can serve as a digital photo frame to display your personal snaps or curated art. extraction.body: Thom Dunn is a writer focusing on home heating and cooling. He once blew up a power strip with a space heater and a Marshall half-stack. We have added the Google TV Streamer (4K) to replace the discontinued Chromecast with Google TV . Google’s Nest Audio and Nest Mini react to voice commands to retrieve news, music, entertainment, and answers to easy questions, and to control lights and appliances throughout the house. With their context-aware search capabilities, ever-growing Actions library, ability to synchronize with multiple Google accounts, and wide support for various smart-home devices, these Google Home speakers bring voice-controlled convenience to (almost) every corner of your life. This is a great choice for anyone looking for an inexpensive multiroom audio system or a way to use their Google accounts to make a voice-controlled smart home even smarter. All of the major smart-speaker platforms (Google Home, Alexa, and Siri) allow you to control a mix of smart-home devices with your voice, adding an extra layer of convenience and accessibility to your smart-home system. We mostly prefer Alexa because it works with a greater number of devices, but if you want a deeper integration with all things Google, or if you already have a Google Home speaker, there’s no reason to switch platforms. (We do have Alexa device and HomeKit device guides for owners of those systems.) One of the advantages of the Nest Audio over other smart-home speakers is that it uses Google for search results, and Google usually provides more-satisfying answers than other search engines. In addition, it can tie in with multiple Google accounts, distinguishing between them by the sound of each different voice. That voice-control expertise means the Nest Audio is great at providing information from your calendars, reminders, Maps data, and more. Or, with the Nest Mini , you can add these capabilities for just $50. And, of course, you can set up your Nest Audio to control your lights as well as Internet of Things–enabled air conditioners , sprinklers , robot vacuums , and more. Below we’ve selected the best Google Home–compatible devices from all of our smart-home reviews. This model has useful Scenes (presets of color and dimness) and emits bold colors, yet it’s cheaper than most smart bulbs. The WiZ 60W A19 Color LED is our top smart LED light bulb pick because it produces bold colors, has useful preset Scenes, is easy to use, can connect to other smart devices without needing a hub, and is still budget-friendly. Note, however, that this Philips bulbs line isn’t directly compatible with Philips Hue bulbs. This reliable, affordable dimmer switch uses Wi-Fi so it doesn’t need a hub, and it works with Google Home and other platforms. TP-Link’s Kasa Smart Wi-Fi Light Switch Dimmer KS220 is our top in-wall smart light-switch pick for a reason—it’s reliable, easy to use, and affordable enough that you can reasonably add a bunch of them around the house. This dimmer switch connects directly to your Wi-Fi network and has three buttons to control lighting (on/off and dim), and the easy-to-navigate app allows you to customize the controls, create automated schedules, and control grouped switches simultaneously. Since the KS220 integrates with Google Home, you can tie lights to voice commands and make specific requests like “Hey Google, dim the living room to 25%.” This easy-to-install, sharp-looking deadbolt works flawlessly, is intuitive to use, and provides robust security. The Schlage Encode Smart WiFi Deadbolt provides fast, easy keyless entry to your home using a straightforward keypad (though there is a keyway as a failsafe). The Google Home app allows you to unlock the door remotely, though it does require inputting a PIN code. And to program new codes for guests and visitors, you’ll still need to rely on the free Schlage app. Google’s newest streamer makes it easier to find, organize and revisit your favorite media than any other player. In addition to Google Home it supports Matter smart home connectivity. The Google TV Streamer (4K) , which replaced the discontinued Chromecast with Google TV , is our favorite media streamer —though it does cost twice as much. It excels at making it intuitive and easy to access video content, which is the most important of its jobs. It doesn’t take much time to notice it’s far faster, and even more responsive than competing models, thanks in part to the addition of 10 times as much internal storage as the Chromecast. The Google TV Streamer supports 4K HDR video streaming with Dolby Vision and Dolby Atmos and also supports Matter, which means you can opt to integrate it with other Google Home devices, but also interact with smart platforms like Apple Home or Amazon Alexa. Included is a Bluetooth remote control which supports voice search and works splendidly, though it doesn’t have a hands-free option. The Tailwind iQ3 Smart WiFi Garage Door Opener is the most responsive and reliable smart garage-door controller we tested. Tailwind solved the common issues of false alerts and unreliable geofencing for opening and closing, thanks to a hardwired door sensor and a unique Bluetooth/GPS technology that lets you control the door hands-free. The downside is that it is slightly more complicated to install than other options. The TP-Link Tapo Wire-Free Magnetic Security Camera is the best cordless outdoor Wi-Fi home security camera we’ve found so far. It can accurately distinguish between people, animals, vehicles, and general motion. And in testing it delivers clear images day and night. It’s also inexpensive and can run up to 300 days on a single charge (we averaged three to four months of use during testing). As cool as it is to have a little robot helper that zips around your house and cleans your floors and carpets, it’s even better when you can just sit back and tell your automated vacuum cleaner what to do, without even having to push a button. The Roborock Q5+ works with Google Home, so you can make it start, stop, pause, resume, and go home using voice commands . Our reviewer did note that pronunciation is important when using voice commands with any smart-home platform, but it appears to be a common complaint among Roborock users. The TP-Link Kasa Smart Wi-Fi Plug Slim (EP25) works reliably, has an app that’s easy to use, and can track usage of lamps, fans, or whatever else you plug into it. You can also schedule the plug to go on and off based on the time of day and the day of the week, as well as local sunrise and sunset. And you can turn those same devices on and off on the fly using the app or voice controls when paired with the Google Home app. If you want to take that convenience outside, the TP-Link Tapo TP25 Outdoor Plug is built to weather the outdoors, with an operating-temperature range of -4 to 122 degrees Fahrenheit. It supports Matter, and it features two outlets that you can control independently using the sound of your voice. One of the smallest and most powerful sous vide options available, this model adds your Google smart speaker to the cooking process to tweak temperatures and provide extra help in the kitchen. Sous vide is French for “under vacuum,” and it’s a method of cooking that lets you make restaurant-quality dishes at home by submerging your food in a vacuum-sealed bag in a heated water bath. Home versions of the sous vide have been available for a while but have only recently become more affordable. Although it’s not our top-pick sous vide appliance, the Breville Joule Turbo is impressively high-tech, letting you check on your steak or tweak temperatures through Google Assistant—integrated voice commands. And, of course, you can ask Google Assistant for help with recipes, measurements, and timers. Nest’s smart thermostat features a large, crisp, and useful display and wide compatibility with HVAC systems. Nothing warms up a cold day better than telling your thermostat to turn up the heat instead of having to crawl out from under the blankets to do it manually. Our Runner-up smart thermostat , the Google Nest Learning Thermostat (3rd generation) , lets you raise or lower the temperature or switch to a preprogrammed Away or Home setting, with just a few words. If you’re willing to take a leap of faith, you can allow the Nest to learn your habits and then create a schedule that should match your preferences (you can always tweak it as you like manually or using app or voice commands). This dimmer switch connects directly to your Wi-Fi network and has three buttons to control lighting (on/off and dim), and the easy-to-navigate app allows you to customize the controls, create automated schedules, and control grouped switches simultaneously. Since the KS220 integrates with Google Home, you can tie lights to voice commands and make specific requests like “Hey Google, dim the living room to 25%.”
This easy-to-install, sharp-looking deadbolt works flawlessly, is intuitive to use, and provides robust security.

The Schlage Encode Smart WiFi Deadbolt provides fast, easy keyless entry to your home using a straightforward keypad (though there is a keyway as a failsafe). The Google Home app allows you to unlock the door remotely, though it does require inputting a PIN code. And to program new codes for guests and visitors, you’ll still need to rely on the free Schlage app.
Google’s newest streamer makes it easier to find, organize and revisit your favorite media than any other player. In addition to Google Home it supports Matter smart home connectivity.

The Google TV Streamer (4K) , which replaced the discontinued Chromecast with Google TV , is our favorite media streamer —though it does cost twice as much. It excels at making it intuitive and easy to access video content, which is the most important of its jobs. It doesn’t take much time to notice it’s far faster, and even more responsive than competing models, thanks in part to the addition of 10 times as much internal storage as the Chromecast. The Google TV Streamer supports 4K HDR video streaming with Dolby Vision and Dolby Atmos and also supports Matter, which means you can opt to integrate it with other Google Home devices, but also interact with smart platforms like Apple Home or Amazon Alexa. Included is a Bluetooth remote control which supports voice search and works splendidly, though it doesn’t have a hands-free option.

The Tailwind iQ3 Smart WiFi Garage Door Opener is the most responsive and reliable smart garage-door controller we tested. Tailwind solved the common issues of false alerts and unreliable geofencing for opening and closing, thanks to a hardwired door sensor and a unique Bluetooth/GPS technology that lets you control the door hands-free. The downside is that it is slightly more complicated to install than other options.

The TP-Link Tapo Wire-Free Magnetic Security Camera is the best cordless outdoor Wi-Fi home security camera we’ve found so far. It can accurately distinguish between people, animals, vehicles, and general motion. And in testing it delivers clear images day and night. It’s also inexpensive and can run up to 300 days on a single charge (we averaged three to four months of use during testing).

As cool as it is to have a little robot helper that zips around your house and cleans your floors and carpets, it’s even better when you can just sit back and tell your automated vacuum cleaner what to do, without even having to push a button. The Roborock Q5+ works with Google Home, so you can make it start, stop, pause, resume, and go home using voice commands . Our reviewer did note that pronunciation is important when using voice commands with any smart-home platform, but it appears to be a common complaint among Roborock users.

The TP-Link Kasa Smart Wi-Fi Plug Slim (EP25) works reliably, has an app that’s easy to use, and can track usage of lamps, fans, or whatever else you plug into it. You can also schedule the plug to go on and off based on the time of day and the day of the week, as well as local sunrise and sunset. And you can turn those same devices on and off on the fly using the app or voice controls when paired with the Google Home app.

If you want to take that convenience outside, the TP-Link Tapo TP25 Outdoor Plug is built to weather the outdoors, with an operating-temperature range of -4 to 122 degrees Fahrenheit. It supports Matter, and it features two outlets that you can control independently using the sound of your voice.
One of the smallest and most powerful sous vide options available, this model adds your Google smart speaker to the cooking process to tweak temperatures and provide extra help in the kitchen.

Sous vide is French for “under vacuum,” and it’s a method of cooking that lets you make restaurant-quality dishes at home by submerging your food in a vacuum-sealed bag in a heated water bath. Home versions of the sous vide have been available for a while but have only recently become more affordable.

Although it’s not our top-pick sous vide appliance, the Breville Joule Turbo is impressively high-tech, letting you check on your steak or tweak temperatures through Google Assistant—integrated voice commands. And, of course, you can ask Google Assistant for help with recipes, measurements, and timers.
Nest’s smart thermostat features a large, crisp, and useful display and wide compatibility with HVAC systems.

Nothing warms up a cold day better than telling your thermostat to turn up the heat instead of having to crawl out from under the blankets to do it manually. Our Runner-up smart thermostat , the Google Nest Learning Thermostat (3rd generation) , lets you raise or lower the temperature or switch to a preprogrammed Away or Home setting, with just a few words. If you’re willing to take a leap of faith, you can allow the Nest to learn your habits and then create a schedule that should match your preferences (you can always tweak it as you like manually or using app or voice commands).

extraction.body: Nabu Casa — the commercial side of the Open Home Foundation, which runs Home Assistant — just launched the Home Assistant Connect Aux-2, a multi-function box designed to help you bring more non-smart devices into your smart home. It’s part of Home Assistant’s ongoing efforts to become more user-friendly. I’ve been testing the Aux-2 for a couple days and I’ve found it unsurprisingly useful and surprisingly easy to set up. The Aux-2 is a $69 box about the size of a deck of cards. Its USB port lets you plug in a Nabu Casa Z-Wave or Zigbee antenna in case your Home Assistant hub isn’t in a good spot. And you can connect an amplifier or powered speakers to its audio jack to stream music to older audio equipment. All of these things leverage Home Assistant’s capabilities as an open-source platform. The Aux-2 is based on ESPHome, an open platform for making DIY smart home devices from cheap, flexible ESP boards, and it uses existing Home Assistant/ESPHome integrations for all its features. The serial integration was developed earlier this year; Music Assistant and SendSpin, which power the audio-out feature, are in active development. I have a Home Assistant install, but even after several years it is not my primary smart home platform simply because of friction and time constraints. Instead, I have a hodgepodge of Google Home, Apple Home, and a few devices that are only in Home Assistant. But the Aux-2’s capabilities perfectly intersect with two things I’d been meaning to do anyway, one of which I’m already using Home Assistant for. First, I have a garage fridge, because I live in Texas. I also have children, which means sometimes the fridge or freezer door gets left open. A couple years ago, I set up a few Aqara temperature sensors, connected to Home Assistant via a now-discontinued Zigbee dongle, and set up an automation to alert me if the fridge or freezer get too warm. But they frequently drop connection (probably because they’re inside a fridge in the garage), they chew through coin cell batteries, and they have no displays, which means I also have a cheap Acu-rite hygrometer in the fridge so I can see the temperature without pulling out my phone. Someone tipped me off to Govee’s Bluetooth hygrometers, but I’d need a Bluetooth proxy to get them into Home Assistant. I also have a set of in-wall speakers in my living room that I’ve never used. Do I try to get them to work with my four Sonos speakers? Setting up the Aux-2 was much easier than I expected. Mercifully, they maintained their Bluetooth connection through three walls and a fridge, and now my fridge monitoring setup works again. The audio capability took a little longer, but most of that was spent hooking the speakers up to the amp I ended up buying and setting up Music Assistant, which I didn’t have installed. Music Assistant lives on your Home Assistant hardware and can play from many different services — from Spotify to YouTube Music to local files and more — and to many different outputs, like Sonos, Wiim, AirPlay, Google Cast, and others, but they all need to be configured, and that took a beat. I can now play music to the in-wall speakers using Music Assistant. Sendspin, the whole-home audio standard (also developed by the Open Home Foundation) is supposed to be able to let you group speakers from different protocols under certain conditions, but I haven’t gotten that working yet. The Aux-2 doesn’t do anything you couldn’t do already with an ESP32 board and various accessories, or even other ESP-based devices. The Apollo Automations Cast-1, for example, costs $35 and supports the same music-casting and Bluetooth proxy features I’m actually using from the Aux-2 at the moment. You could bodge together something even cheaper with DIY parts. Both Nabu Casa and Apollo fund the Open Home Foundation, which develops Home Assistant and ESPHome (and Sendspin and Music Assistant), and both provide hardware that’s a little easier to use than DIY options. I bought a three-pack of ESP32 boards for $16 three years ago. But now that I’ve used the Aux-2 and dipped my toe into the ESPHome waters, maybe I will.

extraction.body: Home Assistant works with a huge number of smart home devices, but it doesn't work with everything. If you have smart home tech that you've not been able to connect to Home Assistant in the past, it's worth checking again. Command a vast range of devices, with or without an internet connection. Home Assistant releases updates on a monthly cycle, with smaller patch releases during the month. Each monthly update adds new features to Home Assistant, and these always include new integrations that have been officially added to Home Assistant. There are usually a significant number of integrations added each month. For example, the 2026.4 release included 14 new integrations, including Infrared, UniFi Access, WiiM, and Autoskope. Over the past 12 months, there have been no fewer than four new integrations in any release, with some months adding as many as 17. This doesn't include custom components that you can install via HACS that are not officially supported integrations. Many of these custom components allow you to connect smart home devices that aren't supported by Home Assistant integrations, and some custom components go on to become official integrations. Home Assistant Green is a pre-built hub directly from the Home Assistant team. It's a plug-and-play solution that comes with everything you need to set up Home Assistant in your home without needing to install the software yourself. Some new Home Assistant integrations only allow you to connect a limited number of smart devices from a specific brand. There are some, however, that open up access to a whole swathe of smart home devices. One such example is the Infrared integration, which was added in Home Assistant 2026.4. The Infrared integration adds native support for controlling IR devices such as TVs or AC units using Home Assistant. In the past, to do so, you needed to use manual workarounds or custom integrations, but Home Assistant now has a dedicated native platform for infrared control. It means that you can turn cheap ESP32 devices into infrared proxies that can send and receive IR signals and control them directly from Home Assistant. For example, you can send commands to your TV as if you were pressing the buttons on your remote, and use them to turn on the TV, change the channels, turn up the volume, and more. Currently, there's only an LG Infrared integration that will let you control an LG straight out of the box, but for other IR devices, you can use the remote.learn_command action to learn the commands that your remote sends out, and the remote.send_command action to send these commands from your IR proxy. It means that in theory, you can add almost any IR device that uses a remote to Home Assistant. Infrared devices aren't the only devices that you can add to Home Assistant. There's support for all the major protocols, including those that you might not expect. For example, if you have Bluetooth smart devices around your home, you may assume that you can't hook these up to Home Assistant due to the limited range of Bluetooth. However, you can also use ESP32 devices as Bluetooth proxies and place them near your Bluetooth devices. These proxies can receive commands over Wi-Fi from Home Assistant and send out the relevant Bluetooth signals to your Bluetooth devices, controlling them as if they were already within Bluetooth range of your Home Assistant server. Home Assistant also has mature support for Matter, and continues to add new Matter features. Home Assistant 2026.4 included an update that allows you to manage users and PIN codes for Matter-compatible smart locks directly from within Home Assistant. If you have Matter devices, Home Assistant is a great way to connect and control them. If you want to see if a smart home device you own will work with Home Assistant, there are a few things you can do. The first is to see if the device is automatically discovered. Power the device on and ensure it's connected, and you may find that it appears in Home Assistant's list of discovered devices. If it isn't, the next step is to search for an official integration. On the Integrations page, click the Add Integration button and type the brand of your device to see if any results appear. If they do, install the integration and follow the setup instructions to connect your device. If there's no official integration, you can try HACS. This is a store of community-created custom components, many of which allow you to connect specific brands of smart home devices. If you can't find a custom component in the HACS store, try searching online, as some require manual installation. If nothing works, you can try the Home Assistant community forums . You may find that someone is working on a solution. Home Assistant supports a huge range of smart home devices, and the list continues to grow. Before replacing old gear or assuming a device won't work, it's worth checking Home Assistant again. Support may have arrived since the last time you checked. We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful. The best of How-To Geek, directly in your inbox.

sources.title: The Best Smart Home Devices We've Tested for 2026 - PCMag
passages: Editors' Note, June 17, 2026: With this update, we made several changes to our list of recommended smart home devices.
All of our picks have been vetted for currency and availability.

I'm PCMag's managing editor for consumer electronics, overseeing an experienced team of analysts covering smart home, home entertainment, wearables, fitness and health tech, and various other product categories.
I have been with PCMag for more than 10 years, and in that time have written more than 6,000 articles and reviews for the site.
I previously served as an analyst focused on smart home and wearable devices, and before that I was a reporter covering consumer tech news.
I'm also a yoga instructor, and have been actively teaching group and private classes for nearly a decade.
These days, there's a smart version of pretty much every home device you can think of.

extraction.body: Trained exclusively on our massive library of expert buying advice, finding the right tech to fit your life has never been easier. We've tested hundreds of smart home products in more than 20 categories to help determine which ones are best for every room in (and out of) the house. I’m PCMag’s senior writer covering smart home and wearable devices. I’ve been reporting on tech professionally for nearly a decade and have been obsessing about it for much longer than that. Prior to joining PCMag, I made educational videos for an electronics store called Abt Electronics in Illinois, and before that, I spent eight years covering the smart home market for CNET. I'm PCMag's managing editor for consumer electronics, overseeing an experienced team of analysts covering smart home, home entertainment, wearables, fitness and health tech, and various other product categories. I have been with PCMag for more than 10 years, and in that time have written more than 6,000 articles and reviews for the site. I previously served as an analyst focused on smart home and wearable devices, and before that I was a reporter covering consumer tech news. I'm also a yoga instructor, and have been actively teaching group and private classes for nearly a decade. These days, there's a smart version of pretty much every home device you can think of. These products (usually) connect to the internet, so you can control them from your phone through a companion app. Most also work with various forms of voice control. What follows is a rundown of the best smart devices we've tested for every area of the house. We have arranged our products by room to help keep things organized, but that doesn't mean you can't use most of these gadgets just about anywhere. Make sure to check back soon, as we regularly test new products and update this guide accordingly. Editors' Note, June 17, 2026: With this update, we made several changes to our list of recommended smart home devices. All of our picks have been vetted for currency and availability. At the ultimate smart home, you're met with technology before you even step through the front door. Some of the most useful connected home gadgets reside in the front yard, starting with outdoor security cameras . Our top pick overall for keeping tabs on your home from your phone is the Aqara Camera Hub G5 Pro . This high-resolution, weather-resistant security camera provides sharp video, color night vision, and AI-powered motion detection and alerts. Better yet, it acts as a hub for other smart home devices with built-in support for the Matter , Thread , and Zigbee protocols. For those times you want to check whether it's a delivery person or an unwanted solicitor knocking on your door, a video doorbell will let you see who's there without getting up from the couch. Beyond this convenience, video doorbells can serve as the first line of defense against property theft, home invasion, and porch pirates. They not only let you see and speak with the person outside, but they also record footage of visitors approaching your door while you're away or unable to answer. Our favorite model, the Arlo Video Doorbell , delivers clear HD or 2K video with a wide 180-degree diagonal field of view, allowing for either a wired or wireless setup. It works with many third-party devices and supports voice control. Another piece of technology you might want on your front door is a smart lock . Arguably the most important part of a truly connected home, these devices offer both security and convenience, allowing you to come and go as you please, while also monitoring who enters and leaves your home when you're away. Our current top pick is the Ultraloq Bolt Fingerprint , which adds HomeKit support to our previous favorite while remaining a dependable and versatile smart lock that lets you gain entry or lock up with your voice and fingerprint, as well as via keypad, mobile app, or traditional keys. If you want privacy but still like to let the sun in, the Feather River Doors Smart Glass offers the best of both worlds. This smart entry door switches between opaque and transparent glass at the push of a button or a voice command. When it comes to living room technology, televisions and soundbars are the obvious stars of the show. However, many other gadgets aim to enhance the ambiance, convenience, and security of your primary living space. For starters, a smart speaker is a must for the living room. Beyond playing music, our favorite models serve as a central command center, letting you control nearly any other connected home gadget by voice. The first step in choosing one is deciding which voice assistance platform is the right fit for your home: Alexa, Google Assistant, or Siri. All three support most major smart home device brands. If Alexa is your voice assistant of choice, we suggest the Amazon Echo Dot Max as an affordable option with impressive sound quality. If you prefer Google, we recommend waiting to see how the upcoming Google Home Speaker fares. And if you prefer Siri, you can get a HomePod or a HomePod mini . If you choose this route, make sure that any other smart home devices you purchase are compatible with Apple HomeKit or Matter . Meanwhile, the Sonos Era 300 and 100 support Alexa but not Google Assistant or Siri. As an alternative or in addition to a smart speaker, you might want a smart display . They offer the same hands-free voice assistant features as a smart speaker, but with a useful touch screen on which you can view live feeds from your smart doorbell or security camera, make video calls, and control your connected gadgets with a few taps. When not in use, your living room smart display can serve as a digital photo frame to display your personal snaps or curated art. The Alexa-powered Amazon Echo Show 11 and the Google Assistant-powered Google Nest Hub Max are among our favorites for the living room, while smaller options are more suitable for kitchen counters and bedrooms. One of the easiest and most affordable ways to upgrade your living room is to replace your standard incandescent bulbs with smart light bulbs that support app and voice control. After upgrading, you won't ever have to get up off the couch to flip the light switch again. Beyond offering greater convenience than traditional bulbs, smart lights use less energy and last longer, ultimately saving you money in the long run. Whether you're a master chef or an Uber Eats power user, the best smart kitchen gadgets can bring serious convenience to the heart of your home. Can't decide what's for dinner? Need to quickly convert fluid ounces to cups? Searching for a cilantro substitute? Sounds like you need a smart display on your countertop. With Alexa or Google Assistant in your kitchen, you can also quickly set timers, add items to your grocery list, and play your favorite cooking music, all with just the sound of your voice. Amazon's Echo Show 8 is our favorite kitchen companion. It's just the right size for countertops, will keep you entertained with great speakers and a sharp display, and can help you search for and execute recipes when you need cooking inspiration and guidance. Once you settle on a recipe, the top smart kitchen appliances can help you with every step of the cooking process. The Tovala Smart Oven allows you to bake, broil, roast, and steam food through app control and QR codes, making it one of the smartest countertop ovens available. Tovala's optional meal kits are pricey but flavorful, and its multi-step cooking programs can help you whip up chef-level entrees. When it's time to clean up after dinner, a good robot vacuum can take care of the floors for you. As a budget-friendly option , the affordable TP-Link Tapo RV30 Max Plus impressed us with its efficient navigation and self-emptying dustbin, both rare features for its sub-$300 price. You could also consider a premium self-emptying robot vacuum , such as the Ecovacs Deebot X8 Pro Omni , the top all-in-one robot for cleaning your floors. It features a self-emptying dustbin, a mop that refreshes itself as it works, and a built-in voice assistant. For homes with pets , we highly recommend the iRobot Roomba j9+ , which comes with a POOP (Pet Owner Official Promise) guarantee: If the robot fails to avoid solid pet waste within one year of your purchase, the company will provide a new one at no additional cost. To scrub away streaks, you need a good robot mop . The iRobot Braava Jet m6 is an excellent mop-only option; however, all the hybrid models mentioned above also work well as mops. The temperature of your room can have a big impact on your sleep quality. A room that is too hot or too cold can make it difficult to drift off and stay asleep throughout the night. According to Harvard Medical School , the ideal sleeping temperature for most people is around 65 to 68 degrees Fahrenheit. If you don't have central air, you might want to consider a smart air conditioner . They typically allow for app and voice control, and support scheduling, which can help reduce your energy costs. The GE Profile Clearview Smart Air Conditioner cools quickly and quietly, thanks to an innovative, split-housing design that places the bulk of the unit below the window line. The noisiest pieces are left outside, and you can still see out of your window. A smart air purifier can help you monitor your indoor air quality and breathe more easily, especially if you suffer from allergies and asthma. The Dyson Big+Quiet Formaldehyde BP03 , our all-around favorite model, is both a capable three-stage HEPA air purifier that can rid your home of harmful pollutants and an oscillating fan with Wi-Fi connectivity for phone and voice control. For relaxing smart lighting , the Philips Hue Iris Table Lamp supports up to 16 million colors and routines to help you wake up or fall asleep. You can schedule it to turn off after you fall asleep or simply tell it that you're ready to go to bed with Amazon Alexa or Google Assistant voice commands. It's easy to set up, and its 570-lumen maximum output allows it to get nice and bright when you want it to. A smart speaker can make for an excellent bedside companion. One of our favorite models for the bedroom is the Amazon Echo Dot . It won't crowd your nightstand, and lets you set alarms, play music, check the weather, and control other compatible smart home devices—all with the sound of your voice. Similarly, a smart display offers all the benefits of a smart speaker and organizes your smart home controls on a single screen, conveniently located on your bedside table. The second-generation Nest Hub is small enough for nightstands and features sensors that allow it to track your sleep, overnight respiration rate, coughing, and snoring, as well as any light and temperature changes in your room, all without a camera or requiring you to wear a separate device to bed. It then offers useful insights to help improve your shut-eye. If you prefer Alexa, our top choice for a smart display in the bedroom is the third-generation Echo Show 5 . It won't track your sleep, but it features a camera (which you can disable if you prefer) for video calls and remote home monitoring. Finally, if you have little ones, a smart baby monitor will let you watch, entertain, and soothe your child in their crib. The Nanit Pro Complete Monitoring System requires a significant investment, but it's the best smart baby monitor we've tested, especially for first-time and/or anxious parents. It records your baby's sleep and wake times down to the minute, which can help you narrow down a bedtime for your little cherub. It can also alert you if your baby stops breathing to preempt the possibility of sudden infant death syndrome. Water and tech don't usually mix, but that hasn't stopped a swell of connected bathroom gadgets, from high-tech toilets that can clean themselves to smart scales that can measure a lot more than just your weight. Whether you're lucky enough to have a dedicated workout room or just an empty corner with enough space for a yoga mat, the smart home gym equipment market offers a wealth of options for improving your fitness. Smart fitness devices, such as the Peloton Cross Training Bike+ , allow for a level of interactivity far beyond their more affordable, non-connected counterparts. The Cross Training Bike+ and other smart fitness machines offer guided classes with knowledgeable instructors and/or customized workouts and programs tailored to your goals and current fitness level. It's like having a personal trainer in the comfort, safety, and privacy of your own home. Indoor cycling on a smart stationary bike can help you burn calories, boost your cardiovascular endurance, and elevate your mood. Peloton motivates you through metrics and competition, while the SoulCycle At-Home Bike offers a more meditative, dance-focused experience. In addition to your high-tech car and e-bike , the garage is probably where you store many of your outdoor smart home devices . One of our favorites, the Rachio 3 smart sprinkler controller, can help you keep your beloved lawn looking green and lush while saving money on water. It installs in minutes and lets you control your in-ground sprinkler system from anywhere using your phone. It can also automatically reschedule watering cycles when significant rainfall is forecasted, a standout feature that performed well in our tests. Our tour of the ultimate smart home wouldn't be complete without a visit to the backyard. The best outdoor smart home devices can help you maintain a green yard, a blue pool, and a safe property. They also make it easy to create a warm and inviting ambiance for backyard parties. To set the mood for your next barbecue or pool party, you need a good outdoor-friendly speaker that can withstand splashes and rain. Opt for the Sonos Play if you're looking for a powerful but compact speaker that combines durability and smart features. It offers outstanding audio, long battery life, and boasts a rugged IP67 weatherproof rating. It also offers hands-free voice control with Alexa or the first-party Sonos assistant. If you don't need voice control on your patio, consider the Sony ULT Field 7 for our favorite blend of size and sound quality, or explore our budget-friendly option, the Anker Soundcore Motion 300 . Thanks to outdoor-friendly smart lights , the party doesn't need to stop when the sun goes down. The fun and festive Govee Lynx Dream Bluetooth & Wi-Fi Outdoor String Lights are designed for the patio, featuring a weatherproof build and easy installation. You can control these multicolor lights with your voice via Alexa or Google Assistant or through their well-designed companion app. Govee offers a variety of preset scenes to choose from, allowing you to set the mood, or you can utilize Music Sync mode for a party atmosphere.

passages: Nvidia's board is preparing to oust Jensen Huang and could meet as soon as Wednesday, the Wall Street Journal reported, after the Times reported his relationship with Nvidia executive Kimberly Powell; Nvidia fell 7.4% after hours to $160.95 (6:30 PM ET).

That came three days after Huang told employees he had been unfaithful to his wife, following reports that linked him to Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore's Megaspeed whom U.S. officials suspect of spying for China.
China calls that claim groundless, and Huang has not been accused of a crime.

On Thursday morning, Nvidia announced Huang’s resignation, saying CFO Colette Kress has been appointed interim CEO.
Huang and Powell, who are both married to other people, were allegedly captured together at a hotel in San Jose during Nvidia’s GTC developer conference in March, two unnamed sources told the Times.
Nvidia’s stock fell more than 7 percent in after-hours trading Wednesday.
The Nvidia board will meet as soon as Wednesday night to decide on Huang’s future at the company, according to the Journal.
Rumors about a potential affair between the two had long circulated at Nvidia, an unnamed source told CNBC, partially because Powell does not have a health or science background.

Since Nvidia and Huang confirmed an extramarital relationship with Megaspeed executive and alleged spy Alice Huang and a subsequent investigation over the weekend, the company has said it retained former US attorney Joon H.

If Jensen Huang is indeed forced to leave his position as CEO, Nvidia will face a major challenge in finding a successor capable of maintaining its technology strategy, partner relationships, and investor confidence.
