coreStoryFacts.text: Nvidia's board is preparing to oust Jensen Huang and could meet as soon as Wednesday, the Wall Street Journal reported, after the Times reported his relationship with Nvidia executive Kimberly Powell; Nvidia fell 7.4% after hours to $160.95 (6:30 PM ET).

That came three days after Huang told employees he had been unfaithful to his wife, following reports that linked him to Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore's Megaspeed whom U.S. officials suspect of spying for China.
China calls that claim groundless, and Huang has not been accused of a crime.
The first-day drops were small in both cases, under 3%.
Nvidia has already fallen more than that after hours tonight alone.
What separated the two outcomes came later, and it was mostly about two things: whether the board had a successor ready on day one, and whether the business underneath was healthy.
Intel had neither, and its stock lagged for the year that followed.
Huang being removed immediately could be challenging for Nvidia since it does not have a succession plan in place," Gil Luria of D.A.
Davidson told Reuters after the Journal's report.
Huang co-founded the company in 1993 and has run it ever since, which makes him harder to replace than Krzanich or Easterbrook, who were both hired managers.
Baird analysts Tristan Gerra and Tyler Bomba wrote earlier Wednesday that a CEO change was growing more likely and that an outside hire would be favored.
Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives has said Nvidia would be worth 25% to 30% less without Huang.
On the other side, Nvidia's business is far healthier than Intel's was in 2018, and a Blind survey found 88% of 232 Nvidia employees want Huang to stay.
For a holder with $100,000 in Nvidia, about 621 shares at the after-hours price, the two histories frame the range.
Neither history includes a founder, so the real range is probably wider in both directions.
A relationship with a direct report turns the board's problem into one that boards have handled before, and twice in the past decade the CEO had to go.
Here is what happened to shareholders those two times.
On Sunday, November 3, 2019, McDonald's said its board had fired CEO Steve Easterbrook for a consensual relationship with an employee, which violated company policy.
In August 2020 the company sued Easterbrook, saying he had hidden other relationships, and in 2021 he agreed to return more than $105 million in pay.

Chief financial officer Bob Swan ran the company as interim CEO for seven months before the board gave him the job in January 2019, while Intel was also struggling to get its next generation of chips into production.
A fast, credible choice was the difference between the two cases above.

extraction.body: Nvidia's board of directors is reportedly preparing for an emergency meeting to decide the future of CEO Jensen Huang, following his extramarital affair with a woman suspected of being a spy. Nvidia's board of directors is preparing to hold a meeting to discuss the possibility of terminating CEO Jensen Huang's tenure, according to information published by the Wall Street Journal on Wednesday (November 11), citing sources familiar with the matter. Sources indicate the meeting could take place as early as Wednesday, focusing on deciding the future of Nvidia's most powerful leader. This move comes after Huang was accused of having two extramarital affairs, one of which involved a woman named Alice Huang, a figure suspected by US intelligence of being a spy. Previously, the New York Times also reported that Jensen Huang had an extramarital affair with a senior female executive at Nvidia who reported directly to him. According to the New York Times , the woman is Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of healthcare . The newspaper cited five former employees of the company to confirm the information about the relationship between the two. If the above information is verified and the board of directors decides to change leadership, Nvidia will face one of the biggest personnel changes since becoming the world's most valuable technology company. Nvidia has not immediately responded to requests for comment on the above information. The new information was released just days after Jensen Huang admitted to infidelity with his wife. At the same time, Nvidia's board of directors was investigating the possibility that he was the target of a foreign intelligence operation. At the heart of the controversy is the relationship between Jensen Huang and Alice Huang. According to U.S. intelligence reports mentioned earlier, this woman is suspected of acting as an intermediary, facilitating the delivery of Nvidia chips to Chinese businesses. This is a particularly sensitive issue for Nvidia, as the company is at the center of the artificial intelligence ( AI ) technology competition between the US and China. The company's AI chips are not only a major source of revenue but are also considered one of the most important strategic assets of the US technology industry. Therefore, the questions surrounding Jensen Huang's personal relationships are no longer simply a matter of private life. If evidence emerges showing that he was exploited to access information or facilitate technology transfer, the case could become a national security issue and directly impact Nvidia's business operations. The fact that the board is considering the possibility that Jensen Huang may have been the target of a foreign intelligence operation speaks to the seriousness of the crisis. However, there is currently no public information confirming that Mr. Huang is involved in any illegal activities. The scandal quickly impacted investor sentiment. Nvidia shares fell about 8% in after-hours trading on Wednesday, following reports of a potential CEO change. Notably, since information about the relationship between Jensen Huang and Alice Huang emerged, Nvidia's stock has lost more than $300 billion in market capitalization. For a trillion-dollar company, this decline indicates that investors are particularly concerned about governance risks and the ability to maintain stability in the leadership structure. Jensen Huang is not only the CEO of Nvidia but also a highly influential figure in global AI development strategy. Under his leadership, the company has risen to dominate the market for chips used in training artificial intelligence models and operating services like OpenAI's ChatGPT. The possibility of Jensen Huang stepping down as CEO could create a significant leadership vacuum at Nvidia, a company currently valued at around $4 trillion and playing a crucial role in the competition for AI dominance between the US and China. For many years, Huang was considered the heart and soul of Nvidia. His strategic vision helped the company transform from a graphics processor manufacturer into a critical computing infrastructure provider for the global AI wave. If Jensen Huang is indeed forced to leave his position as CEO, Nvidia will face a major challenge in finding a successor capable of maintaining its technology strategy, partner relationships, and investor confidence.

sources.title: MSCI Removes Strategy From Indexes: What It Means for MSTR and Bitcoin - Brave New Coin
passages: MSCI’s index deletion creates a new financing test for Strategy.
Here is what passive selling could mean for MSTR and future Bitcoin purchases.
The index provider’s November review lists Strategy A among deletions from the MSCI USA Index, effective after the close of business on November 30.
The decision changes an important source of shareholder demand.
It does not remove MSTR from Nasdaq or require Strategy to sell its Bitcoin.

MSCI is removing Strategy from its global equity indexes, giving Bitcoin investors a new question to confront: what happens to a major corporate buyer when some of the funds holding its shares have to leave?
Brave New Coin reaches 1M+ engaged crypto enthusiasts a month through our website, podcast, newsletters, and YouTube.
Get your brand in front of key decision-makers and early adopters in 2026.
The company also disputes the classification behind the decision.
Its response argues that Bitcoin treasury activity constitutes an operating business.
The risks to MSTR and BTC are related, but they are not interchangeable.
An investor selling Strategy shares transfers ownership of the company to another buyer.
Those figures describe Strategy’s consultation-era assessment, rather than a fresh measurement of every fund’s position on November 12.
Holdings, prices and trading activity can change before implementation.
They nevertheless give investors a more concrete starting point than treating every dollar of MSTR’s market value as exposed to compulsory selling.
The larger issue is the connection between share demand and financing.
Strategy has raised capital through common stock, preferred securities and debt to support its Bitcoin strategy.
Losing a group of benchmark-driven shareholders could make that capital-raising process less favourable if it contributes to a weaker share price.
It would therefore be premature to equate an estimated amount of stock selling with the same amount of Bitcoin selling.
Forecasts built on other index providers also excluding Strategy require those additional decisions to occur.
Strategy now faces a test of demand for its corporate Bitcoin model outside one major benchmark family.
In its consultation response , Strategy said MSCI-linked funds held approximately 13 million shares, representing 3.1% of basic shares outstanding.
BNC’s earlier report on Strategy’s Bitcoin purchases and preferred-share buybacks showed the competing uses of capital.
The index removal adds another consideration to those allocation choices.

Markus Thielen, founder of 10x Research, told CoinDesk : “We don’t expect any spillover into Bitcoin itself.” His assessment is an analyst opinion, not assurance that market sentiment or future corporate purchases will be unaffected.
This is why a company holding Bitcoin and a fund holding Bitcoin can produce very different investment results.
A change in how the equity is valued can matter even when the Bitcoin price is unchanged.
For funds mandated to replicate an index, membership matters regardless of the portfolio manager’s personal view of Bitcoin.
That makes this a scheduled portfolio event rather than another round of speculation about whether digital asset treasury companies belong in equity benchmarks.

The decision changes an important source of shareholder demand. It does not remove MSTR from Nasdaq or require Strategy to sell its Bitcoin. The published review confirms the deletion and its timetable. That makes this a scheduled portfolio event rather than another round of speculation about whether digital asset treasury companies belong in equity benchmarks. For funds mandated to replicate an index, membership matters regardless of the portfolio manager’s personal view of Bitcoin. Once a constituent leaves, a tracking portfolio normally adjusts its exposure to match. Other investors can still buy the stock, including funds using different benchmarks or discretionary mandates. That distinction is crucial. An index exit removes one reason to own shares; it does not erase every reason. Nor does the announcement establish the price at which buyers and sellers will meet when portfolios rebalance. In its consultation response , Strategy said MSCI-linked funds held approximately 13 million shares, representing 3.1% of basic shares outstanding. The company argued that this was less than one day’s trading volume and called the proposal “misguided.” Those figures describe Strategy’s consultation-era assessment, rather than a fresh measurement of every fund’s position on November 12. Holdings, prices and trading activity can change before implementation. They nevertheless give investors a more concrete starting point than treating every dollar of MSTR’s market value as exposed to compulsory selling. The company also disputes the classification behind the decision. Its response argues that Bitcoin treasury activity constitutes an operating business. MSCI’s index eligibility decision and Strategy’s accounting position answer different questions: how a benchmark is constructed, and how a company describes its activities. The larger issue is the connection between share demand and financing. Strategy has raised capital through common stock, preferred securities and debt to support its Bitcoin strategy. Losing a group of benchmark-driven shareholders could make that capital-raising process less favourable if it contributes to a weaker share price. Consider the economics without assuming an outcome. When investors pay a substantial premium for a company’s underlying assets, issuing new shares can raise more capital relative to the asset exposure represented by those shares. A smaller premium reduces that advantage. The calculation also depends on liabilities, financing terms and the security being issued. This is why a company holding Bitcoin and a fund holding Bitcoin can produce very different investment results. Shareholders in the company also own its financing decisions, operating activities and corporate obligations. A change in how the equity is valued can matter even when the Bitcoin price is unchanged. Strategy’s third-quarter results reported $21.23 billion of capital raised year to date as of October 25. That historical figure illustrates the scale of financing in the business; it should not be confused with proceeds guaranteed to remain available after the index decision. BNC’s earlier report on Strategy’s Bitcoin purchases and preferred-share buybacks showed the competing uses of capital. The index removal adds another consideration to those allocation choices. The risks to MSTR and BTC are related, but they are not interchangeable. An investor selling Strategy shares transfers ownership of the company to another buyer. That transaction does not itself instruct Strategy to liquidate coins. Markus Thielen, founder of 10x Research, told CoinDesk : “We don’t expect any spillover into Bitcoin itself.” His assessment is an analyst opinion, not assurance that market sentiment or future corporate purchases will be unaffected. The more plausible transmission channel is indirect: weaker equity demand could influence financing terms, which could affect the pace or attractiveness of future purchases. Whether that happens depends on management’s response, other funding sources and investor appetite beyond MSCI-linked portfolios. It would therefore be premature to equate an estimated amount of stock selling with the same amount of Bitcoin selling. They involve different assets, different decision-makers and potentially different dates. Forecasts built on other index providers also excluding Strategy require those additional decisions to occur. Three developments can make the consequences clearer: disclosures about the actual rebalancing exposure, changes in Strategy’s financing activity, and management’s capital-allocation decisions. Share-price weakness alone cannot identify how much selling came from index funds rather than discretionary investors. The effective date also matters for interpreting headlines. MSCI announced the change in advance; implementation is scheduled for the November 30 close. Markets can respond before that date, and passive portfolios do not necessarily execute every adjustment in an identical way. Strategy now faces a test of demand for its corporate Bitcoin model outside one major benchmark family. For BTC holders, the useful question is whether the decision changes the company’s future ability to buy, rather than assuming its existing coins must suddenly come onto the market. (Bloomberg) -- MSCI Inc. has dropped Strategy Inc. from its global equity benchmarks, potentially triggering billions of dollars in stock sales and adding fresh pressure to the financing model behind Michael Saylor's vast Bitcoin holdings.

That distinction is crucial. An index exit removes one reason to own shares; it does not erase every reason. The company also disputes the classification behind the decision. Its response argues that Bitcoin treasury activity constitutes an operating business. MSCI’s index eligibility decision and Strategy’s accounting position answer different questions: how a benchmark is constructed, and how a company describes its activities. The larger issue is the connection between share demand and financing. Strategy has raised capital through common stock, preferred securities and debt to support its Bitcoin strategy. Losing a group of benchmark-driven shareholders could make that capital-raising process less favourable if it contributes to a weaker share price. Consider the economics without assuming an outcome. When investors pay a substantial premium for a company’s underlying assets, issuing new shares can raise more capital relative to the asset exposure represented by those shares. A smaller premium reduces that advantage. The calculation also depends on liabilities, financing terms and the security being issued. This is why a company holding Bitcoin and a fund holding Bitcoin can produce very different investment results. Shareholders in the company also own its financing decisions, operating activities and corporate obligations. A change in how the equity is valued can matter even when the Bitcoin price is unchanged. That historical figure illustrates the scale of financing in the business; it should not be confused with proceeds guaranteed to remain available after the index decision. The more plausible transmission channel is indirect: weaker equity demand could influence financing terms, which could affect the pace or attractiveness of future purchases. They involve different assets, different decision-makers and potentially different dates. Forecasts built on other index providers also excluding Strategy require those additional decisions to occur. Three developments can make the consequences clearer: disclosures about the actual rebalancing exposure, changes in Strategy’s financing activity, and management’s capital-allocation decisions. MSCI announced the change in advance; implementation is scheduled for the November 30 close. Markets can respond before that date, and passive portfolios do not necessarily execute every adjustment in an identical way. Strategy now faces a test of demand for its corporate Bitcoin model outside one major benchmark family. Strategy Inc NASDAQ MSTR , the bitcoin treasury and enterprise-software company with 850,364 bitcoin as of Nov. 8, will leave the MSCI USA Index at that close. The final review published on Nov. 11 lists “STRATEGY A” among the deletions. MSCI Inc. NYSE MSCI , the provider of indexes and investment analytics, announced 24 deletions and one addition for its USA benchmark. The closing quote for NASDAQ MSTR was US$122.35 at 4:00 p.m. EST on Nov. 11. MSCI had scheduled its review announcement for shortly after 5:00 p.m. EST, so that closing price does not measure trading after the announcement. The Nov. 30 deletion exposes holders to selling by portfolios seeking to track the benchmark's constituents. MSCI's public list does not quantify tracking funds' Strategy holdings or provide a dollar outflow forecast, so the confirmed removal supplies no verified total for passive selling. The deletion follows MSCI's Oct. 15 adoption of new eligibility rules for its Global Investable Market Indexes. Those changes take effect in the November review, adding corporate issuers classified as non-operating to previously ineligible investment funds, business development companies and other passive investment vehicles. MSCI will first screen for substantial operating assets. Issuers that fail that initial screen face a second test using five financial ratios that the provider describes as non-industry-specific; a security becomes ineligible if it is flagged on at least four. “Current constituents will be removed only if they fail the ineligibility screen in each of the two most recent annual filing periods,” MSCI said in its Oct. 15 announcement. MSCI said it may also use the most recent interim filing, if available. For companies seeking admission, failure in either of the two most recent annual filing periods prevents addition, while buffers also apply to the ratios' eligibility thresholds. The same November review ends interim measures announced on Oct. 10, 2025, for a preliminary list of companies whose digital assets represented at least 50 per cent of total assets. Those measures froze increases in index share counts and inclusion factors, and deferred additions and size-segment migrations. MSCI said eligibility for those companies will instead be assessed under the new methodology. Its Nov. 11 deletion list identifies Strategy's security but does not publish the company's individual screening calculations. Strategy opposed the proposed test in an Aug. 31 letter to MSCI's Equity Index Committee. It asked the provider to withdraw the proposal and argued that the classifications lacked definitions grounded in generally accepted accounting principles. In that letter, Strategy described an enterprise-analytics software business employing more than 1,500 people worldwide and generating nearly US$500 million in annual revenue. It also argued that its bitcoin business qualifies as an operating segment and that it actively uses its holdings to develop bitcoin-backed credit instruments. The Aug. 31 response offered alternatives if MSCI proceeded: revise and republish the methodology, explain its rationale, and apply it only to company filings issued after implementation. MSCI's Oct. 15 decision instead provided for the screening history described above and implementation in November. Strategy's Nov. 9 securities filing reports capital-market transactions from Nov. 2 through Nov. 8. It sold 2,051,348 common shares, including sales not yet settled, generating US$283.8 million net of sales commissions. The company used US$81.9 million of those proceeds to buy 1,036 bitcoin during that reporting period. It reported 850,364 bitcoin held as of Nov. 8, acquired for an aggregate US$64.16 billion including fees and expenses. The filing also allocated US$188.3 million of the common-share proceeds to preferred-share repurchases during the period ending Nov. 8. That financing pattern underpinned Mugglehead's Nov. 9 report on bitcoin purchases and preferred repurchases . As of Nov. 8, Strategy separately reported a US$4.77 billion reserve intended to support preferred dividends and debt interest. It also reported US$146.2 million of cash for broader treasury purposes, including bitcoin purchases and capital management. MSCI's Nov. 11 review used a price cutoff of Oct. 20 and allows updates for corporate events and other relevant adjustments before implementation. Passive funds face a Nov. 30 rebalance that will remove a major bitcoin treasury stock from a U.S. equity benchmark. Strategy Inc NASDAQ MSTR , the bitcoin treasury and enterprise-software company with 850,364 bitcoin as of Nov. 8, will leave the MSCI USA Index at that close.

The final review published on Nov. 11 lists “STRATEGY A” among the deletions. MSCI Inc. NYSE MSCI , the provider of indexes and investment analytics, announced 24 deletions and one addition for its USA benchmark.

The closing quote for NASDAQ MSTR was US$122.35 at 4:00 p.m. EST on Nov. 11. MSCI had scheduled its review announcement for shortly after 5:00 p.m. EST, so that closing price does not measure trading after the announcement.

The Nov. 30 deletion exposes holders to selling by portfolios seeking to track the benchmark's constituents. MSCI's public list does not quantify tracking funds' Strategy holdings or provide a dollar outflow forecast, so the confirmed removal supplies no verified total for passive selling.

The deletion follows MSCI's Oct. 15 adoption of new eligibility rules for its Global Investable Market Indexes. Those changes take effect in the November review, adding corporate issuers classified as non-operating to previously ineligible investment funds, business development companies and other passive investment vehicles.

MSCI will first screen for substantial operating assets. Issuers that fail that initial screen face a second test using five financial ratios that the provider describes as non-industry-specific; a security becomes ineligible if it is flagged on at least four.
“Current constituents will be removed only if they fail the ineligibility screen in each of the two most recent annual filing periods,” MSCI said in its Oct. 15 announcement.

MSCI said it may also use the most recent interim filing, if available. For companies seeking admission, failure in either of the two most recent annual filing periods prevents addition, while buffers also apply to the ratios' eligibility thresholds.

The same November review ends interim measures announced on Oct. 10, 2025, for a preliminary list of companies whose digital assets represented at least 50 per cent of total assets. Those measures froze increases in index share counts and inclusion factors, and deferred additions and size-segment migrations.

MSCI said eligibility for those companies will instead be assessed under the new methodology. Its Nov. 11 deletion list identifies Strategy's security but does not publish the company's individual screening calculations.

Strategy opposed the proposed test in an Aug. 31 letter to MSCI's Equity Index Committee. It asked the provider to withdraw the proposal and argued that the classifications lacked definitions grounded in generally accepted accounting principles.

In that letter, Strategy described an enterprise-analytics software business employing more than 1,500 people worldwide and generating nearly US$500 million in annual revenue. It also argued that its bitcoin business qualifies as an operating segment and that it actively uses its holdings to develop bitcoin-backed credit instruments.

The Aug. 31 response offered alternatives if MSCI proceeded: revise and republish the methodology, explain its rationale, and apply it only to company filings issued after implementation. MSCI's Oct. 15 decision instead provided for the screening history described above and implementation in November.

Strategy's Nov. 9 securities filing reports capital-market transactions from Nov. 2 through Nov. 8. It sold 2,051,348 common shares, including sales not yet settled, generating US$283.8 million net of sales commissions.

The company used US$81.9 million of those proceeds to buy 1,036 bitcoin during that reporting period. It reported 850,364 bitcoin held as of Nov. 8, acquired for an aggregate US$64.16 billion including fees and expenses.

The filing also allocated US$188.3 million of the common-share proceeds to preferred-share repurchases during the period ending Nov. 8. That financing pattern underpinned Mugglehead's Nov. 9 report on bitcoin purchases and preferred repurchases .

As of Nov. 8, Strategy separately reported a US$4.77 billion reserve intended to support preferred dividends and debt interest. It also reported US$146.2 million of cash for broader treasury purposes, including bitcoin purchases and capital management.

MSCI's Nov. 11 review used a price cutoff of Oct. 20 and allows updates for corporate events and other relevant adjustments before implementation. The next scheduled test for Strategy holders is the Nov. 30 closing rebalance, when the announced MSCI USA deletion takes effect.

extraction.body: Nvidia co-founder CEO Jensen Huang has never been as flashy or controversy-prone as AI leaders like OpenAI’s Sam Altman or SpaceXAI’s Elon Musk. Now, the 63-year-old industry kingpin has admitted that he cheated on his wife of 40 years in an affair that could have ramifications beyond Huang’s personal life and potentially impact national security. United States officials believe that Huang’s likely romantic interest, Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, is a Chinese spy who has been feeding information back to Beijing. (Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen, is of no relation to Jensen Huang.) Megaspeed, a Singapore-based AI infrastructure company, had reportedly purchased $4.8 billion in Nvidia chips over the last two years. The U.S. and Singapore have both previously investigated Megaspeed over suspicions that the firm was illegally sharing chips with China. The Justice Department has since taken over the federal investigation into the company, the Times has reported. The story took a sudden new turn on Wednesday. Citing five people who worked at Nvidia, the Times reported that Huang also had an extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell, the company’s vice president of health care, who reports directly to him. Nvidia, Huang and Powell have not confirmed the report. Reached by a Times reporter, Huang reportedly said, “I don’t think you should be talking to me directly,” before hanging up. Separately, the Wall Street Journal reported that Nvidia’s board is preparing to oust Huang , and Nvidia’s shares fell in after-hours trading. The U.S. and China are embroiled in a fierce technological arms race to build the most advanced AI infrastructure, which could shape each country’s economic future, military prowess, and capacity for innovation. Nvidia is valuable in this competition as one of the world’s largest makers of AI chips, which are essential for accelerating AI development. But as an American company, Nvidia faces government restrictions on the sale of its most powerful chips to Chinese entities. As the controversy unfolds, we are organizing the most relevant events into a reverse-chronological timeline to keep you up to date. After reports of a second extramarital affair, Nvidia’s board reportedly plans to meet to discuss Huang’s future at the company, per the Wall Street Journal. Stock fell about 8% in after hours trading on Wednesday and is down 11% in the past five days. Huang famously delegates very little and has about 60 direct reports, he has said . The company has not had an obvious successor or a succession plan. The New York Times reported that Jensen Huang also had an affair with Nvidia vice president of healthcare Kimberly Powell, who reports directly to the CEO. According to the report, Huang and Powell were captured on film “being affectionate” at a hotel during a conference earlier this year. Huang has not responded to a request from three Republican congressman to appear for a closed-door briefing for questioning about his affair with an alleged Chinese spy. House China committee Chairman Moolenaar said Wednesday on Fox Business that if Huang doesn’t agree to the briefing, he’ll likely be subpoenaed . The Nvidia CEO pulled out of upcoming speaking engagements at the ElevenLabs Summit and Anthropic CEO Forum. Alice Huang and her family reportedly built a network of companies in China and Singapore to acquire Nvidia chips, including founding a Chinese company called Shanghai Century Litong. Founded in 2023, it became an Nvidia-preferred cloud partner, giving it priority access to chips, The Information reported . The Information also reported that Shanghai Century Litong facilitated buying $7.5 billion worth of Nvidia’s chips, including banned chips. Nvidia’s head lawyer, Tim Teter, intervened in a 2025 U.S. government probe surrounding the suspected smuggling of AI chips by Megaspeed International, Bloomberg reported . Teter contacted Commerce Under Secretary Jeffrey Kessler asking questions about whether the Trump administration played a role in detaining Alice Huang. In early 2025, Alice Huang and a business partner sought China-based investors for an Asian data center, promising they had no problem in securing GPUs, the Financial Times reported. On Sunday night, President Trump weighed in on Huang’s controversy and showed support for the Nvidia CEO. “I have not spoken to him about it. I just know he’s a fine person, but you never know what’s going on,” Trump said. When asked if Huang should remain chief of Nvidia , Trump said, “I think so. Oh yeah, sure.” Jensen Huang wrote in a letter to Nvidia employees — which was also published as a press release — that he cheated on his wife. “I owe my family and all of you an apology,” Huang told his company. “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.” Huang did not mention Alice Huang by name in the message, but linked his infidelity to “the national security concerns raised in news reports.” “Nvidia’s Board of Directors has initiated an independent investigation. I support the investigation and will cooperate fully. I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America’s national security. I am proud and grateful to be an American,” Huang wrote. Nvidia shares slid over 5% the following day. An Nvidia spokesperson denied that this relationship was something out of the ordinary. “Jensen’s interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected. Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year,” Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo said. He added that “if the U.S. government believes that any person is a threat to American industry, it would let us know.” U.S. officials circulated a secret memo among policymakers that warned that Megaspeed’s Alice Huang, who had a relationship with Jensen Huang, was a spy for China’s Ministry of State Security. This memo was not public knowledge until it was later reported by the New York Times. Secretary of State Marco Rubio supervised the drafting of the memo. Around the same time, per the New York Times’ report , U.S. President Donald Trump was briefed about intelligence findings that possible Chinese spy Alice Huang had formed a close relationship with Jensen Huang. Trump did not act on this information. The Nvidia CEO, an ally of Trump , has repeatedly advocated for the U.S. government to let Nvidia expand its business in China. Megaspeed, a neocloud that used Nvidia chips, had been renting computing power to Chinese internet giant Alibaba and other Chinese companies, the Times reported. A Commerce Department official who had visited Megaspeed’s data center in Malaysia in 2024 had found a hoard of Nvidia equipment that was still packed in boxes and the concern was that this equipment was being directly shipped somewhere else, like China, rather than installed and sold as a cloud service. Jensen Huang had been spotted socializing with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang as early as 2024 in Taiwan, where the Nvidia CEO was born. These investigations into Megaspeed highlighted concerns about the degree to which Nvidia is able to track its chip exports. At the time, an Nvidia spokesperson told press that the company did not have “any reason to believe products had been diverted.” “NVIDIA visited multiple Megaspeed sites yet again earlier this week and confirmed what we previously observed — Megaspeed is running a small commercial cloud, like many other companies throughout the world, as allowed by U.S. export control rules,” the Nvidia spokesperson said at the time. extraction.body: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is at the centre of a controversy that has moved well beyond his personal life. What began as reports of his close relationship with Alice Huang, suspected of spying for China, has developed into a wider national security and corporate governance issue. The controversy has drawn attention from US lawmakers, prompted an independent investigation by Nvidia's board and reportedly raised questions about Huang's future at the company. Here is how the events unfolded, from the initial investigations into a Singapore-based business to the latest developments surrounding the Nvidia chief. October 2025: Chip smuggling investigation The controversy has its roots in investigations into Megaspeed International, a Singapore-based AI infrastructure company and Nvidia customer. In October 2025, authorities in the US and Singapore began investigating the company over suspicions that it was helping Chinese businesses obtain Nvidia chips despite American export restrictions. According to reports, Megaspeed had been renting computing capacity to Chinese internet giant Alibaba and other companies. Concerns grew after a US Commerce Department official visiting one of its data centres in Malaysia in 2024 reportedly discovered Nvidia equipment still packed in boxes, raising questions about whether the hardware was being shipped elsewhere rather than deployed for cloud computing. Huang had also been seen socialising with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang in Taiwan as early as 2024. Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen, is not related to the Nvidia CEO. 2025: Trump reportedly briefed on Huang's relationship US President Donald Trump was reportedly briefed towards the end of 2025 about intelligence findings concerning Alice Huang and her relationship with the Nvidia chief. However, the president did not take action following the briefing, according to the New York Times. Huang has been an ally of Trump and has repeatedly argued that the US government should allow Nvidia to expand its business in China. May 2026: Secret memo raises concerns about suspected Chinese spy The matter took another turn in spring 2026 when a confidential memo circulated among Trump administration officials. The document reportedly identified Alice Huang as a suspected Chinese intelligence operative working for China's Ministry of State Security. According to reports, Secretary of State Marco Rubio supervised the preparation of the memo. It warned policymakers about her alleged relationship with Huang and the potential implications for American national security. October 29, 2026: Huang's relationship with Alice Huang becomes public The controversy became public when the New York Times reported that Jensen Huang had developed a close relationship with Alice Huang, who was already under investigation by American authorities. Nvidia pushed back against suggestions that their interactions were unusual. Company spokesperson John Rizzo said meetings with customers were part of Huang's responsibilities as chief executive, adding that he interacted with thousands of customer executives every year. He also said Nvidia would expect the US government to inform the company if it believed someone posed a threat to American industry. November 5, 2026: Republican lawmakers seek answers from Huang Three Republican committee chairmen asked Huang to attend a closed-door briefing with members of their committees. The lawmakers included John Moolenaar of the House Select Committee on China, Brian Mast of the House Foreign Affairs Committee and Rick Crawford of the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence. Their letter highlighted concerns about China's access to sensitive American technology and information. They said Congress needed to establish whether US national security had been compromised through potential Chinese infiltration. November 8, 2026: Huang apologises for affair as Nvidia, FDA launches investigation Huang addressed the controversy directly in a letter to Nvidia employees, admitting that he had been unfaithful to his wife and apologising to his family and colleagues. Although he did not identify Alice Huang by name, he acknowledged the national security concerns raised in media reports. Huang also confirmed that Nvidia's board had initiated an independent investigation, pledging to cooperate fully and reiterating his commitment to protecting the company and American national security. The admission had an immediate impact on investor sentiment, with Nvidia shares falling more than 5 per cent the following day. US President Donald Trump also weighed in on the controversy on November 8. Despite acknowledging that he did not know all the details, Trump described Huang as a 'fine person' and said he believed the Nvidia chief should remain in charge of the company. November 9-10, 2026: More about Alice Huang's business network Further reporting shed light on the business connections between Alice Huang, her family and Nvidia's chip supply chain. According to reports, Alice Huang and her family had established a network of businesses across China and Singapore to acquire Nvidia processors. One of these was Shanghai Century Litong, a Chinese company founded in 2023 that reportedly became an Nvidia-preferred cloud partner, giving it priority access to chips. The Information reported that the company had facilitated purchases worth $7.5 billion, including chips restricted under US export controls. Separately, Bloomberg reported that Nvidia's head lawyer, Tim Teter, had intervened during a 2025 US government investigation into suspected chip smuggling involving Megaspeed.

extraction.body: Nvidia co-founder CEO Jensen Huang has never been as flashy or controversy-prone as AI leaders like OpenAI’s Sam Altman or SpaceXAI’s Elon Musk. Now, the 63-year-old industry kingpin has admitted that he cheated on his wife of 40 years in an affair that could have ramifications beyond Huang’s personal life and potentially impact national security. United States officials believe that Huang’s likely romantic interest, Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, is a Chinese spy who has been feeding information back to Beijing. (Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen, is of no relation to Jensen Huang.) Megaspeed, a Singapore-based AI infrastructure company, had reportedly purchased $4.8 billion in Nvidia chips over the last two years. The U.S. and Singapore have both previously investigated Megaspeed over suspicions that the firm was illegally sharing chips with China. The Justice Department has since taken over the federal investigation into the company, the Times has reported. The story took a sudden new turn on Wednesday. Citing five people who worked at Nvidia, the Times reported that Huang also had an extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell, the company’s vice president of health care, who reports directly to him. Nvidia, Huang and Powell have not confirmed the report. Reached by a Times reporter, Huang reportedly said, “I don’t think you should be talking to me directly,” before hanging up. Separately, the Wall Street Journal reported that Nvidia’s board is preparing to oust Huang , and Nvidia’s shares fell in after-hours trading. The U.S. and China are embroiled in a fierce technological arms race to build the most advanced AI infrastructure, which could shape each country’s economic future, military prowess, and capacity for innovation. Nvidia is valuable in this competition as one of the world’s largest makers of AI chips, which are essential for accelerating AI development. But as an American company, Nvidia faces government restrictions on the sale of its most powerful chips to Chinese entities. As the controversy unfolds, we are organizing the most relevant events into a reverse-chronological timeline to keep you up to date. After reports of a second extramarital affair, Nvidia’s board reportedly plans to meet to discuss Huang’s future at the company, per the Wall Street Journal. Stock fell about 8% in after hours trading on Wednesday and is down 11% in the past five days. Huang famously delegates very little and has about 60 direct reports, he has said . The company has not had an obvious successor or a succession plan. The New York Times reported that Jensen Huang also had an affair with Nvidia vice president of healthcare Kimberly Powell, who reports directly to the CEO. According to the report, Huang and Powell were captured on film “being affectionate” at a hotel during a conference earlier this year. Huang has not responded to a request from three Republican congressman to appear for a closed-door briefing for questioning about his affair with an alleged Chinese spy. House China committee Chairman Moolenaar said Wednesday on Fox Business that if Huang doesn’t agree to the briefing, he’ll likely be subpoenaed . The Nvidia CEO pulled out of upcoming speaking engagements at the ElevenLabs Summit and Anthropic CEO Forum. Alice Huang and her family reportedly built a network of companies in China and Singapore to acquire Nvidia chips, including founding a Chinese company called Shanghai Century Litong. Founded in 2023, it became an Nvidia-preferred cloud partner, giving it priority access to chips, The Information reported . The Information also reported that Shanghai Century Litong facilitated buying $7.5 billion worth of Nvidia’s chips, including banned chips. Nvidia’s head lawyer, Tim Teter, intervened in a 2025 U.S. government probe surrounding the suspected smuggling of AI chips by Megaspeed International, Bloomberg reported . Teter contacted Commerce Under Secretary Jeffrey Kessler asking questions about whether the Trump administration played a role in detaining Alice Huang. In early 2025, Alice Huang and a business partner sought China-based investors for an Asian data center, promising they had no problem in securing GPUs, the Financial Times reported. On Sunday night, President Trump weighed in on Huang’s controversy and showed support for the Nvidia CEO. “I have not spoken to him about it. I just know he’s a fine person, but you never know what’s going on,” Trump said. When asked if Huang should remain chief of Nvidia , Trump said, “I think so. Oh yeah, sure.” Jensen Huang wrote in a letter to Nvidia employees — which was also published as a press release — that he cheated on his wife. “I owe my family and all of you an apology,” Huang told his company. “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.” Huang did not mention Alice Huang by name in the message, but linked his infidelity to “the national security concerns raised in news reports.” “Nvidia’s Board of Directors has initiated an independent investigation. I support the investigation and will cooperate fully. I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America’s national security. I am proud and grateful to be an American,” Huang wrote. Nvidia shares slid over 5% the following day. An Nvidia spokesperson denied that this relationship was something out of the ordinary. “Jensen’s interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected. Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year,” Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo said. He added that “if the U.S. government believes that any person is a threat to American industry, it would let us know.” U.S. officials circulated a secret memo among policymakers that warned that Megaspeed’s Alice Huang, who had a relationship with Jensen Huang, was a spy for China’s Ministry of State Security. This memo was not public knowledge until it was later reported by the New York Times. Secretary of State Marco Rubio supervised the drafting of the memo. Around the same time, per the New York Times’ report , U.S. President Donald Trump was briefed about intelligence findings that possible Chinese spy Alice Huang had formed a close relationship with Jensen Huang. Trump did not act on this information. The Nvidia CEO, an ally of Trump , has repeatedly advocated for the U.S. government to let Nvidia expand its business in China. Megaspeed, a neocloud that used Nvidia chips, had been renting computing power to Chinese internet giant Alibaba and other Chinese companies, the Times reported. A Commerce Department official who had visited Megaspeed’s data center in Malaysia in 2024 had found a hoard of Nvidia equipment that was still packed in boxes and the concern was that this equipment was being directly shipped somewhere else, like China, rather than installed and sold as a cloud service. Jensen Huang had been spotted socializing with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang as early as 2024 in Taiwan, where the Nvidia CEO was born. These investigations into Megaspeed highlighted concerns about the degree to which Nvidia is able to track its chip exports. At the time, an Nvidia spokesperson told press that the company did not have “any reason to believe products had been diverted.” “NVIDIA visited multiple Megaspeed sites yet again earlier this week and confirmed what we previously observed — Megaspeed is running a small commercial cloud, like many other companies throughout the world, as allowed by U.S. export control rules,” the Nvidia spokesperson said at the time. The claims first surfaced in a New York Times report on October 29. They are unproven publicly, China rejects them, and Nvidia says nothing suggests its secrets were compromised. The story stretches back more than two years, to a US probe of one of Nvidia’s customers. It also lands as Nvidia leans harder into Europe: on October 13, Huang said in Paris that it would announce $2 billion in new European AI deals. Alice Huang, also reported as Huang Le, worked as an executive at Megaspeed. The Times reported that US officials believe she was an asset of China’s Ministry of State Security. The Financial Times reported that officials believed her task was to gather information on Huang, including by pushing him to argue for looser limits on chip exports to China. She has no relation to Jensen Huang. She has not commented publicly, and the FT said it could not reach her. Megaspeed was spun out of a Chinese gaming company in 2023. Trade data cited by the Times indicates that a Malaysia-linked company associated with Megaspeed bought at least $4.8 billion of Nvidia equipment between June 2024 and February 2026. Megaspeed has faced questions over whether chips were diverted to China. Nvidia says those claims were “thoroughly investigated and debunked” last year. “We trust that if we were the target of a genuine threat, the U.S. government would have notified us,” Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo said. Huang wrote to staff: “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.” He did not name the woman and said he would cooperate with the inquiry. Nvidia’s board said a committee of independent directors, assisted by outside counsel, will run it, and that it had “no reason to believe” national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised. Secretary of State Marco Rubio called the matter an “internal corporate matter.” One point is settled: Huang has confirmed the affair. The spying claims rest on reports citing US officials, and nothing public shows that Nvidia’s confidential information was compromised. Huang spent much of October pitching Europe. Nvidia puts its total European commitment at close to $10 billion and does not split it between equity stakes and infrastructure. In the same Paris speech, it flagged planned minority stakes in four French startups: Doctolib, Genesis AI, Pigment and Entalpic. Amounts were not disclosed. Nvidia’s European footprint goes well beyond those four. Trending Topics counted 26 European tech companies Nvidia has backed over three years, including Mistral AI, Wayve, Black Forest Labs, Nscale and ElevenLabs, plus 13 newly announced stakes. By the publication’s own extrapolation from PitchBook data, Nvidia’s commitments equal roughly a tenth of European tech venture funding in 2026, though check sizes are rarely disclosed. For European founders and investors, the worry is simple. A leadership crisis could slow Nvidia’s dealmaking, and tighter US scrutiny of its China ties could change how European governments see the company. The House chairs asked Huang to confirm by November 11 whether he will brief the committees on November 18, one day after Nvidia’s quarterly earnings. The board inquiry has no announced end date, and Washington has given no public sign of how the FBI’s interest affects Huang or Nvidia. Huang is one of AI’s best-known figures and has argued for keeping some chip sales to China open. The FT reported that he lobbied Trump earlier this year to allow exports of Nvidia’s H200 chip. The allegations could strengthen calls for tighter export controls and raise governance questions at a company closely tied to its CEO. Analyst Dan Ives expects Huang to stay for now but warned of a risk he could be removed, depending on what the board finds. Nvidia is also pushing into AI financing, including agreements with six asset managers to mobilise more than $500 billion in third-party capital for AI infrastructure . TFN has also covered Nvidia’s position in the AI chip market and how its dominance is being challenged. If the inquiry clears Huang, does Nvidia’s China exposure still leave it vulnerable in Washington? extraction.body: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is at the centre of a controversy that has moved well beyond his personal life. What began as reports of his close relationship with Alice Huang, suspected of spying for China, has developed into a wider national security and corporate governance issue. The controversy has drawn attention from US lawmakers, prompted an independent investigation by Nvidia's board and reportedly raised questions about Huang's future at the company. Here is how the events unfolded, from the initial investigations into a Singapore-based business to the latest developments surrounding the Nvidia chief. October 2025: Chip smuggling investigation The controversy has its roots in investigations into Megaspeed International, a Singapore-based AI infrastructure company and Nvidia customer. In October 2025, authorities in the US and Singapore began investigating the company over suspicions that it was helping Chinese businesses obtain Nvidia chips despite American export restrictions. According to reports, Megaspeed had been renting computing capacity to Chinese internet giant Alibaba and other companies. Concerns grew after a US Commerce Department official visiting one of its data centres in Malaysia in 2024 reportedly discovered Nvidia equipment still packed in boxes, raising questions about whether the hardware was being shipped elsewhere rather than deployed for cloud computing. Huang had also been seen socialising with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang in Taiwan as early as 2024. Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen, is not related to the Nvidia CEO. 2025: Trump reportedly briefed on Huang's relationship US President Donald Trump was reportedly briefed towards the end of 2025 about intelligence findings concerning Alice Huang and her relationship with the Nvidia chief. However, the president did not take action following the briefing, according to the New York Times. Huang has been an ally of Trump and has repeatedly argued that the US government should allow Nvidia to expand its business in China. May 2026: Secret memo raises concerns about suspected Chinese spy The matter took another turn in spring 2026 when a confidential memo circulated among Trump administration officials. The document reportedly identified Alice Huang as a suspected Chinese intelligence operative working for China's Ministry of State Security. According to reports, Secretary of State Marco Rubio supervised the preparation of the memo. It warned policymakers about her alleged relationship with Huang and the potential implications for American national security. October 29, 2026: Huang's relationship with Alice Huang becomes public The controversy became public when the New York Times reported that Jensen Huang had developed a close relationship with Alice Huang, who was already under investigation by American authorities. Nvidia pushed back against suggestions that their interactions were unusual. Company spokesperson John Rizzo said meetings with customers were part of Huang's responsibilities as chief executive, adding that he interacted with thousands of customer executives every year. He also said Nvidia would expect the US government to inform the company if it believed someone posed a threat to American industry. November 5, 2026: Republican lawmakers seek answers from Huang Three Republican committee chairmen asked Huang to attend a closed-door briefing with members of their committees. The lawmakers included John Moolenaar of the House Select Committee on China, Brian Mast of the House Foreign Affairs Committee and Rick Crawford of the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence. Their letter highlighted concerns about China's access to sensitive American technology and information. They said Congress needed to establish whether US national security had been compromised through potential Chinese infiltration. November 8, 2026: Huang apologises for affair as Nvidia, FDA launches investigation Huang addressed the controversy directly in a letter to Nvidia employees, admitting that he had been unfaithful to his wife and apologising to his family and colleagues. Although he did not identify Alice Huang by name, he acknowledged the national security concerns raised in media reports. Huang also confirmed that Nvidia's board had initiated an independent investigation, pledging to cooperate fully and reiterating his commitment to protecting the company and American national security. The admission had an immediate impact on investor sentiment, with Nvidia shares falling more than 5 per cent the following day. US President Donald Trump also weighed in on the controversy on November 8. Despite acknowledging that he did not know all the details, Trump described Huang as a 'fine person' and said he believed the Nvidia chief should remain in charge of the company. November 9-10, 2026: More about Alice Huang's business network Further reporting shed light on the business connections between Alice Huang, her family and Nvidia's chip supply chain. According to reports, Alice Huang and her family had established a network of businesses across China and Singapore to acquire Nvidia processors. One of these was Shanghai Century Litong, a Chinese company founded in 2023 that reportedly became an Nvidia-preferred cloud partner, giving it priority access to chips. The Information reported that the company had facilitated purchases worth $7.5 billion, including chips restricted under US export controls. Separately, Bloomberg reported that Nvidia's head lawyer, Tim Teter, had intervened during a 2025 US government investigation into suspected chip smuggling involving Megaspeed.

extraction.body: It’s a weird time to launch a new pair of smart glasses. These last few years, Meta has been the dominant player in pushing a fragile smart glasses resurgence. Unfortunately, its privacy reputation led to the “pervert glasses” moniker. Smart glasses have never been more unpopular. But in the past week, I’ve been demoing some new smart glasses from Samsung, Warby Parker, and Gentle Monster. All were made by Samsung and have Google’s Gemini built in via Android XR, Google’s platform for smart glasses and mixed-reality headsets. Pressing two fingers to my temple, Gemini starts translating each language seamlessly in real time. In another demo, a TV chef cooks a “monster pasta” recipe in Korean while people have a conversation behind me. This exact scenario tripped up the Meta Ray-Ban Display’s translation capabilities when I was on vacation. I don’t even have to specify the languages I need translated or, as with Meta’s glasses, download a specific language pair to translate. I asked Gemini to identify my video director, Owen Grove. Gemini told me it knew I was looking at a person, but it can’t identify him because of privacy protections. We pull up a picture of our editor-in-chief, Nilay Patel. There, too, Gemini said that for privacy reasons, it can’t identify a person from a photo either. But what’s striking here is that Google is making an active choice to take facial recognition completely off the table. The Warby Parker and Gentle Monster glasses have the customary privacy LED light that lights up whenever there’s an intent to save visual data. Like Meta’s glasses, there’ll be protections in place to disable the glasses if tampering is detected. However, when I sit down to chat with Juston Payne, Google’s senior director of product management for XR, he says Google intends to go much further than the LED light. “Somebody might come up with some solution [to tamper with privacy LEDs] that our algorithms can’t detect, so then the question becomes: So what can we do?” says Payne. The glasses will only process audio from the glasses-wearer using beam-forming mics. Camera and mic access will also require opt-in permissions. [Image: This photo was taken on a Gentle Monster pair. Google could leave it at that, and Android XR would already have a leg up in the privacy discussion. But Payne says Google plans on using its entire platform to disincentivize glassholes. Google Shopping and Google Ads won’t allow sales or ads for accessories like lens covers for privacy LED lights. Google Play policies will prohibit third-party apps from enabling social livestreaming, real-time facial identification, or changing anything about how the LED light functions. This is less of a concern right now, but it’s a future-focused stance for other Android XR devices or even with devices like Xreal’s Aura glasses. It’s much more expansive than Meta’s more reactive approach so far. Granted, Meta doesn’t have its own app store or a computing platform quite like Android. This still underscores how much more Meta could’ve been doing all along. The one area Meta truly nailed with smart glasses has been style. The company, through its partnership with EssilorLuxottica, has over 100 combinations of frames and lenses. Samsung’s partnerships with Warby Parker and Gentle Monster aren’t too shabby to look at. Warby Parker has three designs and three colors: green, brown, and black. Gentle Monster has six frames — including two that are very Y2K — with bolder designs, colors, and tinted lens options. The Warby Parker collection starts at $395, while Gentle Monster starts at $449. Style-wise, I found both collections were fetching.

But the real problem isn’t just Meta — it’s that when I asked Google AI how to bypass this new security feature, its AI gave me a cheerful step-by-step DIY guide to becoming a creep. All I asked was a simple theoretical question, and Google’s algorithm practically handed me a soldering iron and a ski mask. Both its AI overview and Gemini quickly reveal that Meta’s update is going to be the first of a lot of times Zuck & Co. will be left playing an ongoing game of whack-a-mole with this problem. And given peeping tom Meta glasses mods are now a business , hackers and modders will view this as an obstacle course rather than a hard stop. So rather than just re-report the news you’ve been seeing, I want to go into what else needs to change to truly get rid of this peeping tom behavior once and for all — starting with AI companies putting a block on guiding people how to get around it, and extending into changing the laws to stomp it out. I won’t labor the point too much here, but while a software update and taking down modders' services on its own platform is a start, relying on a trillion-dollar tech company to police itself never quite works out the way you think. Much more needs to be done on a legislative and hardware level: I can’t lie, I do rather like wearing smart glasses for the convenience of their features. But that doesn’t make me blind to this massive problem, and rightly so, people are mad after reading the same stories of secret filming that I have. Meta’s update is essentially putting a better lock on the door of it all, but it ignores the fact that a crowd of people is still trying to kick the door down. Much like Nintendo Switch’s update that was supposed to stop piracy in 2018 or Apple’s software locks on third-party iPhone parts, hackers and modders will eventually find a new way around this. Maybe it’s wiring a tiny internal LED that tricks the camera into thinking the external light is on? That’s what Gemini said anyway (yikes)! Put simply, tech fixes are temporary, but true privacy protection will only happen when society decides that secret recording is socially unacceptable. And that starts with the law treating the creators and facilitators of this tech as criminals — not just innovative tinkerers or innocent content creators. relevantPassages.text: Meta just released an emergency update to stop creeps from disabling the recording light on its smart glasses.
But the real problem isn’t just Meta — it’s that when I asked Google AI how to bypass this new security feature, its AI gave me a cheerful step-by-step DIY guide to becoming a creep.
Unlock and manage exclusive Tom’s Guide member rewards.
Both its AI overview and Gemini quickly reveal that Meta’s update is going to be the first of a lot of times Zuck & Co. will be left playing an ongoing game of whack-a-mole with this problem.
And given peeping tom Meta glasses mods are now a business , hackers and modders will view this as an obstacle course rather than a hard stop.
He has previously written for Laptop Mag, Tom's Hardware, Kotaku, Stuff and BBC Science Focus.
In his spare time, you'll find Jason looking for good dogs to pet or thinking about eating pizza if he isn't already.
I can’t lie, I do rather like wearing smart glasses for the convenience of their features.
Meta's moves usurped by Google practically giving me a soldering iron and a ski mask

extraction.body: Meta has been flirting with retail for years now, however a Business Insider report maintains the company is finally looking to expand its retail footprint beyond its first and only brick-and-mortar location. Citing an internal communication, the report maintains Meta is looking to hire retail staff and roll out more physical stores, which are thought to go beyond the sort of pop-up locations the company experimented with late last year. It’s said the plans could mirror Apple’s retail strategy, although the communication seen by Business Insider is “not broadly known internally yet,” suggesting it’s still early days. While Meta’s latest pop-up in Los Angeles garnered a fair amount of press late last year, since 2016 the company has actually launched numerous pop-up stores in addition to partnering with retailers like Best Buy to offer demo spaces for its line of XR headsets. Beyond pop-ups, the company currently operates a single permanent Meta Store in Burlingame, California , which opened next to its Reality Labs campus in 2022. There, customers can demo Quest 3 and Quest 3S, as well as Ray-Ban Meta smart glasses. The biggest driver for the retail rollout is thought to be Ray-Ban Meta Glasses however, which are built in partnership with French-Italian eyewear conglomerate EssilorLuxottica. In 2024 alone, Meta sold more than 1 million units of its Ray-Ban Meta Glasses , making it what CEO Mark Zuckerberg called at the time “a great start.” Earlier this year, EssilorLuxottica CEO Francesco Milleri said the company had plans to ramp up production capacity to 10 million annual units by the end of 2026. Ray-Ban Meta Glasses, which pack in cameras for photos and video, as well as onboard Meta AI assistant and off-ear speakers, are already available in a number of styles and lens configurations, although that’s likely set to change. Notably, a report from Bloomberg in April alleged the company is aiming to introduce a number of new smart glasses , including a pair with built-in display and a sportier pair from EssilorLuxottica sub-brand Oakley. And the segment is heating up. Google showed off its own pair of smart glasses on stage at Google I/O earlier this month, announcing it’s partnering with eyewear companies Warby Parker and Gentle Monster to release multiple versions of its Android XR Glasses in the near future. Meanwhile, a report from earlier this month alleged Apple is also getting into the smart glasses segment too , as the Cupertino tech giant is reportedly now producing a smart glasses chip based on the low-energy processors used in Apple Watches, which is optimized for power efficiency and the ability to control multiple cameras.

sources.title: Google Has So Many New Smart Glasses Coming Soon. I Wore Them All - CNET
passages: This advanced AR glasses setup, known as Project Aura, is just one of three Google glasses products coming this year.

extraction.body: Google and Samsung’s glasses, left, and Google and Xreal’s Project Aura, right, are two parts of a new wave of Gemini-powered tech arriving this fall. I found myself facing a wall, talking to a smiling molecule that emerged from a vase. I had pinched my fingers over the very real vase, and now a very unreal molecule floated in front of me, googly eyes blinking, as it told me about its properties in ceramic material. This whole chat, AI-generated via Gemini , emerged as a hovering 3D graphic on glasses I was wearing. They were plugged into a phone-sized device running an app that was apparently coded on the fly in just days. This advanced AR glasses setup, known as Project Aura, is just one of three Google glasses products coming this year. And there’s more — also on deck are wireless AI glasses made with Samsung, Gentle Monster and Warby Parker , slated for the fall, ready to compete with Meta's Ray-Ban and Oakley smart glasses . I spent time with all of them, and even a prototype dual-display set of wireless glasses, at Google’s Mountain View campus. Back in December, I’d done a demo as well, but my latest deep dive showed me more, and better, things that all of these glasses can do. I was wowed. Will Google help make smart glasses feel more everyday and useful? Or solve how offputting and potentially threatening their cameras and AI tech make some people feel? My latest set of demos at Google’s campus, part of Google’s AI-centric I/O developer conference , convinced me that they could be the best smart glasses out there. They could even help redefine what smart glasses can be. And they’re the first glasses I’ve seen that really feel ready to work with the apps and services we have on phones already. In 2026 we’ve seen a flood of smart glasses , a category of product that most people don’t wear and many are increasingly wary of . But Google’s Gemini-powered glasses could change what’s possible more than nearly any other glasses I’ve seen so far. The reason, clearly, is the AI and software under the hood — and what Google’s doing to lay groundwork for where Apple is reportedly heading too. That’s even clearer to me now after meeting again with Google’s head of XR, Shahram Izadi, and Samsung’s Jay Kim, head of that company’s MX customer experience division. These are prototype glasses, with custom prescription inserts added for the demo, but these Samsung/Google glasses are lightweight and still have a display in one lens. I test-drove multiple versions of the smart glasses that Google and Samsung are releasing later this year. What I saw were still prototype models, but their more watch- and phone-connected features have more AI skills than Meta’s latest glasses. But they still don’t have prices yet, or even an official name. Called “Intelligent Eyewear” for now, the glasses will be given product names later on by Warby Parker, Gentle Monster and Samsung when they’re released this fall, according to Izadi, who spoke with me at Google’s headquarters. The glasses will all have cameras, microphones and embedded speakers like Meta’s line of smart glasses, and also will come in display-free and single-display versions. The always-on Gemini Live mode on these glasses could follow me around a room and describe plants or tell me how to play a board game. I’ve seen these tricks before. But Google’s advantage over Meta is how these AI tools relay back to apps already on phones, like Google Keep and Google Calendar. Or appear on watches. My room experiences using Gemini Live on the glasses, saved as a record in Google Keep on a connected phone. One of the Warby Parker glasses designs, which I didn’t get to try on, is coming this fall. These glasses feel lighter-weight than Meta’s Ray-Ban Displays: At 49 grams, they felt close to the heft of display-free Meta Ray-Bans. The two Warby Parker and Gentle Monster designs weren’t something I got to try yet, but the prototype pair I wore is meant to represent a similar size and comfort, and they felt good despite having a single display inside one lens. They’re definitely smaller than the equivalent, larger pair of display-enabled Ray-Ban Displays. The Gentle Monster frames have a distinctive look. Photos taken on the Samsung/Google glasses relayed instantly to the connected phone and smartwatch. WearOS watches could act as glasses viewfinders. Photos I took on the glasses popped up moments later on a Pixel Watch worn by one of Google’s team, showing off how a WearOS smartwatch could be a connected camera viewfinder. I tried taking a photo of the room with the glasses and adding Nano Banana effects: a David Lynch vibe and 1930s cartoon characters eating sushi. The image was updated in under a minute on the glasses, and it also popped up on the watch and the phone. Nano Banana’s Lynch-with-cartoon-with-sushi AI reinvention of a photo taken with the glasses. It showed up in-glasses, and on the phone shortly after. The glasses have a touchpad in one arm, which works with angle and double taps and swipes (single tap-hold for Gemini, double finger swipe for volume), and a camera shutter button on the top of one arm. They could also be controlled to some degree with a watch, although I didn’t get to try that. Watch gestures would help, especially since Google doesn’t have anything like Meta’s neural band yet. Google’s also working on dual-display glasses, which might not come until at least 2027. The prototypes I demoed again were notably heavier, and while I also tried this demo last year, this time the quality looked better for playing a Spider-Man clip converted to 3D by YouTube, and playing back 3D models that I could move with tilts and turns of my head, almost like augmented reality. Scrolling widgets moved by in 3D too. The dual-display model is still being finessed, and Izadi and Kim acknowledged that there’s no release timeframe yet. It’s next on deck: maybe next year or the year after. But Izadi expects dual, single and no-display glasses to be on sale together down the road, likely at a range of prices. Samsung’s and Google’s teams admit that the world of wearables is a challenge to figure out and that public apprehension about face tech and camera-enabled glasses is something that still needs to be figured out. Meta’s already faced multiple privacy problems and has muddy lines on its AI privacy policies . Google plans to go into more details on data privacy on its glasses at a fall event, says Izadi. “We’ve been doing a lot of thinking from the very beginning with these kinds of devices. Given the privacy aspects, you have to design with privacy in mind from the very, very beginning and leverage some of the standards that have been set in the AI world,” says Izadi, who adds that a bystander LED indicator, fraud detection for AI and other features are part of the glasses. The prototype glasses I tried run the same experiences as the upcoming Warby Parker and Gentle Monster models. I did my demos of all these glasses using custom inserts matched to my heavily myopic prescription, but Google and Samsung are confident that their range of all-day smart glasses with Warby Parker and Gentle Monster will support prescription ranges including my own, even in display-enabled models. “We are really going deep there,” says Izadi. “This is where some of the partnerships with the eyewear companies have been really important.” Izadi points to the display-enabled Even Realities G2 glasses that I’ve worn using my prescription as “existence proof” that they can be made. I hope so, because I plan to test out Google’s glasses as my everyday pair. Unlike Meta’s prescription support-limited Ray-Ban Displays , it looks like that could actually happen. Google's new Fitbit Air and Gemini-powered health coach, which I’m test driving now, already had me thinking about how fitness and health could be a part of the next wave of glasses. Izadi acknowledges that the glasses could access data like this and interconnect, just not right away. Xreal’s Project Aura supports hand tracking, and it works just like it does on VR headsets to pinch, scroll and control apps. Now let’s get back to that talking molecule demo that stunned me, which came courtesy of Google and Xreal’s Project Aura , one of the most fascinating products I’ve seen in a while. It’s not the first time I’ve tried it, but as Aura readies to launch later this year, this new batch of demos reminded me what amazed me back in December. In many ways, this glasses-plus-processor-puck combo delivers what a VR headset can do, and possibly more, in a little package that also works with your phone, laptop or Steam Deck . It doesn’t work with your phone directly. Instead, it has a processor puck that runs Android XR and Android apps, relaying this to glasses. It’s very much a living model of what Meta's Project Orion prototype AR glasses were going for two years ago when I tried them, but with hardware available now, and with hand tracking via cameras instead of using a gestural neural band like Meta has. Anyone who’s ever tried a pair of display-enabled tethered glasses, like those that Xreal or Viture or TCL sell, might know how good these “headphones for your eyes” can look. Project Aura is better, extending the field of view of its microOLED displays to 70 degrees, effectively enough to fill the glasses and not feel like you’re missing too much. Project Aura comes with its own travel case. The processor puck it uses is about the size of a phone. Aura, as I said last year, can do all the things Samsung’s 6-month-old Galaxy XR mixed reality headset can do — but in a smaller package. The phone-sized processor puck has a touchpad surface and fingerprint ID button, and runs all the Android apps and VR/AR-enabled experiences that Galaxy XR does. The glasses have cameras and depth sensors that can enable hand tracking, pinching and scrolling apps and playing VR games. But this little package can also run a lot of AI-intensive things. Gemini Live can run in conjunction with any app, but you can also plug in other devices via USB-C/DisplayPort. Connecting a Steam Deck meant I could play Hollow Knight on the glasses on the big screen, but also open a YouTube window and drag it next to the game in any position, watching run-throughs. It can support five apps open at once, or have Gemini Live watch my Steam Deck gameplay and give playthrough advice. I could connect an iPhone or a MacBook or any other device and layer it with Gemini Live analysis, too. Samsung and Google glasses on my eyes, Xreal Project Aura perched on my head. When will these concepts converge? Aura will go on sale as an actual product later this year, but at an unknown price. I expect it might be a more expensive product than I’d like, but it’s also truly a shrunken-down set of some of the same pieces that Vision Pro and Galaxy XR were aiming for, in a form I’m more likely to use on the go. It’s part dev kit, part portable VR replacement and preview of where AR glasses that connect with our phones could eventually evolve. Imagine the phone-sized processing puck that Aura uses being the phone in our pockets instead. Current phones can’t do it, but Aura feels like a preview of what’s possible.
