The phone-sized processor puck has a touchpad surface and fingerprint ID button, and runs all the Android apps and VR/AR-enabled experiences that Galaxy XR does. The glasses have cameras and depth sensors that can enable hand tracking, pinching and scrolling apps and playing VR games.

But this little package can also run a lot of AI-intensive things. Gemini Live can run in conjunction with any app, but you can also plug in other devices via USB-C/DisplayPort. Connecting a Steam Deck meant I could play Hollow Knight on the glasses on the big screen, but also open a YouTube window and drag it next to the game in any position, watching run-throughs. It can support five apps open at once, or have Gemini Live watch my Steam Deck gameplay and give playthrough advice. I could connect an iPhone or a MacBook or any other device and layer it with Gemini Live analysis, too.
Samsung and Google glasses on my eyes, Xreal Project Aura perched on my head. When will these concepts converge?

Aura will go on sale as an actual product later this year, but at an unknown price. I expect it might be a more expensive product than I’d like, but it’s also truly a shrunken-down set of some of the same pieces that Vision Pro and Galaxy XR were aiming for, in a form I’m more likely to use on the go. It’s part dev kit, part portable VR replacement and preview of where AR glasses that connect with our phones could eventually evolve.
Imagine the phone-sized processing puck that Aura uses being the phone in our pockets instead. Current phones can’t do it, but Aura feels like a preview of what’s possible.

extraction.body: It’s a weird time to launch a new pair of smart glasses. These last few years, Meta has been the dominant player in pushing a fragile smart glasses resurgence. Unfortunately, its privacy reputation led to the “pervert glasses” moniker. Smart glasses have never been more unpopular. But in the past week, I’ve been demoing some new smart glasses from Samsung, Warby Parker, and Gentle Monster. All were made by Samsung and have Google’s Gemini built in via Android XR, Google’s platform for smart glasses and mixed-reality headsets. Pressing two fingers to my temple, Gemini starts translating each language seamlessly in real time. In another demo, a TV chef cooks a “monster pasta” recipe in Korean while people have a conversation behind me. This exact scenario tripped up the Meta Ray-Ban Display’s translation capabilities when I was on vacation. I don’t even have to specify the languages I need translated or, as with Meta’s glasses, download a specific language pair to translate. I asked Gemini to identify my video director, Owen Grove. Gemini told me it knew I was looking at a person, but it can’t identify him because of privacy protections. We pull up a picture of our editor-in-chief, Nilay Patel. There, too, Gemini said that for privacy reasons, it can’t identify a person from a photo either. But what’s striking here is that Google is making an active choice to take facial recognition completely off the table. The Warby Parker and Gentle Monster glasses have the customary privacy LED light that lights up whenever there’s an intent to save visual data. Like Meta’s glasses, there’ll be protections in place to disable the glasses if tampering is detected. However, when I sit down to chat with Juston Payne, Google’s senior director of product management for XR, he says Google intends to go much further than the LED light. “Somebody might come up with some solution [to tamper with privacy LEDs] that our algorithms can’t detect, so then the question becomes: So what can we do?” says Payne. The glasses will only process audio from the glasses-wearer using beam-forming mics. Camera and mic access will also require opt-in permissions. [Image: This photo was taken on a Gentle Monster pair. Google could leave it at that, and Android XR would already have a leg up in the privacy discussion. But Payne says Google plans on using its entire platform to disincentivize glassholes. Google Shopping and Google Ads won’t allow sales or ads for accessories like lens covers for privacy LED lights. Google Play policies will prohibit third-party apps from enabling social livestreaming, real-time facial identification, or changing anything about how the LED light functions. This is less of a concern right now, but it’s a future-focused stance for other Android XR devices or even with devices like Xreal’s Aura glasses. It’s much more expansive than Meta’s more reactive approach so far. Granted, Meta doesn’t have its own app store or a computing platform quite like Android. This still underscores how much more Meta could’ve been doing all along. The one area Meta truly nailed with smart glasses has been style. The company, through its partnership with EssilorLuxottica, has over 100 combinations of frames and lenses. Samsung’s partnerships with Warby Parker and Gentle Monster aren’t too shabby to look at. Warby Parker has three designs and three colors: green, brown, and black. Gentle Monster has six frames — including two that are very Y2K — with bolder designs, colors, and tinted lens options. The Warby Parker collection starts at $395, while Gentle Monster starts at $449. Style-wise, I found both collections were fetching.

Samsung’s partnerships with Warby Parker and Gentle Monster aren’t too shabby to look at.
Warby Parker has three designs and three colors: green, brown, and black.
Gentle Monster has six frames — including two that are very Y2K — with bolder designs, colors, and tinted lens options.
The Warby Parker collection starts at $395, while Gentle Monster starts at $449.
Style-wise, I found both collections were fetching.
extraction.headline: I tried Google’s AI glasses and Meta’s finally got real competition
extraction.description: The Android XR experience is better thanks to Gemini, Google’s privacy protections are more proactive, and Warby Parker and Gentle Monster add style.

relevantPassages.text: All were made by Samsung and have Google’s Gemini built in via Android XR, Google’s platform for smart glasses and mixed-reality headsets.
I don’t even have to specify the languages I need translated or, as with Meta’s glasses, download a specific language pair to translate.
However, when I sit down to chat with Juston Payne, Google’s senior director of product management for XR, he says Google intends to go much further than the LED light.
These last few years, Meta has been the dominant player in pushing a fragile smart glasses resurgence.
It’s much more expansive than Meta’s more reactive approach so far.
But what’s striking here is that Google is making an active choice to take facial recognition completely off the table.
Google could leave it at that, and Android XR would already have a leg up in the privacy discussion.
But Payne says Google plans on using its entire platform to disincentivize glassholes.
Granted, Meta doesn’t have its own app store or a computing platform quite like Android.
This still underscores how much more Meta could’ve been doing all along.

extraction.body: Meta has been flirting with retail for years now, however a Business Insider report maintains the company is finally looking to expand its retail footprint beyond its first and only brick-and-mortar location. Citing an internal communication, the report maintains Meta is looking to hire retail staff and roll out more physical stores, which are thought to go beyond the sort of pop-up locations the company experimented with late last year. It’s said the plans could mirror Apple’s retail strategy, although the communication seen by Business Insider is “not broadly known internally yet,” suggesting it’s still early days. While Meta’s latest pop-up in Los Angeles garnered a fair amount of press late last year, since 2016 the company has actually launched numerous pop-up stores in addition to partnering with retailers like Best Buy to offer demo spaces for its line of XR headsets. Beyond pop-ups, the company currently operates a single permanent Meta Store in Burlingame, California , which opened next to its Reality Labs campus in 2022. There, customers can demo Quest 3 and Quest 3S, as well as Ray-Ban Meta smart glasses. The biggest driver for the retail rollout is thought to be Ray-Ban Meta Glasses however, which are built in partnership with French-Italian eyewear conglomerate EssilorLuxottica. In 2024 alone, Meta sold more than 1 million units of its Ray-Ban Meta Glasses , making it what CEO Mark Zuckerberg called at the time “a great start.” Earlier this year, EssilorLuxottica CEO Francesco Milleri said the company had plans to ramp up production capacity to 10 million annual units by the end of 2026. Ray-Ban Meta Glasses, which pack in cameras for photos and video, as well as onboard Meta AI assistant and off-ear speakers, are already available in a number of styles and lens configurations, although that’s likely set to change. Notably, a report from Bloomberg in April alleged the company is aiming to introduce a number of new smart glasses , including a pair with built-in display and a sportier pair from EssilorLuxottica sub-brand Oakley. And the segment is heating up. Google showed off its own pair of smart glasses on stage at Google I/O earlier this month, announcing it’s partnering with eyewear companies Warby Parker and Gentle Monster to release multiple versions of its Android XR Glasses in the near future. Meanwhile, a report from earlier this month alleged Apple is also getting into the smart glasses segment too , as the Cupertino tech giant is reportedly now producing a smart glasses chip based on the low-energy processors used in Apple Watches, which is optimized for power efficiency and the ability to control multiple cameras.

extraction.body: Google and Samsung’s glasses, left, and Google and Xreal’s Project Aura, right, are two parts of a new wave of Gemini-powered tech arriving this fall. I found myself facing a wall, talking to a smiling molecule that emerged from a vase. I had pinched my fingers over the very real vase, and now a very unreal molecule floated in front of me, googly eyes blinking, as it told me about its properties in ceramic material. This whole chat, AI-generated via Gemini , emerged as a hovering 3D graphic on glasses I was wearing. They were plugged into a phone-sized device running an app that was apparently coded on the fly in just days. This advanced AR glasses setup, known as Project Aura, is just one of three Google glasses products coming this year. And there’s more — also on deck are wireless AI glasses made with Samsung, Gentle Monster and Warby Parker , slated for the fall, ready to compete with Meta's Ray-Ban and Oakley smart glasses . I spent time with all of them, and even a prototype dual-display set of wireless glasses, at Google’s Mountain View campus. Back in December, I’d done a demo as well, but my latest deep dive showed me more, and better, things that all of these glasses can do. I was wowed. Will Google help make smart glasses feel more everyday and useful? Or solve how offputting and potentially threatening their cameras and AI tech make some people feel? My latest set of demos at Google’s campus, part of Google’s AI-centric I/O developer conference , convinced me that they could be the best smart glasses out there. They could even help redefine what smart glasses can be. And they’re the first glasses I’ve seen that really feel ready to work with the apps and services we have on phones already. In 2026 we’ve seen a flood of smart glasses , a category of product that most people don’t wear and many are increasingly wary of . But Google’s Gemini-powered glasses could change what’s possible more than nearly any other glasses I’ve seen so far. The reason, clearly, is the AI and software under the hood — and what Google’s doing to lay groundwork for where Apple is reportedly heading too. That’s even clearer to me now after meeting again with Google’s head of XR, Shahram Izadi, and Samsung’s Jay Kim, head of that company’s MX customer experience division. These are prototype glasses, with custom prescription inserts added for the demo, but these Samsung/Google glasses are lightweight and still have a display in one lens. I test-drove multiple versions of the smart glasses that Google and Samsung are releasing later this year. What I saw were still prototype models, but their more watch- and phone-connected features have more AI skills than Meta’s latest glasses. extraction.body: Exclusive: Ed Miliband says sci-fi scenarios of destruction ‘now regular occurrences’, as he prepares to address Cop31 The national security of all countries is at risk from the climate crisis, as “science fiction” scenarios of widespread destruction are already coming true and economic shocks from fossil fuels are now the norm rather than the exception, the UK’s foreign secretary is to warn world leaders gathered in Turkey . Ed Miliband will tell the Cop31 UN climate summit on Wednesday that security and defence objectives are the new “frontier” of climate action, because the rapid heating of the planet will lead to food shortages, widespread economic disruption, migration and conflict. “National security is the next frontier of the fight for climate action; the scenarios once of science fiction are now regular occurrences in the daily news,” Miliband told the Guardian before his speech to world leaders and governments in Antalya . “We should be clear that climate breakdown is one of the greatest national security threats we face . Food security, threats to infrastructure, and population movements [are resulting from the climate crisis],” he said. In a veiled swipe at the Conservatives and Reform UK, which want to scrap efforts to cut greenhouse gas emissions, he added: “Those who seek to stick their heads in the sand on climate are putting our national security at risk.” Miliband arrived in Turkey on Tuesday evening for the two-day leaders’ summit segment on Wednesday and Thursday of the fortnight-long Cop31 talks, which started on Monday. Andy Burnham, the UK prime minister, is expected to travel on Wednesday for a series of bilateral meetings with fellow world leaders on Thursday. Anthony Albanese, the prime minister of Australia, and the Turkish president, Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, will open the leaders’ summit segment on Wednesday. There will also be speeches by the UN secretary general, António Guterres, President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva of Brazil, which hosted last year’s Cop, and the prime minister of Ethiopia, Abiy Ahmed, who will host next year’s meeting. However, several heads of leading countries are skipping this year’s Cop , including China’s Xi Jinping, India’s Narendra Modi, France’s Emmanuel Macron and Germany’s Friedrich Merz. The European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, will attend. Miliband will argue that the world must now face the consequences of failures to cut carbon emissions over the past three decades. “It is a disaster for people and the planet, and we must reckon with its implications,” he will tell audiences at Cop31 on Wednesday. “It will drive hardship and insecurity for billions of people.” He will note that an “overshoot” of the crucial threshold of 1.5C of global heating above preindustrial levels, is now inevitable, as temperatures have exceeded that level for two years and are unlikely to subside significantly. This “overshoot” requires stronger policies to ensure heating does not accelerate, and to seek ways of returning temperatures to safer levels in decades to come. Fossil fuel shocks, such as the soaring oil price seen this year after the start of the Iran war, which has led to rampant inflation and interest rate rises from central banks in an effort to control it, will wreak further harm, according to Miliband. He told the Guardian: “A new era of global insecurity means fossil fuel shocks are now the norm – the fossil fuel rollercoaster is here to stay. First Russia, now Iran, next others, have identified global chokepoints and systemic overreliance [on fossil fuels] and the vulnerability of countries around the world that they expose.” He said the only answer was to “double down” on measures to cut greenhouse gas emissions and build resilience to the effects of extreme weather. “Next year will be the year of climate fightback, as governments, movements and communities across the world step up to defend our shared home.” Miliband will call for more investment in clean energy and efforts to use it for transport and heating, as well as urgent action to cut methane, a powerful greenhouse gas, and protect and expand forests. However, Burnham’s government is under fire in the UK for a series of recent and looming policy interventions that campaigners say will push the country off-track from its target of net zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050, and set a poor example to the rest of the world. The government plans to weaken a mandate for carmakers to ensure more of their vehicles are electric by 2030, and has given the green light to a new gasfield, Jackdaw, in the North Sea, while considering licensing a new oilfield, Rosebank , west of Shetland.

extraction.body: Exclusive: Ed Miliband says sci-fi scenarios of destruction ‘now regular occurrences’, as he prepares to address Cop31 The national security of all countries is at risk from the climate crisis, as “science fiction” scenarios of widespread destruction are already coming true and economic shocks from fossil fuels are now the norm rather than the exception, the UK’s foreign secretary is to warn world leaders gathered in Turkey . Ed Miliband will tell the Cop31 UN climate summit on Wednesday that security and defence objectives are the new “frontier” of climate action, because the rapid heating of the planet will lead to food shortages, widespread economic disruption, migration and conflict. “National security is the next frontier of the fight for climate action; the scenarios once of science fiction are now regular occurrences in the daily news,” Miliband told the Guardian before his speech to world leaders and governments in Antalya . “We should be clear that climate breakdown is one of the greatest national security threats we face . Food security, threats to infrastructure, and population movements [are resulting from the climate crisis],” he said. In a veiled swipe at the Conservatives and Reform UK, which want to scrap efforts to cut greenhouse gas emissions, he added: “Those who seek to stick their heads in the sand on climate are putting our national security at risk.” Miliband arrived in Turkey on Tuesday evening for the two-day leaders’ summit segment on Wednesday and Thursday of the fortnight-long Cop31 talks, which started on Monday. Andy Burnham, the UK prime minister, is expected to travel on Wednesday for a series of bilateral meetings with fellow world leaders on Thursday. Anthony Albanese, the prime minister of Australia, and the Turkish president, Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, will open the leaders’ summit segment on Wednesday. There will also be speeches by the UN secretary general, António Guterres, President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva of Brazil, which hosted last year’s Cop, and the prime minister of Ethiopia, Abiy Ahmed, who will host next year’s meeting. However, several heads of leading countries are skipping this year’s Cop , including China’s Xi Jinping, India’s Narendra Modi, France’s Emmanuel Macron and Germany’s Friedrich Merz. The European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, will attend. Miliband will argue that the world must now face the consequences of failures to cut carbon emissions over the past three decades. “It is a disaster for people and the planet, and we must reckon with its implications,” he will tell audiences at Cop31 on Wednesday. “It will drive hardship and insecurity for billions of people.” He will note that an “overshoot” of the crucial threshold of 1.5C of global heating above preindustrial levels, is now inevitable, as temperatures have exceeded that level for two years and are unlikely to subside significantly. This “overshoot” requires stronger policies to ensure heating does not accelerate, and to seek ways of returning temperatures to safer levels in decades to come. Fossil fuel shocks, such as the soaring oil price seen this year after the start of the Iran war, which has led to rampant inflation and interest rate rises from central banks in an effort to control it, will wreak further harm, according to Miliband. He told the Guardian: “A new era of global insecurity means fossil fuel shocks are now the norm – the fossil fuel rollercoaster is here to stay. First Russia, now Iran, next others, have identified global chokepoints and systemic overreliance [on fossil fuels] and the vulnerability of countries around the world that they expose.” He said the only answer was to “double down” on measures to cut greenhouse gas emissions and build resilience to the effects of extreme weather. “Next year will be the year of climate fightback, as governments, movements and communities across the world step up to defend our shared home.” Miliband will call for more investment in clean energy and efforts to use it for transport and heating, as well as urgent action to cut methane, a powerful greenhouse gas, and protect and expand forests. However, Burnham’s government is under fire in the UK for a series of recent and looming policy interventions that campaigners say will push the country off-track from its target of net zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050, and set a poor example to the rest of the world. The government plans to weaken a mandate for carmakers to ensure more of their vehicles are electric by 2030, and has given the green light to a new gasfield, Jackdaw, in the North Sea, while considering licensing a new oilfield, Rosebank , west of Shetland.

candidates.policy: Single canonical evidence pack for downstream writer, claim-verification and editorial stages. Downstream stages must not silently replace or expand factual evidence outside this pack.

sources.title: Exclusive-PLA-linked Chinese university bought Nvidia H200 chips despite US blacklist, records show - Yahoo! Finance Canada
passages: BEIJING, Nov 11 (Reuters) - A Chinese university with deep ties to the People's Liberation Army bought Nvidia's powerful H200 AI chips last month despite being on a US export blacklist, procurement records show, highlighting gaps in Washington's efforts to curb China's access to advanced technology.
Shenzhen University bought three H100 processors, another high-end Nvidia AI chip banned by the US, for ‌769,800 yuan in September.
Wuhan University of Technology bought a server containing an H100 chip for ​355,000 yuan in June and four A100 chips in a ​separate 344,000 yuan purchase, the records show.

A Reuters review of 26 Chinese procurement and corporate records from ​this ​year found universities and research institutions buying US-restricted Nvidia chips or renting access to Nvidia-powered computing services that use such chips through domestic ​suppliers.
It also rented access to servers containing eight Nvidia A100 chips and eight A800 chips.
The A100 and A800 are banned from export to all Chinese entities, though the H200 is the most advanced of those cited in Northwestern Polytechnical's procurement records.
The US Commerce ⁠Department added the university to its trade blacklist, known as the Entity List, in 2001 over its alleged involvement in missile-proliferation activities and military research.

The January licensing rules also require safeguards to prevent blacklisted entities and military end-users from remotely accessing chips exported under the policy, which covers H200 processors and less advanced models.
Last week, Reuters reported that small quantities of H200 ​chips had reached China through indirect routes while Beijing withheld approval for large-scale imports.
The chips were purchased for its management school from Shaanxi Bosuan Network Technology rather than directly from Nvidia, the record shows.
The universities named in the ‌records did not respond to requests for comment.

Wuhan University of Technology bought a server containing an H100 chip for ​355,000 yuan in June and four A100 chips in a ​separate 344,000 yuan purchase, the records show. A Reuters review of 26 Chinese procurement and corporate records from ​this ​year found universities and research institutions buying US-restricted Nvidia chips or renting access to Nvidia-powered computing services that use such chips through domestic ​suppliers. It also rented access to servers containing eight Nvidia A100 chips and eight A800 chips. The A100 and A800 are banned from export to all Chinese entities, though the H200 is the most advanced of those cited in Northwestern Polytechnical's procurement records. The US Commerce ⁠Department added the university to its trade blacklist, known as the Entity List, in 2001 over its alleged involvement in missile-proliferation activities and military research. The January licensing rules also require safeguards to prevent blacklisted entities and military end-users from remotely accessing chips exported under the policy, which covers H200 processors and less advanced models. Last week, Reuters reported that small quantities of H200 ​chips had reached China through indirect routes while Beijing withheld approval for large-scale imports. The chips were purchased for its management school from Shaanxi Bosuan Network Technology rather than directly from Nvidia, the record shows. The universities named in the ‌records did not respond to requests for comment.

extraction.body: BEIJING, Nov 11 (Reuters) - A Chinese university with deep ties to the People's Liberation Army bought Nvidia's powerful H200 AI chips last month despite being on a US export blacklist, procurement records show, highlighting gaps in Washington's efforts to curb China's access to advanced technology. The findings come as Nvidia and its CEO Jensen Huang face mounting scrutiny in Washington over his lobbying for looser restrictions on ‌sales of AI chips to China, following reports alleging he was targeted by a Chinese spying operation. Huang has argued that continued US sales to China would preserve American technological leadership and keep Chinese customers reliant on ‌US technology. But some US lawmakers say access to Nvidia's most powerful AI chips can speed China's development of AI systems for weapons design, intelligence analysis and military modernisation. Both Democrats and Republicans in Congress have urged stronger controls on China's access to advanced AI chips, such as chip-tracking requirements and greater ​congressional oversight of exports. Three Republican congressional committee chairmen have requested a briefing with Huang on November 18 over his reported contacts with an alleged Chinese intelligence operative. Northwestern Polytechnical University, a member of China's "Seven Sons of National Defense" group of elite defence-focused universities, bought two H200 chips last month for 874,700 yuan ($123,000), according to an October 21 procurement record on its website. The chips were purchased for its management school from Shaanxi Bosuan Network Technology rather than directly from Nvidia, the record shows. The H200 is among Nvidia's most capable chips for training and running advanced AI systems and is subject to US export licence approvals, which are normally denied for blacklisted institutions such as Northwestern Polytechnical. Northwestern Polytechnical also bought access this year to H200 chips and other powerful Nvidia AI processors through five ‌contracts for rented computing capacity from Chinese companies, procurement records show. Reuters is reporting the ⁠chip purchases and computing contracts for the first time. Northwestern Polytechnical, Nvidia and the US Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security, which oversees export controls, did not respond to requests for comment. Reuters could not determine contact details for Shaanxi Bosuan Network Technology. Based in the northwestern city of Xian, Northwestern Polytechnical conducts research related to military aircraft, missiles and satellites. The US Commerce ⁠Department added the university to its trade blacklist, known as the Entity List, in 2001 over its alleged involvement in missile-proliferation activities and military research. It tightened the restrictions in 2019, making licences for exports of controlled US technology to the university subject to a policy of denial in most circumstances. Northwestern Polytechnical's purchases show how Chinese institutions with military ties continue to obtain US AI computing power through domestic suppliers, either by buying chips outright or renting access to servers containing them. A Reuters review of 26 Chinese procurement and corporate records from ​this ​year found universities and research institutions buying US-restricted Nvidia chips or renting access to Nvidia-powered computing services that use such chips through domestic ​suppliers. Several had close links to China's defence industry or military research. The universities named in the ‌records did not respond to requests for comment. US President Donald Trump's administration began allowing some H200 exports to China on a case-by-case basis in January. But that policy did not lift the separate restrictions applying to Entity List organisations such as Northwestern Polytechnical. The January licensing rules also require safeguards to prevent blacklisted entities and military end-users from remotely accessing chips exported under the policy, which covers H200 processors and less advanced models. In addition to the management school's outright purchase of the two H200 chips, procurement records show the university's cybersecurity school awarded two seven-month contracts in January for access to servers containing eight H200 chips each. The contracts, worth 441,700 yuan and 441,000 yuan, covered fine-tuning AI models and reinforcement-learning training. It also rented access to servers containing eight Nvidia A100 chips and eight A800 chips. The A100 and A800 are banned from export to all Chinese entities, though the H200 is the most advanced of those cited in Northwestern Polytechnical's procurement records. In April, another ‌university institute bought computing services requiring at least 24 A100 chips in a 375,000 yuan contract for structural and fluid-dynamics simulations. The awards went ​to several little-known Chinese technology suppliers. The records offered scant information about where the processors originated or where the rented servers operated. Under Chinese law, ​public procurement agencies must verify that suppliers can fulfil orders before announcing winning bidders and signing contracts. The ​procurement records show a wider market for restricted Nvidia AI chips and computing services at Chinese universities. Shenzhen University bought three H100 processors, another high-end Nvidia AI chip banned by the US, for ‌769,800 yuan in September. Wuhan University of Technology bought a server containing an H100 chip for ​355,000 yuan in June and four A100 chips in a ​separate 344,000 yuan purchase, the records show. Beihang University, another of the Seven Sons of National Defense universities, bought four A800 processors for 489,000 yuan in April. Beihang has close ties to China's aerospace and defence industries and conducts research for military aviation and space programmes. Two government procurement announcements in July and September named suppliers selected to provide computing services using Nvidia H800 and A800 chips restricted from export to China to the University of Chinese ​Academy of Sciences. One listed H800 access at 10 yuan per chip-hour. A separate January ‌procurement award named a supplier of six A100 chips worth 484,800 yuan for a Shenzhen-based public institution. Reuters has previously reported that Chinese institutions acquired restricted Nvidia chips embedded in servers made by Super Micro Computer, ​Dell and Gigabyte through domestic resellers. Reuters has also documented an underground market in China for restricted Nvidia chips sourced from overseas inventories and third-country intermediaries. Last week, Reuters reported that small quantities of H200 ​chips had reached China through indirect routes while Beijing withheld approval for large-scale imports. (Reporting by Eduardo Baptista; Editing by Jamie Freed)

sources.title: PLA-Linked Chinese University Buys Nvidia H200 AI Chips Despite US Blacklist
passages: A Chinese university with close links to the country’s military has purchased two of Nvidia’s powerful H200 artificial intelligence (AI) chips despite being on a US export blacklist, Reuters reported.
Why Is The Chinese University On US Blacklist?

Reuters reviewed 26 Chinese procurement and corporate records from this year and found instances of universities and research institutions purchasing US-restricted Nvidia chips or renting access to computing services powered by them through domestic suppliers.

Nvidia, Chinese University Yet To Respond Reuters said Northwestern Polytechnical University, Nvidia and the US Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security, which oversees export controls, did not respond to requests for comment.

Huang has argued that allowing American companies to continue selling AI chips to China would help preserve US technological leadership while keeping Chinese customers dependent on American technology.
The university also rented computing capacity from servers containing eight Nvidia A100 chips and eight A800 chips.
In another instance, a university institute in April purchased computing services requiring at least 24 A100 chips under a contract worth 375,000 yuan.
According to Reuters, the latest purchase is not the only instance of the university obtaining access to Nvidia’s restricted processors.
The licensing framework also requires safeguards to prevent blacklisted institutions and military end-users from remotely accessing chips exported under the policy.
The purchases come amid growing scrutiny in Washington over Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s efforts to secure greater access to the Chinese market.
The transaction highlights how Chinese institutions with military connections may continue accessing advanced American computing technology despite Washington’s export restrictions.
The H200 is among Nvidia’s most powerful processors for developing and running advanced AI systems.
Exports of the chips to restricted institutions require US government approval, with licence applications for blacklisted entities such as Northwestern Polytechnical generally subject to denial.
US Restrictions On Nvidia Chip Exports To China The administration of US President Donald Trump began allowing certain H200 exports to China on a case-by-case basis in January.

coreStoryFacts.text: BEIJING, Nov 11 (Reuters) - A Chinese university with deep ties to the People's Liberation Army bought Nvidia's powerful H200 AI chips last month despite being on a US export blacklist, procurement records show, highlighting gaps in Washington's efforts to curb China's access to advanced technology.
Shenzhen University bought three H100 processors, another high-end Nvidia AI chip banned by the US, for ‌769,800 yuan in September.
Wuhan University of Technology bought a server containing an H100 chip for ​355,000 yuan in June and four A100 chips in a ​separate 344,000 yuan purchase, the records show.

A Reuters review of 26 Chinese procurement and corporate records from ​this ​year found universities and research institutions buying US-restricted Nvidia chips or renting access to Nvidia-powered computing services that use such chips through domestic ​suppliers.
It also rented access to servers containing eight Nvidia A100 chips and eight A800 chips.
The A100 and A800 are banned from export to all Chinese entities, though the H200 is the most advanced of those cited in Northwestern Polytechnical's procurement records.
The US Commerce ⁠Department added the university to its trade blacklist, known as the Entity List, in 2001 over its alleged involvement in missile-proliferation activities and military research.

The January licensing rules also require safeguards to prevent blacklisted entities and military end-users from remotely accessing chips exported under the policy, which covers H200 processors and less advanced models.
Last week, Reuters reported that small quantities of H200 ​chips had reached China through indirect routes while Beijing withheld approval for large-scale imports.
The chips were purchased for its management school from Shaanxi Bosuan Network Technology rather than directly from Nvidia, the record shows.
The universities named in the ‌records did not respond to requests for comment.

A Chinese university with close links to the country’s military has purchased two of Nvidia’s powerful H200 artificial intelligence (AI) chips despite being on a US export blacklist, Reuters reported.
Why Is The Chinese University On US Blacklist?

Reuters reviewed 26 Chinese procurement and corporate records from this year and found instances of universities and research institutions purchasing US-restricted Nvidia chips or renting access to computing services powered by them through domestic suppliers.

Nvidia, Chinese University Yet To Respond Reuters said Northwestern Polytechnical University, Nvidia and the US Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security, which oversees export controls, did not respond to requests for comment.

Huang has argued that allowing American companies to continue selling AI chips to China would help preserve US technological leadership while keeping Chinese customers dependent on American technology.
The university also rented computing capacity from servers containing eight Nvidia A100 chips and eight A800 chips.
In another instance, a university institute in April purchased computing services requiring at least 24 A100 chips under a contract worth 375,000 yuan.
According to Reuters, the latest purchase is not the only instance of the university obtaining access to Nvidia’s restricted processors.
The licensing framework also requires safeguards to prevent blacklisted institutions and military end-users from remotely accessing chips exported under the policy.
The purchases come amid growing scrutiny in Washington over Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s efforts to secure greater access to the Chinese market.
The transaction highlights how Chinese institutions with military connections may continue accessing advanced American computing technology despite Washington’s export restrictions.
The H200 is among Nvidia’s most powerful processors for developing and running advanced AI systems.
Exports of the chips to restricted institutions require US government approval, with licence applications for blacklisted entities such as Northwestern Polytechnical generally subject to denial.

extraction.body: BEIJING, Nov 11 (Reuters) - A Chinese university with deep ties to the People's Liberation Army bought Nvidia's powerful H200 AI chips last month despite being on a US export blacklist, procurement records show, highlighting gaps in Washington's efforts to curb China's access to advanced technology. The findings come as Nvidia and its CEO Jensen Huang face mounting scrutiny in Washington over his lobbying for looser restrictions on ‌sales of AI chips to China, following reports alleging he was targeted by a Chinese spying operation. Huang has argued that continued US sales to China would preserve American technological leadership and keep Chinese customers reliant on ‌US technology. But some US lawmakers say access to Nvidia's most powerful AI chips can speed China's development of AI systems for weapons design, intelligence analysis and military modernisation. Both Democrats and Republicans in Congress have urged stronger controls on China's access to advanced AI chips, such as chip-tracking requirements and greater ​congressional oversight of exports. Three Republican congressional committee chairmen have requested a briefing with Huang on November 18 over his reported contacts with an alleged Chinese intelligence operative. Northwestern Polytechnical University, a member of China's "Seven Sons of National Defense" group of elite defence-focused universities, bought two H200 chips last month for 874,700 yuan ($123,000), according to an October 21 procurement record on its website. The chips were purchased for its management school from Shaanxi Bosuan Network Technology rather than directly from Nvidia, the record shows. The H200 is among Nvidia's most capable chips for training and running advanced AI systems and is subject to US export licence approvals, which are normally denied for blacklisted institutions such as Northwestern Polytechnical. Northwestern Polytechnical also bought access this year to H200 chips and other powerful Nvidia AI processors through five ‌contracts for rented computing capacity from Chinese companies, procurement records show. Reuters is reporting the ⁠chip purchases and computing contracts for the first time. Northwestern Polytechnical, Nvidia and the US Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security, which oversees export controls, did not respond to requests for comment. Reuters could not determine contact details for Shaanxi Bosuan Network Technology. Based in the northwestern city of Xian, Northwestern Polytechnical conducts research related to military aircraft, missiles and satellites. The US Commerce ⁠Department added the university to its trade blacklist, known as the Entity List, in 2001 over its alleged involvement in missile-proliferation activities and military research. It tightened the restrictions in 2019, making licences for exports of controlled US technology to the university subject to a policy of denial in most circumstances. Northwestern Polytechnical's purchases show how Chinese institutions with military ties continue to obtain US AI computing power through domestic suppliers, either by buying chips outright or renting access to servers containing them. A Reuters review of 26 Chinese procurement and corporate records from ​this ​year found universities and research institutions buying US-restricted Nvidia chips or renting access to Nvidia-powered computing services that use such chips through domestic ​suppliers. Several had close links to China's defence industry or military research. The universities named in the ‌records did not respond to requests for comment. US President Donald Trump's administration began allowing some H200 exports to China on a case-by-case basis in January. But that policy did not lift the separate restrictions applying to Entity List organisations such as Northwestern Polytechnical. The January licensing rules also require safeguards to prevent blacklisted entities and military end-users from remotely accessing chips exported under the policy, which covers H200 processors and less advanced models. In addition to the management school's outright purchase of the two H200 chips, procurement records show the university's cybersecurity school awarded two seven-month contracts in January for access to servers containing eight H200 chips each. The contracts, worth 441,700 yuan and 441,000 yuan, covered fine-tuning AI models and reinforcement-learning training. It also rented access to servers containing eight Nvidia A100 chips and eight A800 chips. The A100 and A800 are banned from export to all Chinese entities, though the H200 is the most advanced of those cited in Northwestern Polytechnical's procurement records. In April, another ‌university institute bought computing services requiring at least 24 A100 chips in a 375,000 yuan contract for structural and fluid-dynamics simulations. The awards went ​to several little-known Chinese technology suppliers. The records offered scant information about where the processors originated or where the rented servers operated. Under Chinese law, ​public procurement agencies must verify that suppliers can fulfil orders before announcing winning bidders and signing contracts. The ​procurement records show a wider market for restricted Nvidia AI chips and computing services at Chinese universities. Shenzhen University bought three H100 processors, another high-end Nvidia AI chip banned by the US, for ‌769,800 yuan in September. Wuhan University of Technology bought a server containing an H100 chip for ​355,000 yuan in June and four A100 chips in a ​separate 344,000 yuan purchase, the records show. Beihang University, another of the Seven Sons of National Defense universities, bought four A800 processors for 489,000 yuan in April. Beihang has close ties to China's aerospace and defence industries and conducts research for military aviation and space programmes. Two government procurement announcements in July and September named suppliers selected to provide computing services using Nvidia H800 and A800 chips restricted from export to China to the University of Chinese ​Academy of Sciences. One listed H800 access at 10 yuan per chip-hour. A separate January ‌procurement award named a supplier of six A100 chips worth 484,800 yuan for a Shenzhen-based public institution. Reuters has previously reported that Chinese institutions acquired restricted Nvidia chips embedded in servers made by Super Micro Computer, ​Dell and Gigabyte through domestic resellers. Reuters has also documented an underground market in China for restricted Nvidia chips sourced from overseas inventories and third-country intermediaries. Last week, Reuters reported that small quantities of H200 ​chips had reached China through indirect routes while Beijing withheld approval for large-scale imports. (Reporting by Eduardo Baptista; Editing by Jamie Freed)

Reuters also could not find contact details for Shaanxi Bosuan Network Technology.Why is the Chinese university on the US blacklist?Northwestern Polytechnical University is based in Xi'an, a city in northwestern China.

It conducts research related to military aircraft, missiles and satellites, according to Reuters.The US Commerce Department added the university to its trade blacklist, officially known as the Entity List, in 2001.
The US government took this step over the university's alleged involvement in missile-proliferation activities and military research.Washington tightened the restrictions in 2019.
It made the export of controlled American technology to the university subject to a policy of denial in most cases.
This means companies generally cannot export restricted US technology to the institution without government approval.Reuters reviewed 26 Chinese procurement and corporate records from this year.

The review found that Chinese universities and research institutions were buying US-restricted Nvidia chips or renting access to computing services powered by these processors through Chinese suppliers.

Several of the institutions identified in the records had close links to China's defence industry or military research programmes.How did the university access restricted Nvidia chips?US President Donald Trump's administration started allowing some exports of Nvidia H200 chips to China on a case-by-case basis in January.

However, this policy did not remove the separate restrictions on organisations listed on the US Entity List, including Northwestern Polytechnical University.Apart from buying two H200 chips for its management school, Northwestern Polytechnical University's cybersecurity school also signed two contracts in January to rent computing services.
Each contract covered access to servers containing eight H200 chips for seven months.The two contracts were worth 441,700 yuan and 441,000 yuan.

The rented computing power was meant to be used for fine-tuning AI models and reinforcement-learning training, according to procurement records.The contracts were awarded to several relatively unknown Chinese technology companies.

However, the procurement records provided very little information about where the Nvidia processors originally came from or where the rented servers were located.Other Chinese universities also bought restricted Nvidia chipsShenzhen University purchased three Nvidia H100 processors in September for 769,800 yuan.

The H100 is another high-end Nvidia AI chip that the US has banned from export to China.Also read: US midterms could fuel AI trade as data centre curbs favour Microsoft, AmazonWuhan University of Technology purchased a server containing an Nvidia H100 chip for 355,000 yuan in June.

It also bought four Nvidia A100 chips in a separate transaction worth 344,000 yuan, according to procurement records.Beihang University, another member of China's Seven Sons of National Defense group, purchased four Nvidia A800 processors in April for 489,000 yuan.Two government procurement announcements published in July and September named companies selected to provide computing services using Nvidia H800 and A800 chips to the University of Chinese Academy of Sciences.

Both chip models are restricted from export to China.Restricted Nvidia chips are reaching China through other routesLast week, Reuters reported that small quantities of Nvidia H200 chips had already reached China through indirect routes.

However, Beijing had not approved large-scale imports of the processors.The latest purchases highlight the challenges facing Washington as it tries to stop advanced American AI chips from reaching Chinese institutions with military links.
Despite export restrictions, procurement records show that some Chinese universities are continuing to access these processors through domestic companies and rented computing services.

extraction.body: The United States has requested that Russia submit a proposal for a future security agreement with Europe, including steps to ease tensions on the continent. This marks a shift in US policy as part of broader efforts to end the war in Ukraine. According to sources cited by Axios, the United States has asked Russia to submit a new proposal for a future security agreement with Europe, which would include steps from the Russian side to ease tensions with the continent. The significance of this move, according to the site, lies in the fact that Russia has sought for years to conclude a European security agreement that would limit NATO's expansion and reduce its military presence in Eastern Europe. Although the US previously rejected these demands, it now appears open to them - one way or another - as part of a broader deal to end the war in Ukraine. However, many European governments view the US administration's approach with deep suspicion. A US official said that Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, envoys of President Donald Trump, will meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow today, Thursday, to renew this request. They also hope that Putin will allow European representatives to participate in the next round of peace talks between Russia and Ukraine. At the same time, according to "Axios," Kushner and Witkoff are expected to travel from Moscow to Dublin to meet with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky on the evening of the same Thursday. Tuesday and Wednesday saw the first meeting between Ukrainian and Russian officials with American mediators present since February, when these meetings were suspended due to the war on Iran. After Abu Dhabi Talks, Trump's Envoys Head to Moscow to Meet Putin In recent weeks, Witkoff and Kushner met with both Putin and Zelensky, creating a certain momentum. Putin agreed to resume peace talks and release US citizen Steven Hubbard, whom Russia had detained in 2022. Kushner and Witkoff, in cooperation with First Lady Melania Trump and her team, also succeeded in mediating a humanitarian ceasefire in the city of "Oleshki." The talks began in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday, with the participation of Witkoff, Kushner, and the commander of US forces in Europe, General Alexus Grynkewich, who took on the role of mediation between the Russian and Ukrainian sides. The two parties agreed on a prisoner exchange deal, which Kushner and Ukrainian negotiator David Arakhamia described as potentially "the largest since the outbreak of the war," according to "Axios." US and Ukrainian officials stated that the exact number of prisoners to be released would be determined during meetings scheduled for Thursday with Putin and Zelensky. Before and after the talks, the US and Ukrainian negotiating teams briefed a delegation comprising senior diplomats from Germany, the United Kingdom, France, Italy, the European Union, and NATO on the latest developments.

passages: Source : Scoop: U.S. asks Russia to propose new security agreement with Europe , by Barak Ravid , Axios , Nov 11, 2026
The request hands Moscow the opening text and leaves European governments waiting on Russian terms.
A security agreement between Russia and Europe would settle questions the war has kept open, including military posture across the continent and the sanctions tied to the conflict.
Each of those questions touches governments that have spent years rebuilding defenses and energy trade around the assumption of a hostile Russia.
The order of work now runs through Moscow, where officials must put terms on paper before Washington and European capitals can judge anything concrete.
Washington and its European allies then work from that text.
For now, the next concrete terms depend on what Moscow writes, and every capital watching the process will judge the request by the document Russia brings back.

extraction.body: The Trump administration asked Russia to draft a proposed security agreement with Europe as the first day of trilateral talks on Ukraine opened in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday. The request hands Moscow the opening text and leaves European governments waiting on Russian terms. The United States asked Russia to propose a new security agreement with Europe as the first day of trilateral talks on Ukraine opened in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday. President Trump's envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner attended the session with UAE Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Abdullah bin Zayed Al Nahyan. The request gives Moscow the pen. Russia writes the opening draft of any agreement that sets security terms between Russia and Europe. Washington and its European allies then work from that text. A first proposal anchors the range of positions at the table. The government that wrote it starts from its own language, while the recipients spend their capital pulling the draft toward their terms. That advantage is why the choice of who drafts carries as much weight as the content. The order of work now runs through Moscow, where officials must put terms on paper before Washington and European capitals can judge anything concrete. The request also separates two tracks. One track covers the war in Ukraine. The other covers the security relationship between Russia and Europe after the fighting stops. A security agreement between Russia and Europe would settle questions the war has kept open, including military posture across the continent and the sanctions tied to the conflict. Each of those questions touches governments that have spent years rebuilding defenses and energy trade around the assumption of a hostile Russia. Washington gains a test of Russian intent. A draft that European governments can negotiate shows a path toward a deal. A draft built on demands no European government could sign measures the distance the talks still have to travel. European capitals face a coordination task before that text arrives. Each government holds its own red lines on force levels and on the sanctions regime, and a Russian proposal will expose where those red lines differ. Divided European positions would give Moscow room to negotiate around the bloc instead of with it. The UAE holds a seat at the table. Abdullah bin Zayed's presence at the trilateral talks gives Abu Dhabi a direct role in diplomacy over European security, and the Gulf capital now hosts the channel where the parties to the war meet. Two U.S. envoys in the room at the same session signals the weight Washington puts on the process. The talks continue in Abu Dhabi. For now, the next concrete terms depend on what Moscow writes, and every capital watching the process will judge the request by the document Russia brings back. coreStoryFacts.text: Axios: US asks Russia to propose new security agreement with Europe
Trump’s envoys are expected to meet Putin in Moscow on Thursday.
According to Axios’ sources, they intend to raise the matter of a new Russia-Europe security agreement again.
One of the Axios interlocutors, however, said that its implementation will be possible only after the war in Ukraine ends.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy will not agree to the deal until he knows what the future holds for security guarantees.
That’s why the security issue is so important, the source explained.
The document should also specify what proportionate measures Russia is ready to take to ease tensions with European countries.
Witkoff and Kushner have added that European representatives should also participate in the talks so as to discuss such matters more seriously.

According to sources cited by Axios, the United States has asked Russia to submit a new proposal for a future security agreement with Europe, which would include steps from the Russian side to ease tensions with the continent.
This marks a shift in US policy as part of broader efforts to end the war in Ukraine.
The two parties agreed on a prisoner exchange deal, which Kushner and Ukrainian negotiator David Arakhamia described as potentially "the largest since the outbreak of the war," according to "Axios."
A US official said that Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, envoys of President Donald Trump, will meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow today, Thursday, to renew this request.
They also hope that Putin will allow European representatives to participate in the next round of peace talks between Russia and Ukraine.
In recent weeks, Witkoff and Kushner met with both Putin and Zelensky, creating a certain momentum.
Putin agreed to resume peace talks and release US citizen Steven Hubbard, whom Russia had detained in 2022.
Source : Scoop: U.S. asks Russia to propose new security agreement with Europe , by Barak Ravid , Axios , Nov 11, 2026
The request hands Moscow the opening text and leaves European governments waiting on Russian terms.
A security agreement between Russia and Europe would settle questions the war has kept open, including military posture across the continent and the sanctions tied to the conflict.
Each of those questions touches governments that have spent years rebuilding defenses and energy trade around the assumption of a hostile Russia.
The order of work now runs through Moscow, where officials must put terms on paper before Washington and European capitals can judge anything concrete.
Washington and its European allies then work from that text.
For now, the next concrete terms depend on what Moscow writes, and every capital watching the process will judge the request by the document Russia brings back.

The United States has asked Russia to prepare a new proposal for a future security agreement with Europe that would include steps by the Russian Federation aimed at reducing tensions on the continent.
Axios reports this, citing two informed sources, according to UNN .

This marks a shift in US policy as part of broader efforts to end the war in Ukraine. According to sources cited by Axios, the United States has asked Russia to submit a new proposal for a future security agreement with Europe, which would include steps from the Russian side to ease tensions with the continent. The significance of this move, according to the site, lies in the fact that Russia has sought for years to conclude a European security agreement that would limit NATO's expansion and reduce its military presence in Eastern Europe. Although the US previously rejected these demands, it now appears open to them - one way or another - as part of a broader deal to end the war in Ukraine. However, many European governments view the US administration's approach with deep suspicion. A US official said that Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, envoys of President Donald Trump, will meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow today, Thursday, to renew this request. They also hope that Putin will allow European representatives to participate in the next round of peace talks between Russia and Ukraine. At the same time, according to "Axios," Kushner and Witkoff are expected to travel from Moscow to Dublin to meet with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky on the evening of the same Thursday. Tuesday and Wednesday saw the first meeting between Ukrainian and Russian officials with American mediators present since February, when these meetings were suspended due to the war on Iran. After Abu Dhabi Talks, Trump's Envoys Head to Moscow to Meet Putin In recent weeks, Witkoff and Kushner met with both Putin and Zelensky, creating a certain momentum. Putin agreed to resume peace talks and release US citizen Steven Hubbard, whom Russia had detained in 2022. Kushner and Witkoff, in cooperation with First Lady Melania Trump and her team, also succeeded in mediating a humanitarian ceasefire in the city of "Oleshki." The talks began in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday, with the participation of Witkoff, Kushner, and the commander of US forces in Europe, General Alexus Grynkewich, who took on the role of mediation between the Russian and Ukrainian sides. The two parties agreed on a prisoner exchange deal, which Kushner and Ukrainian negotiator David Arakhamia described as potentially "the largest since the outbreak of the war," according to "Axios." US and Ukrainian officials stated that the exact number of prisoners to be released would be determined during meetings scheduled for Thursday with Putin and Zelensky. Before and after the talks, the US and Ukrainian negotiating teams briefed a delegation comprising senior diplomats from Germany, the United Kingdom, France, Italy, the European Union, and NATO on the latest developments.

passages: Source : Scoop: U.S. asks Russia to propose new security agreement with Europe , by Barak Ravid , Axios , Nov 11, 2026
The request hands Moscow the opening text and leaves European governments waiting on Russian terms.
A security agreement between Russia and Europe would settle questions the war has kept open, including military posture across the continent and the sanctions tied to the conflict.
Each of those questions touches governments that have spent years rebuilding defenses and energy trade around the assumption of a hostile Russia.
The order of work now runs through Moscow, where officials must put terms on paper before Washington and European capitals can judge anything concrete.
Washington and its European allies then work from that text.
For now, the next concrete terms depend on what Moscow writes, and every capital watching the process will judge the request by the document Russia brings back.

extraction.body: The Trump administration asked Russia to draft a proposed security agreement with Europe as the first day of trilateral talks on Ukraine opened in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday. The request hands Moscow the opening text and leaves European governments waiting on Russian terms. The United States asked Russia to propose a new security agreement with Europe as the first day of trilateral talks on Ukraine opened in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday. President Trump's envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner attended the session with UAE Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Abdullah bin Zayed Al Nahyan. The request gives Moscow the pen. Russia writes the opening draft of any agreement that sets security terms between Russia and Europe. Washington and its European allies then work from that text. A first proposal anchors the range of positions at the table. The government that wrote it starts from its own language, while the recipients spend their capital pulling the draft toward their terms. That advantage is why the choice of who drafts carries as much weight as the content. The order of work now runs through Moscow, where officials must put terms on paper before Washington and European capitals can judge anything concrete. The request also separates two tracks. One track covers the war in Ukraine. The other covers the security relationship between Russia and Europe after the fighting stops. A security agreement between Russia and Europe would settle questions the war has kept open, including military posture across the continent and the sanctions tied to the conflict. Each of those questions touches governments that have spent years rebuilding defenses and energy trade around the assumption of a hostile Russia. Washington gains a test of Russian intent. A draft that European governments can negotiate shows a path toward a deal. A draft built on demands no European government could sign measures the distance the talks still have to travel. European capitals face a coordination task before that text arrives. Each government holds its own red lines on force levels and on the sanctions regime, and a Russian proposal will expose where those red lines differ. Divided European positions would give Moscow room to negotiate around the bloc instead of with it. The UAE holds a seat at the table. Abdullah bin Zayed's presence at the trilateral talks gives Abu Dhabi a direct role in diplomacy over European security, and the Gulf capital now hosts the channel where the parties to the war meet. Two U.S. envoys in the room at the same session signals the weight Washington puts on the process. The talks continue in Abu Dhabi. For now, the next concrete terms depend on what Moscow writes, and every capital watching the process will judge the request by the document Russia brings back. The Trump administration seeks to negotiate simultaneously on a new security architecture between Europe and Russia and a peace agreement between Russia and Ukraine. However, according to a source familiar with the White House's position, the implementation of security arrangements will be possible only after an agreement to end the war has been concluded. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said ahead of the talks in Abu Dhabi that Europe would discuss a new security architecture only after the war in Ukraine ends. At the same time, according to two informed sources, European officials who were in Abu Dhabi this week agreed to work on both tracks in parallel. They emphasized, however, that final decisions on the architecture of European security would be made only after the war in Ukraine ends. The United States hopes that involving European representatives in the peace talks will encourage their governments to discuss and agree on a broader security agreement more actively before the war ends. "Zelensky will not agree to a deal until he knows what will happen next with the security guarantees; Putin also wants to know this. That is why the security issue is so important," the source said. The source added that the United States had made it clear to European countries that it would not agree to a security agreement with Russia unless Europe and Ukraine supported it. extraction.body: From recruitment of U.S. students to allegations surrounding Nvidia's Jensen Huang affair, reports point to one Chinese intelligence agency: the Ministry of State Security. The opaque government entity — which lacks an official website other than one supporting whistleblowers — has gained prominence with Beijing's growing emphasis on national security since 2023. The ministry oversees a range of provincial and national-level bureaus, including for intelligence gathering. While the MSS is not Beijing's only intelligence entity , the ministry has often been named in high-profile cases. Following hacking attempts on U.S. entities, the U.S. Treasury Department has in recent years sanctioned Chinese entities and individuals it alleges are affiliated with MSS. The Financial Times and The New York Times this month reported, citing sources, that U.S. government intelligence believe the MSS recruited businesswoman Alice Huang to gather information on Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. The two are not related. Jensen Huang admitted to an affair over the weekend, but it remains unclear whether any sensitive information was shared. The MSS earlier this year approached an individual who knows Alice Huang — to find out more information about her business and connections, The FT reported Wednesday, citing the person who was questioned . The FT report said it was unclear whether she was suspected of any wrongdoing, and that the MSS inquiry followed news of a Singapore probe into the company related to chip-smuggling allegations. China established its Ministry of State Security in 1983, in part to respond to risks from the country's new openness to foreigners after roughly three decades of tightly closed borders, according to research by Sheena Chestnut Greitens, an associate professor at the University of Texas-Austin. The MSS appears to have gained political influence under Chinese President Xi Jinping to "strengthen China's protections against espionage and foreign infiltration," Greitens wrote last year in China Leadership Monitor. The publication is run by Minxin Pei, non-resident senior fellow of the German Marshall Fund of the United States. In 2023 MSS launched a social media account on the WeChat messaging platform to increase public awareness of security issues. An article published Tuesday criticized an unidentified individual with a Chinese surname for fabricating allegations to a foreign organization that a colleague was a spy, after learning the colleague had secured an overseas posting that the individual had wanted. China's MSS is separate from China's Cyberspace Administration as well as the Ministry of Public Security, whose Minister Wang Xiaohong met with then-U.S. Secretary of State Antony Blinken. But the entities can work together. In September, State Security Minister Chen Yixin published a rare article in the cyberspace regulator's magazine about the need to improve artificial intelligence governance and prevent related security risks. The piece came out just as prominent U.S. AI company executives warned about the risks from uncontrolled development of the technology. Chen has met with his Vietnamese and Laotian counterparts in Beijing this year, according to official Chinese readouts. Beijing has increasingly targeted the U.S. tech sector in an attempt to narrow the gap in artificial intelligence capabilities, Matt Pearl, director of the strategic technologies program at the U.S.-based think tank Center for Strategic and International Studies, previously told CNBC. An MSS agent allegedly posed as a Stanford student for years in order to gather sensitive information, the Silicon Valley university's newspaper reported last year. The report also cited "Stanford experts on Chinese intelligence-gathering efforts who wished to remain anonymous" as saying the MSS used civilians as a way to "quietly extract the know-how behind American innovation." Other cases reinforce the trend, although not necessarily tied to MSS directly. In June, U.S.-based cybersecurity giant CrowdStrike said Chinese entities broadly accounted for more than half of state-sponsored intrusions targeting technology companies, especially their AI assets, in the 12 months through March 31. Brian Abbott, founder and CEO of U.S.-based start-up Agentiq Capital, previously told CNBC that he believed an employee he hired from China last year was an agent of Beijing who purposely altered code and website content to prevent the company from getting venture capital funding. The individual was dismissed earlier this year, Abbott said, and the company filed a complaint with the FBI. CNBC was unable to independently verify the allegation or a connection to MSS. Separately, U.S. investigators believed a former senior U.S. Federal Reserve official passed information about the central bank to a Chinese government spy . Got a confidential news tip? extraction.body: From recruitment of U.S. students to allegations surrounding Nvidia's Jensen Huang affair, reports point to one Chinese intelligence agency: the Ministry of State Security. The opaque government entity — which lacks an official website other than one supporting whistleblowers — has gained prominence with Beijing's growing emphasis on national security since 2023. The ministry oversees a range of provincial and national-level bureaus, including for intelligence gathering. While the MSS is not Beijing's only intelligence entity , the ministry has often been named in high-profile cases. Following hacking attempts on U.S. entities, the U.S. Treasury Department has in recent years sanctioned Chinese entities and individuals it alleges are affiliated with MSS. The Financial Times and The New York Times this month reported, citing sources, that U.S. government intelligence believe the MSS recruited businesswoman Alice Huang to gather information on Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. The two are not related. Jensen Huang admitted to an affair over the weekend, but it remains unclear whether any sensitive information was shared. The MSS earlier this year approached an individual who knows Alice Huang — to find out more information about her business and connections, The FT reported Wednesday, citing the person who was questioned . The FT report said it was unclear whether she was suspected of any wrongdoing, and that the MSS inquiry followed news of a Singapore probe into the company related to chip-smuggling allegations. China established its Ministry of State Security in 1983, in part to respond to risks from the country's new openness to foreigners after roughly three decades of tightly closed borders, according to research by Sheena Chestnut Greitens, an associate professor at the University of Texas-Austin. The MSS appears to have gained political influence under Chinese President Xi Jinping to "strengthen China's protections against espionage and foreign infiltration," Greitens wrote last year in China Leadership Monitor. The publication is run by Minxin Pei, non-resident senior fellow of the German Marshall Fund of the United States. In 2023 MSS launched a social media account on the WeChat messaging platform to increase public awareness of security issues. An article published Tuesday criticized an unidentified individual with a Chinese surname for fabricating allegations to a foreign organization that a colleague was a spy, after learning the colleague had secured an overseas posting that the individual had wanted. China's MSS is separate from China's Cyberspace Administration as well as the Ministry of Public Security, whose Minister Wang Xiaohong met with then-U.S. Secretary of State Antony Blinken. But the entities can work together. In September, State Security Minister Chen Yixin published a rare article in the cyberspace regulator's magazine about the need to improve artificial intelligence governance and prevent related security risks. The piece came out just as prominent U.S. AI company executives warned about the risks from uncontrolled development of the technology. Chen has met with his Vietnamese and Laotian counterparts in Beijing this year, according to official Chinese readouts. Beijing has increasingly targeted the U.S. tech sector in an attempt to narrow the gap in artificial intelligence capabilities, Matt Pearl, director of the strategic technologies program at the U.S.-based think tank Center for Strategic and International Studies, previously told CNBC. An MSS agent allegedly posed as a Stanford student for years in order to gather sensitive information, the Silicon Valley university's newspaper reported last year. The report also cited "Stanford experts on Chinese intelligence-gathering efforts who wished to remain anonymous" as saying the MSS used civilians as a way to "quietly extract the know-how behind American innovation." Other cases reinforce the trend, although not necessarily tied to MSS directly. In June, U.S.-based cybersecurity giant CrowdStrike said Chinese entities broadly accounted for more than half of state-sponsored intrusions targeting technology companies, especially their AI assets, in the 12 months through March 31. Brian Abbott, founder and CEO of U.S.-based start-up Agentiq Capital, previously told CNBC that he believed an employee he hired from China last year was an agent of Beijing who purposely altered code and website content to prevent the company from getting venture capital funding. The individual was dismissed earlier this year, Abbott said, and the company filed a complaint with the FBI. CNBC was unable to independently verify the allegation or a connection to MSS. Separately, U.S. investigators believed a former senior U.S. Federal Reserve official passed information about the central bank to a Chinese government spy . Got a confidential news tip? An article published Tuesday criticized an unidentified individual with a Chinese surname for fabricating allegations to a foreign organization that a colleague was a spy, after learning the colleague had secured an overseas posting that the individual had wanted.
China's MSS is separate from China's Cyberspace Administration as well as the Ministry of Public Security, whose Minister Wang Xiaohong met with then-U.S. Secretary of State Antony Blinken.

But the entities can work together. In September, State Security Minister Chen Yixin published a rare article in the cyberspace regulator's magazine about the need to improve artificial intelligence governance and prevent related security risks. The piece came out just as prominent U.S. AI company executives warned about the risks from uncontrolled development of the technology.
Chen has met with his Vietnamese and Laotian counterparts in Beijing this year, according to official Chinese readouts.

Beijing has increasingly targeted the U.S. tech sector in an attempt to narrow the gap in artificial intelligence capabilities, Matt Pearl, director of the strategic technologies program at the U.S.-based think tank Center for Strategic and International Studies, previously told CNBC.
An MSS agent allegedly posed as a Stanford student for years in order to gather sensitive information, the Silicon Valley university's newspaper reported last year.

The report also cited "Stanford experts on Chinese intelligence-gathering efforts who wished to remain anonymous" as saying the MSS used civilians as a way to "quietly extract the know-how behind American innovation."
Other cases reinforce the trend, although not necessarily tied to MSS directly.

In June, U.S.-based cybersecurity giant CrowdStrike said Chinese entities broadly accounted for more than half of state-sponsored intrusions targeting technology companies, especially their AI assets, in the 12 months through March 31.

Brian Abbott, founder and CEO of U.S.-based start-up Agentiq Capital, previously told CNBC that he believed an employee he hired from China last year was an agent of Beijing who purposely altered code and website content to prevent the company from getting venture capital funding.
The individual was dismissed earlier this year, Abbott said, and the company filed a complaint with the FBI. CNBC was unable to independently verify the allegation or a connection to MSS.
Separately, U.S. investigators believed a former senior U.S. Federal Reserve official passed information about the central bank to a Chinese government spy .
