extraction.body: Nvidia has long been closely tied to one person: Jensen Huang. The company’s co-founder and CEO has become its public face, remains deeply involved in daily operations and has played a central role in its rise during the artificial intelligence boom. But an investigation into an alleged foreign intelligence effort involving Huang is putting the spotlight on a question Nvidia has rarely had to confront, who could run the company without him?Huang acknowledged an affair in a message to employees on Sunday. Nvidia’s board has since launched an independent investigation into whether he was targeted by a foreign intelligence agency.The board has said it has confidence in Huang and has no reason to believe that national security or Nvidia’s secrets were compromised. The company has not announced any change to his role. Still, the investigation has brought renewed attention to Nvidia’s lack of a publicly identified successor. Its shares fell more than 4% on Monday, even as the broader market rallied sharply.Nvidia has no obvious replacement for Jensen HuangHuang’s influence at Nvidia goes well beyond his role as CEO. Around 60 executives report directly to him, and he remains closely involved in the company’s daily operations, as per a CNBC report. Nvidia’s flat management structure gives senior leaders direct access to him, but it also means there is no obvious second-in-command.“Jensen is Nvidia. Nvidia is Jensen,” Bernstein analyst Stacy Rasgon told CNBC. He described Huang as someone who runs the company from the top and effectively pulls the strings.Melius Research analysts have also said Nvidia has no clear successor. They had expected Huang to remain in the role for at least another 10 years.Huang owns just over 3% of Nvidia’s outstanding shares and is one of its 11 board members. His ownership stake is relatively small compared with those of some other high-profile technology founders.Nvidia’s financial filings do not specifically identify Huang as a key person. The company instead says it relies on the services of its longstanding executive team. Its filings also warn that a failure to plan for succession, transfer knowledge and manage leadership transitions could affect strategic planning, execution and long-term performance.135691857Could Jensen Huang’s children eventually lead NvidiaThe Nvidia's CEO two adult children, Madison and Spencer, both work at Nvidia and hold senior positions. Their roles have attracted attention amid questions about the company’s future leadership, although neither has been publicly named as a successor.Madison Huang is a senior director of product marketing and has mainly focused on Nvidia’s Omniverse software division. She has accompanied her father on business trips and is part of a small group known as “The Band,” which helps him prepare presentations, according to the Wall Street Journal report cited by the New York Post.Her brother, Spencer Huang, works as a product line manager in Nvidia’s robotics division. Both siblings earned more than $1.2 million in fiscal 2026, according to company disclosures cited by the newspaper.Reportedly Huang had told a close friend his dream was for one of his children to eventually run Nvidia. However, the company has not announced a family succession plan or indicated that either child is being prepared to take over as CEO.Huang has reportedly said he does not believe in succession planning.Alleged Chinese intelligence links put Huang under scrutinyThe investigation follows reports that a businesswoman named Alice Huang was suspected of having links to China’s Ministry of State Security.The New York Times first reported the allegation, citing people briefed on intelligence circulated in a memo among Trump administration officials in the spring. China rejected the claim as a smear.Alice Huang has worked at Singapore-based Megaspeed, a company that rents AI computing capacity to firms in Asia. Some US officials have raised concerns that Megaspeed may have been involved in smuggling Nvidia computing chips in violation of export controls. Those concerns have not been presented as proof of wrongdoing.Nvidia’s board said it launched the independent investigation after recent reports that its founder and CEO had been the target of a foreign intelligence effort. The company has maintained that it has confidence in Huang and sees no reason to believe its secrets or national security were compromised.The issue has also reached Washington. Lawmakers from both parties have called for briefings, while Democrats have pushed for investigations and new legislation to prevent advanced AI chips from supporting China’s military. Senator Elizabeth Warren raised the issue on X.135691349Nvidia has experienced executives but no easy replacementNvidia has senior executives with deep technical experience. Melius Research pointed to the company’s strengths in networking, hyperscale computing and high-performance computing, along with the expertise of Chief Technology Officer Michael Kagan and Chief Scientist Bill Dally.That experience could help keep the business running if Huang were unable to lead it. But Melius analysts said his energy and ability to maintain confidence in the AI trade would be difficult to replace.Partner and senior managing director at Yorkville Ives Dan Ives told the New York Post that the possibility of Huang being removed was a clear risk for investors. He said no one on Nvidia’s management team could step into the CEO role seamlessly, adding to the uncertainty surrounding the stock.Rothschild & Co. Redburn analyst Timm Schulze-Melander told CNBC that Huang could be forced to step aside if the investigation uncovered something materially more serious than an undisclosed relationship.135684584135687674

extraction.body: I’m sitting in front of my TV, puppy nuzzled up next to me, with four HomePods spread around my living room — two flanking my TV and one at either end of my couch — connected to the brand new Apple TV 4K. There hasn’t been an Apple surround sound system until now, and since it was announced, I was excited to try it out. And let me tell you, watching a pod race with an all-Apple audio setup is a whole lot of fun. Surround sound across four HomePods is one of the flagship features of the fourth-gen Apple TV 4K, which is out tomorrow for $300. It’s an expensive streaming box — double and in some cases quadruple the price of competing options — that tries to earn its place in your living room with premium and convenient new features: a powerful chip, lots of storage, a trackable remote, and lots of AI. If you’re deep in the Apple ecosystem and willing to splurge, the box is a solid choice. Compared to the 2022 model, it’s the same size, in the same finish, with the same number of ports (in the same configuration), showing the same interface, with the same HDR support. Where things are upgraded is largely on the inside: there’s a more powerful chip — the A19, which first showed up in the iPhone 17 — and 128GB of storage by default, which was previously an upgrade. The flip side is that there is no lower-cost 64GB model anymore, which is a shame because I don’t think most people need any more than that. There is one small quality of life change, though. It shows up in the Find My app on your phone, which does a great job of pinpointing the remote’s location; it can also make a sound when you can’t spot it. For a busy family like mine, this is great when one of us unintentionally brings the remote into the kitchen or bedroom (or when it’s buried in the cushions or pillows of the couch). Siri AI is here, too, though it’s also coming to second- and third-gen Apple TV 4Ks with tvOS 27.2. The new Siri can be pretty great, when it works, especially when using personal context to understand your requests. If Apple Intelligence is enabled on your iPhone or iPad and it’s on the same network as the Apple TV 4K, the box can recognize your voice and securely connect to your device to help personalize answers to you. But even when I clarified, “No, the show he messaged about yesterday,” Siri wasn’t able to find it. The Apple TV 4K also had trouble recognizing my voice from one moment to the next. I asked Siri about his competitor Marcus Samuelsson’s restaurant Hav & Mar — where it is, what type of food it serves, if it had any accolades (I found out it was awarded two stars by The New York Times), and when it would be open during an upcoming trip to New York City. My iPhone was still on the coffee table in front of me and on the Wi-Fi network, so the connection between it and the Apple TV 4K should have been strong enough for personal context to work without issue. My days of testing overlapped with the F1 Brazilian Grand Prix, which is broadcast on Apple TV. When live coverage of the race started, I asked Siri, “Play the F1 Brazilian Grand Prix.” Instead of the race, it started the music track “Hymn of the Racers” by the 1995 band F1. “Play the São Paulo F1 Grand Prix” played the song “São Paulo,” a collaboration between The Weeknd and Anitta. “Play Empire Strikes Back” started the Star Wars film on Disney Plus in seconds without having to mention the streaming service. But as it stands right now, Siri AI is still very much a beta project and needs some work and refinement to be consistently useful. You can talk to Siri using the Apple TV remote, but the new model also has far-field microphones built into the box, so you can talk aloud from anywhere. One of the concerns I had when it was announced that the Apple TV 4K was getting far-field mics was whether it would even be able to hear me while in my home theater stand, but that wasn’t an issue for me. Whenever I said “Hey Siri,” I could see it activated on my TV screen. Then there’s the new feature I had the most fun with: home theater surround. Apple added the ability to use two second-generation HomePods as a stereo pair (with Atmos) a couple of years ago. But as the hub for a home theater, the Apple TV 4K can now connect with four HomePods for a more immersive experience than what you can get with just your (almost certainly terrible) TV speakers. This is the setup I tested, with a pair of second-gen HomePods in front and a pair of HomePod Mini 2s in back. With all of the speakers connected to your Apple Home, each speaker emits a gentle pinging sound and a wash of pink noise that sounds like ocean waves, while a ripple of color moves across the TV screen corresponding to the color on the top of each HomePod to make sure positioning is correct. The speakers and the Apple TV 4K need to be a part of the same Apple Home and set up by the same user. My wife’s Apple account is the primary on our Apple Home, and even though we’re all a part of the same Apple family, when I set up the 4K TV with my account, it couldn’t see any of the speakers. This is not a major issue, but it can make setup more difficult. It’s not the same heart-rattling rumble a dedicated subwoofer can provide, but for a smaller space (and one with neighbors) it’s a good amount of bass. (I do hope Apple decides to make a standalone wireless subwoofer for the setup, though.) The front HomePods create a very convincing phantom center channel, making dialog sound like it’s coming right from the screen.

Apple added the ability to use two second-generation HomePods as a stereo pair (with Atmos) a couple of years ago.
But as the hub for a home theater, the Apple TV 4K can now connect with four HomePods for a more immersive experience than what you can get with just your (almost certainly terrible) TV speakers.
This is the setup I tested, with a pair of second-gen HomePods in front and a pair of HomePod Mini 2s in back.

With all of the speakers connected to your Apple Home, each speaker emits a gentle pinging sound and a wash of pink noise that sounds like ocean waves, while a ripple of color moves across the TV screen corresponding to the color on the top of each HomePod to make sure positioning is correct.
The speakers and the Apple TV 4K need to be a part of the same Apple Home and set up by the same user.
My wife’s Apple account is the primary on our Apple Home, and even though we’re all a part of the same Apple family, when I set up the 4K TV with my account, it couldn’t see any of the speakers.
This is not a major issue, but it can make setup more difficult.

It’s not the same heart-rattling rumble a dedicated subwoofer can provide, but for a smaller space (and one with neighbors) it’s a good amount of bass. (I do hope Apple decides to make a standalone wireless subwoofer for the setup, though.) The front HomePods create a very convincing phantom center channel, making dialog sound like it’s coming right from the screen.

Years after debuting in a crowded\u00a0 video streaming \u00a0market, Apple TV has found its niche by prioritizing quality over quantity. Just as Apple makes premium hardware and software, Apple TV offers premium original entertainment, including acclaimed shows, Oscar-winning films, and sophisticated sports offerings. Apple TV also has impressive premium features: Subscribers can stream shows in 4K, download content for offline viewing on iOS, and enjoy ad-free viewing. Still, its library is far more limited than you'd expect from an industry heavyweight, a problem that has become more noticeable as the service has grown more expensive. Editors' Choice winners Hulu , Netflix , and Peacock offer far more variety with their paid subscriptions. After its most recent price increase, Apple TV\u2014not to be confused with the Apple TV 4K media hub\u2014now costs $14.99 per month (you can save money by signing up for an annual subscription at $119.99). Apple offers a seven-day trial, but you must provide a payment method. Purchasers of new Apple devices get a year of free access. See our story on how to cancel your Apple TV subscription for detailed info on the cancellation process. You can also get Apple TV through one of several Apple One subscription bundles. The Individual plan includes Apple Arcade , Apple Music , Apple TV, and 50GB of iCloud storage for $21.95 per month. The $27.95-per-month Family tier boosts the iCloud storage to 200GB, and you can share the service with up to six family members.\u00a0The $39.95-per-month Premier option has Apple Fitness+, Apple News+, and 2TB of iCloud storage. Other video streaming services offer bundles, too. For example, you can pay $21.99 per month to get ESPN Select and the ad-supported versions of Disney+ and Hulu. Apple TV is now more expensive than many other top streaming services. Peacock starts at $8.99 per month, and Netflix starts at $8.99 per month. However, those are for the ad-supported tiers. Apple TV lacks commercials. Hulu and HBO Max 's ad-supported plans are less expensive than Apple's, at $11.99 and $10.99 per month, respectively. If you don't want to pay anything for your entertainment, our roundup of the best free video streaming services has options worth checking out. Our top free pick, Tubi , includes popular and offbeat network shows and movies. You can subscribe to Apple TV on iPhones, iPads , and Macs, \u00a0as well as via\u00a0tv.apple.com\u00a0in your web browser . Support extends to select LG, Samsung, and Sony smart TVs, as well as\u00a0 media streaming devices \u00a0that support the Apple TV app, such as Roku units. Apple now offers Apple TV apps for video game consoles and Android devices. Apple TV's original catalog includes Central Park , an animated musical series about a family who lives in the famous park; Little Voice , a romantic comedy; Mythic Quest , a video game-themed workplace comedy; Tehran , a co-produced spy-thriller revolving around the Israeli-Iranian conflict; Tiny World , a nature documentary series; and real-life tech drama WeCrashed . Apple promises new shows every month and new episodes every week. However, the total number of exclusive titles (shows and movies) is approximately 300. Netflix, on the other hand, has thousands of originals. You won't find fan favorites from broadcast networks or older shows to bolster Apple TV's offerings. Disney+, on the other hand, debuted with a staggering number of shows and movies from its vast catalog and a trove of 21st Century Fox content, in addition to the promise of new originals, such as Daredevil: Born Again . None of the other services we've reviewed depend entirely on brand-new original shows. HBO Max, Netflix, and Prime Video are the current leaders in producing original content. Among Amazon Prime's most notable shows are The Boys , Invincible , and Undone . HBO Max is highly regarded for its original shows, both past and present, including Game of Thrones , Lanterns , and The Wire . Netflix's blockbuster originals include Ozark, Squid Game, and Tiger King . All these services also offer non-original shows and movies. There's a clear value in the third-party content that pads out the vast catalogs of services like Hulu and Prime Video. Apple certainly has the resources to build up its library, but you should weigh the show and movie reviews before subscribing. For what it's worth, though, Apple TV originals like Ted Lasso and Severance have become acclaimed hits and genuine parts of current pop culture. Apple TV's library includes several documentaries and feature-length films, such as Beastie Boys Story , a documentary about the band directed by Spike Jonze; Greyhound , a WWII thriller starring Tom Hanks; and the comedy On The Rocks, which stars Bill Murray, Rashida Jones, and Marlon Wayans. Coda was the first streaming-funded film to win the Academy Award for Best Picture. Cinephiles should check out our roundup of the best movie streaming services for a more comprehensive selection. Look to\u00a0 The Criterion Channel , Filmatique,\u00a0 Mubi , or Ovid for good selections of classic and independent films. The service also offers sports. With Apple TV, you can stream F1 and Friday night\u00a0 MLB games , which are included with your existing subscription.\u00a0Multiview lets you watch multiple live games at once on Apple TV devices. I tested Apple TV on an iPhone . Apple TV's interface is clear and easy to navigate, with buttons for Watch Now, Library, and Search at the bottom. In the app, Apple Originals live in your Watch Now and Library tabs alongside HBO, Showtime , and Starz content. Note that you can't sort shows by network unless you are a subscriber. Tapping the standard cloud-plus-down-arrow icon next to an episode listing lets you download a show for offline viewing. Downloading a show may take several minutes, given the large file sizes. I watched an episode of The Morning Show over Wi-Fi, and the stream was generally sharp. I didn't like that you had to back out of the playback screen to the show listing to play the next episode. Note that Apple TV integrates with iOS's built-in parental control options, which makes things simple. Although Apple's marketing primarily highlights the Apple TV streaming service on devices that support the Apple TV app, you can still sign up for the service and watch shows in a web browser. In testing, Apple TV's web interface seems less polished than the Apple TV app. For instance, you can browse and watch only Apple TV content\u2014none of the other services that you can subscribe to via the Apple TV app appear here. The Apple TV website is elegant, but, like many of the service's shows, the experience is only surface-deep. All the shows appear in a wide list. Selecting a show brings you to a description page with the show's available episodes, cast information, and other Apple TV recommendations. You can also search for shows and add them to your Up Next list. Want to access account settings? Click the profile icon in the upper-right corner of the screen to view your billing information and change your subscription. Likewise, you can set up parental control restrictions, but note that these limitations are not profile-based; whatever settings you choose apply to everyone using that account on the web. I watched several episodes from The Morning Show , See , and For All Mankind in Chrome and Edge on a 1080p monitor , and the shows looked and sounded excellent. Playback controls are standard, with a draggable progress bar, forward and rewind buttons, a volume slider, and accessibility options in the lower-right corner. Apple TV offers many languages and closed-caption options, too. In addition, you can tweak the size and position of the text on the screen to make it more readable or fire up clearly labeled audio descriptions. Apple TV's technical features are impressive. As noted, subscribers can download content for offline viewing on iOS devices via the Apple TV app. HBO Max, Netflix, Prime Video, and Showtime also offer offline viewing. Hulu only offers this capability to subscribers of its premium ad-free tier. Apple TV users can share a subscription and stream with up to six people via Apple's Family Sharing feature. Apple says that Originals are \"subtitled and/or dubbed in nearly 40 languages, including Subtitles for the Deaf and Hard-of-Hearing (SDH) or closed captions,\" and that they support audio descriptions in eight languages. Netflix and Prime Video also support Audio Descriptions. This accessibility feature adds vocal narration to scenes to explain character movements, settings, and other on-screen actions that are not discernible from character dialogue. These accessibility options outclass those found in competitors. 4K streaming, HDR, Dolby Atmos, and Dolby Vision support round out the list of Apple TV's tech specs. Only select devices, such as the Apple TV 4K, support all these capabilities. Netflix and Prime Video offer some original shows in 4K, with sporadic support for Dolby Atmos and Dolby Vision . Since most launch shows support these high-end standards, the service, combined with the Apple TV 4K, could be very attractive to home theater enthusiasts. You should use a VPN to protect your internet traffic from nosy ISPs and malicious actors on a network. Many video streaming services block VPN traffic because a VPN can also let you spoof your location and potentially access location-restricted content. Apple plans to offer Apple TV in over 100 countries with the same content, so that shouldn't be an issue. I streamed content from Apple TV via the web with a desktop connected to a US-based Mullvad VPN server.

extraction.body: I’m sitting in front of my TV, puppy nuzzled up next to me, with four HomePods spread around my living room — two flanking my TV and one at either end of my couch — connected to the brand new Apple TV 4K. There hasn’t been an Apple surround sound system until now, and since it was announced, I was excited to try it out. And let me tell you, watching a pod race with an all-Apple audio setup is a whole lot of fun. Surround sound across four HomePods is one of the flagship features of the fourth-gen Apple TV 4K, which is out tomorrow for $300. It’s an expensive streaming box — double and in some cases quadruple the price of competing options — that tries to earn its place in your living room with premium and convenient new features: a powerful chip, lots of storage, a trackable remote, and lots of AI. If you’re deep in the Apple ecosystem and willing to splurge, the box is a solid choice. Compared to the 2022 model, it’s the same size, in the same finish, with the same number of ports (in the same configuration), showing the same interface, with the same HDR support. Where things are upgraded is largely on the inside: there’s a more powerful chip — the A19, which first showed up in the iPhone 17 — and 128GB of storage by default, which was previously an upgrade. The flip side is that there is no lower-cost 64GB model anymore, which is a shame because I don’t think most people need any more than that. There is one small quality of life change, though. It shows up in the Find My app on your phone, which does a great job of pinpointing the remote’s location; it can also make a sound when you can’t spot it. For a busy family like mine, this is great when one of us unintentionally brings the remote into the kitchen or bedroom (or when it’s buried in the cushions or pillows of the couch). Siri AI is here, too, though it’s also coming to second- and third-gen Apple TV 4Ks with tvOS 27.2. The new Siri can be pretty great, when it works, especially when using personal context to understand your requests. If Apple Intelligence is enabled on your iPhone or iPad and it’s on the same network as the Apple TV 4K, the box can recognize your voice and securely connect to your device to help personalize answers to you. But even when I clarified, “No, the show he messaged about yesterday,” Siri wasn’t able to find it. The Apple TV 4K also had trouble recognizing my voice from one moment to the next. I asked Siri about his competitor Marcus Samuelsson’s restaurant Hav & Mar — where it is, what type of food it serves, if it had any accolades (I found out it was awarded two stars by The New York Times), and when it would be open during an upcoming trip to New York City. My iPhone was still on the coffee table in front of me and on the Wi-Fi network, so the connection between it and the Apple TV 4K should have been strong enough for personal context to work without issue. My days of testing overlapped with the F1 Brazilian Grand Prix, which is broadcast on Apple TV. When live coverage of the race started, I asked Siri, “Play the F1 Brazilian Grand Prix.” Instead of the race, it started the music track “Hymn of the Racers” by the 1995 band F1. “Play the São Paulo F1 Grand Prix” played the song “São Paulo,” a collaboration between The Weeknd and Anitta. “Play Empire Strikes Back” started the Star Wars film on Disney Plus in seconds without having to mention the streaming service. But as it stands right now, Siri AI is still very much a beta project and needs some work and refinement to be consistently useful. You can talk to Siri using the Apple TV remote, but the new model also has far-field microphones built into the box, so you can talk aloud from anywhere. One of the concerns I had when it was announced that the Apple TV 4K was getting far-field mics was whether it would even be able to hear me while in my home theater stand, but that wasn’t an issue for me. Whenever I said “Hey Siri,” I could see it activated on my TV screen. Then there’s the new feature I had the most fun with: home theater surround. Apple added the ability to use two second-generation HomePods as a stereo pair (with Atmos) a couple of years ago. But as the hub for a home theater, the Apple TV 4K can now connect with four HomePods for a more immersive experience than what you can get with just your (almost certainly terrible) TV speakers. This is the setup I tested, with a pair of second-gen HomePods in front and a pair of HomePod Mini 2s in back. With all of the speakers connected to your Apple Home, each speaker emits a gentle pinging sound and a wash of pink noise that sounds like ocean waves, while a ripple of color moves across the TV screen corresponding to the color on the top of each HomePod to make sure positioning is correct. The speakers and the Apple TV 4K need to be a part of the same Apple Home and set up by the same user. My wife’s Apple account is the primary on our Apple Home, and even though we’re all a part of the same Apple family, when I set up the 4K TV with my account, it couldn’t see any of the speakers. This is not a major issue, but it can make setup more difficult. It’s not the same heart-rattling rumble a dedicated subwoofer can provide, but for a smaller space (and one with neighbors) it’s a good amount of bass. (I do hope Apple decides to make a standalone wireless subwoofer for the setup, though.) The front HomePods create a very convincing phantom center channel, making dialog sound like it’s coming right from the screen.

Now, I'm a senior writer, using the skills I acquired at Northwestern University to write about dating apps, meal kits, programming software, website builders, video streaming services, and video games. I was previously a senior editor at Geek.com and have written for The A.V. Club, Kotaku, and Paste Magazine. I'm the author of the gaming history book Video Game of the Year: A Year-by-Year Guide to the Best, Boldest, and Most Bizarre Games from Every Year Since 1977 , and the reason everything you know about Street Sharks is a lie. I use the newest Android and iOS smartphones for testing, but I currently use an iPhone 14 as my personal phone. I just hate that we gave up headphone jacks. I've always favored gaming laptops over desktops. On that note, I have a 16-inch HP Envy with an Intel Core i9-13900H CPU and Nvidia GeForce RTX 4060 GPU. No matter what machine I’m working on, an alarming amount of my personal and professional life revolves around cloud-synced Google Drive files. For food subscriptions, my household sticks with CookUnity and HelloFresh for meals. Video streaming is a bit more complicated. While there are too many services to list, we're subscribed to most of the major ones. These days, I find myself drawn to HBO Max's movies and shows, as well as Peacock's reality trash. I've been a lifelong Nintendo fan, and I sincerely believe the Nintendo Switch will go down as one of the best gaming consoles of all time. It has an unbelievable library of new and old games from Nintendo and third-party companies. The handheld/console hybrid approach makes playing games so much more flexible, a legacy that continues with the Nintendo Switch 2 and Valve’s Steam Deck. Apple TV also has impressive premium features: Subscribers can stream shows in 4K, download content for offline viewing on iOS, and enjoy ad-free viewing. Still, its library is far more limited than you'd expect from an industry heavyweight, a problem that has become more noticeable as the service has grown more expensive. Editors' Choice winners Hulu , Netflix , and Peacock offer far more variety with their paid subscriptions. After its most recent price increase, Apple TV\u2014not to be confused with the Apple TV 4K media hub\u2014now costs $14.99 per month (you can save money by signing up for an annual subscription at $119.99). Apple offers a seven-day trial, but you must provide a payment method. Purchasers of new Apple devices get a year of free access. The Apple TV 4K has been our favourite streamer and an Award-winner since its release in 2021, and now there is a new generation with a more powerful chip and smaller casework. With plenty of subtle upgrades across the board, from general usability improvements to a blazing-fast new processor inside, the new Apple TV 4K is already shaping up to be a nice upgrade over the last model – and did we mention that it's cheaper? In a surprisingly un-Apple move, the 3rd Generation Apple TV 4K is actually cheaper than the previous model . It starts at £149 / $130 / AU$219 for the 64GB model, or £169 / $150 / $250 for the 128GB model, which also adds an Ethernet connection. For reference, the previous generation model started at £169 / $179 / $249. The Apple TV 4K’s nearest competitor is the Amazon Fire TV Cube which costs £140 / $130 / AU$219. The Apple TV 4K’s price point puts it at the premium end of the market, as it’s double the price of the Amazon Fire TV Stick 4K and Google Chromecast with Google TV . Is it worth the extra money? Read on to find out. The Apple TV 4K retains the modest and boxy design of its predecessor, coming in a matte and glossy black combo finish. It’s embellished with an Apple logo on top, and you’ll find an HDMI 2.1 socket and a power connection on the rear, as well as an ethernet port if you opt for the more expensive model. While it may look almost identical to the previous generation, this Apple TV is actually a tad smaller and it's around the size of a trio of stacked CDs. The reduction in size is made possible because Apple’s engineers have opted for a fanless design this time around. The unit’s aesthetics are sleek and low-key enough to practically disappear into an entertainment set-up, and it can be easily tucked behind a TV if needed. The high-quality aluminium remote has hardly changed since the previous model. There is one difference, however, and that is a USB-C port replacing the Lightning connector. We’re just waiting on the iPhone and AirPods to ditch Lightning now so that we can charge all of our Apple gadgets with one cable. It now uses an A15 Bionic processor, the same one found in the iPhone 14 . It's joined by 4GB of RAM (up from 3GB last year), and the usability gains are noticeable as the TV 4K flies through menus and frankly refuses to stutter or glitch. It’s easy to navigate, and isn’t crammed with advertisements unlike Amazon ’s Fire OS platform; that being said it certainly guides you towards Apple’s services where it can, such as Apple TV+ and iTunes Movies. The powerful internal specs and HDMI 2.1 connection allow for 4K HDR streaming up to 60Hz, although there’s no word on 4K/120 quite yet. Why is this worth noting? Well, the Apple TV 4K can be used to access Apple Arcade and you can even connect a PS5, Xbox Series X or Nintendo Switch controller for a proper gameplay experience. Apple’s streaming box supports all the HDR formats of its predecessor including HDR10, HLG and Dolby Vision , however, Apple has added HDR10+ to the roster this year. This is of course a win for Samsung TV owners, as Samsung still refuses to include Dolby Vision on its sets. The Apple TV extends Dolby support into the audio department too, with Dolby Atmos as well as Apple’s own Spatial Audio platform for both movies, TV and music from Apple Music and Tidal . You can download a host of movie and TV streaming, music streaming and lifestyle apps via the App Store. You’ll find all the usual suspects here including Netflix , Disney Plus and Amazon Prime Video to name a few, as well as region-specific apps such as BBC iPlayer, All 4, ITVX, My 5 and Now in the UK and HBO Max , Peacock and Hulu in the US. It's not all about streaming here, as you can access iTunes to buy music, movies and TV shows to add to your digital library. extraction.body: AI agents are all the rage, but they’re not quite as capable as their purveyors would have you believe. Efforts to benchmark agents doing complex tasks show that they aren’t typically reliable enough to function without close supervision. LiveBench 2.0 shows Claude Fable 5.2 and ChatGPT-6 Astra succeeding on 82.9 and 75.6 out of 100 tasks, respectively, and an effort by the AI infrastructure company EON to test agents in a simulated corporate environment found the most successful model tested, Claude Opus 4.8, performed tasks at 76.8% accuracy. Now, a startup known as Plurai wants to boost those numbers with the same techniques that put self-driving cars on the street: Simulations using synthetic data based on a company’s own digital systems, meant to prepare models to tackle difficult edge cases. Co-founders Ilan Kadar and Elad Levi previously worked for Nexar, which develops autonomous driving technology. Kadar worked with Waymo to simulate and evaluate its end-to-end deep learning driving software. “The moment that we saw the wave of AI agents, we saw the same pattern: That it is very easy to build a demo, but [hard] to get something that will be reliable and cost effective,” Kadar told TechCrunch. “Since we saw the same pattern, the same pitch was that we want to build this simulation layer.” On Wednesday, the startup said it had raised $13 million in seed funding to make that happen. The round was led by Team8, with participation from U&I, Velocity, and Mercer. Like the end-to-end models trained to drive cars, AI agents are probabilistic systems operating in unpredictable environments. When pressed by customers, agents tasked with booking travel can ignore spending policies. Or, when tasked with querying one database, agents can reliably provide an answer, but combining information from multiple datasets tends to gum up the works. A long conversation with a customer service bot can overwhelm an agent with too much context and lead to wrong turns. To fix that, Plurai creates a digital twin of the company’s electronic systems, including the knowledge base and tools that an agent will have access to in production. It then maps all the possible flows of the agents and uses that graph to prepare the model with evaluations and fixes for possible edge cases. The platform works alongside existing agentic tools like Claude Code, Codex, Copilot, and Cursor. However, Kadar says the company’s real promise is using the data it gathers to post-train small, open-weight models tailored to individual customer needs. Tests performed in cooperation with Nvidia and Nebius showed the company’s models outperforming midtier frontier models at lower costs. “We can take a large language model, we can take the task, decompose it into a smaller task using the simulation, train [an open-weight] model, and using the simulation, verify that the quality is higher or comparable to the frontier model, and an order or two orders of magnitude cost reduction,” he said. Reah Miyara, a Google DeepMind researcher who backed Plurai as an angel investor, said the company’s edge comes from understanding failure modes in production, and generating synthetic data to tune models. As businesses try to optimize their AI expense, Plurai’s approach could prove a real advantage, since IT leaders are seeing that “frontier-capable models are out of distribution with my specific data, and the cost of these things isn’t sustainable in the long term,” Miyara said. Meanwhile, robots powered by AI models built for specific tasks are in the field right now, working for customers and gathering valuable real-world data. “My view is that no matter how smart OpenAI and Anthropic model will be — and they will be much smarter — they will not know your business and your policy,” Kadar said.

When pressed by customers, agents tasked with booking travel can ignore spending policies. Or, when tasked with querying one database, agents can reliably provide an answer, but combining information from multiple datasets tends to gum up the works. A long conversation with a customer service bot can overwhelm an agent with too much context and lead to wrong turns.

To fix that, Plurai creates a digital twin of the company’s electronic systems, including the knowledge base and tools that an agent will have access to in production. It then maps all the possible flows of the agents and uses that graph to prepare the model with evaluations and fixes for possible edge cases. The platform works alongside existing agentic tools like Claude Code, Codex, Copilot, and Cursor.

However, Kadar says the company’s real promise is using the data it gathers to post-train small, open-weight models tailored to individual customer needs. Tests performed in cooperation with Nvidia and Nebius showed the company’s models outperforming midtier frontier models at lower costs.

“We can take a large language model, we can take the task, decompose it into a smaller task using the simulation, train [an open-weight] model, and using the simulation, verify that the quality is higher or comparable to the frontier model, and an order or two orders of magnitude cost reduction,” he said.

Reah Miyara, a Google DeepMind researcher who backed Plurai as an angel investor, said the company’s edge comes from understanding failure modes in production, and generating synthetic data to tune models. As businesses try to optimize their AI expense, Plurai’s approach could prove a real advantage, since IT leaders are seeing that “frontier-capable models are out of distribution with my specific data, and the cost of these things isn’t sustainable in the long term,” Miyara said.

Plurai hopes analogies between AI agents in physical and digital environments can prove predictive: While powerful general AI models are imbuing robots with fascinating capabilities, they aren’t yet reliable enough to be deployed widely. Meanwhile, robots powered by AI models built for specific tasks are in the field right now, working for customers and gathering valuable real-world data.
“My view is that no matter how smart OpenAI and Anthropic model will be — and they will be much smarter — they will not know your business and your policy,” Kadar said.

IT Home, November 12: Apple has released a technical article today detailing its Secure Enclave security architecture in Apple Silicon chips, explaining how this system prevents raw audio and video data collected by the camera and microphone from being accessed by the operating system, applications, or even Apple itself.
Apple also manages memory access permissions through the Secure Page Table Monitor (SPTM), ensuring that the main operating system kernel cannot read data stored in Secure Exclaves’ dedicated memory.
Secure Exclaves are built around three key aspects: data isolation, controlled communication interfaces, and secure indication mechanisms.
In terms of communication, Apple developed a communication mechanism called Secure IPC, written in Swift, which restricts data exchange between components through predefined interfaces.

At the underlying technology level, Apple states that the microkernel of Secure Enclaves uses a capability-based mechanism to manage permissions; system components do not have default access to other components or hardware resources and can only interact after receiving explicit authorization.

extraction.body: IT Home, November 12: Apple has released a technical article today detailing its Secure Enclave security architecture in Apple Silicon chips, explaining how this system prevents raw audio and video data collected by the camera and microphone from being accessed by the operating system, applications, or even Apple itself. Apple's Security Engineering and Architecture (SEAR) team and Core OS team published an article titled "Secure Exclaves and Ambient Sensing" on the Apple Security Research blog on November 12, detailing the design principles, underlying architecture, and real-world applications of Secure Exclaves. Apple states that as devices become increasingly capable of perceiving their environment, cameras and microphones need to continuously process surrounding information. For example, devices must identify whether a user is nearby, detect specific voice commands, and determine if someone is currently using the device. These features require processing sensitive audio and video data, but this does not mean the device must continuously record or store this information. To this end, Apple has introduced Secure Exclaves, which process camera and microphone data in a separate, isolated execution environment. According to Apple, in environmental awareness mode, raw audio and video data are not transmitted to the main operating system, applications, or Apple itself, and are discarded after processing. The system only provides necessary metadata externally, such as whether specific sounds have been detected, whether a registered user has been identified, and the user’s location. Secure Exclaves are built around three key aspects: data isolation, controlled communication interfaces, and secure indication mechanisms. In terms of data isolation, Secure Exclaves operate in a processor execution environment separate from the main operating system and utilize Apple’s custom L4 microkernel. Apple also manages memory access permissions through the Secure Page Table Monitor (SPTM), ensuring that the main operating system kernel cannot read data stored in Secure Exclaves’ dedicated memory. In terms of communication, Apple developed a communication mechanism called Secure IPC, written in Swift, which restricts data exchange between components through predefined interfaces. Each sandbox can access only explicitly authorized resources, and only reviewed, necessary information is passed to the main operating system. For security purposes, Apple has designed a dedicated Exclave Indicator Controller to manage when camera and microphone data may leave the isolated environment. When an application requires full access to sensor data, the system must first ensure that the corresponding indicator light or on-screen prompt is displayed and has remained visible for the required duration before allowing data transmission. Apple also introduced the application of Secure Exclaves on HomeView. The device can recognize up to six registered users via its camera and microphone while determining whether users are near the device. The camera enclave detects faces and generates relevant data, while the microphone enclave processes audio information, which is then inferred through a dedicated neural network engine enclave queue. Ultimately, the system will only pass metadata such as user identity, location, and recognition confidence to the main operating system, not raw images or audio. The operating system can use this information to adjust the display content of features like Calendar, Messages, and Apple Music. IT Home notes that Secure Exclaves are also applied to the camera, microphone, and screen indicators on the iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max, and iPhone Duo, as well as the camera indicators on MacBook Neo and HomeView. Apple used the "Hey Siri" voice wake-up feature on the iPhone 18 Pro as an example to explain how this system works: the device first listens for the wake word using a low-power Always-On Processor (AOP); when a potential "Hey Siri" command is detected, the audio buffer is passed to the Audio Isolation Zone for processing, followed by a second round of recognition by the Siri Isolation Zone. Before confirming the wake word, the main operating system receives only a notification that Siri needs to be awakened, not the audio data. Audio transmission to the Siri service is permitted only after the user enters an active interaction state and the system completes the display of the microphone indicator and security checks. Apple explains that the screen indicator feature is not solely rendered by the operating system. For devices with a screen indicator, a dedicated display isolation zone checks the actual pixels displayed on the screen, including color, shape, duration, and brightness, to ensure the indicator is genuinely visible to users and to prevent malicious software from misleading users by hiding or falsifying the indicator. At the underlying technology level, Apple states that the microkernel of Secure Enclaves uses a capability-based mechanism to manage permissions; system components do not have default access to other components or hardware resources and can only interact after receiving explicit authorization. Apple has also performed formal verification on the microkernel, using mathematical methods to verify that the C language implementation conforms to predefined functional specifications, thereby uncovering low-level logic issues that traditional software testing may miss. However, Apple also emphasized that the current formal verification is being implemented incrementally and does not yet cover all parts of the microkernel.

passages: We believe Secure Exclaves are the most advanced architecture for ambient sensing in the industry, defining an ambitious new level of security and privacy for these use cases.
Some of the secure sensing workloads that run in Secure Exclaves need access to high-performance inference hardware to run demanding machine learning models.
To enable this, we extended the Apple Neural Engine (ANE) by adding isolated workload queues, like those we use in the SEP.
Memory filters protect those queues from being modified or accessed by the main OS, and switching from an isolated to a standard queue flushes any local storage to prevent information leaks.
Microkernel capabilities are used to control the IPC connections of every exclave.
By default, exclaves are unable to communicate or even refer to one another.
An exclave may only initiate IPC if it has an explicit capability to an IPC connection.
Next, Secure Exclaves must account for the other coprocessors and sensors connected to the Apple silicon fabric.
The coprocessor secure compartment is also built on top of the exclaves microkernel, maintaining security assurance continuity across the application processor and coprocessors.
This propagates the memory isolation property throughout the system.
Traditional inter-process communication (IPC) mechanisms are designed for maximum flexibility, providing open-ended interfaces that can be composed with arbitrary complexity when moving data.
For Secure Exclaves, we approached the problem from the opposite angle, and set out to design IPC primitives that could enable tightly restricted, completely predictable communication.
This capability relies on ambient sensing : using the microphone and camera to understand the surrounding environment and recognize an enrolled user’s voice and face.
Our goal is to keep ambient sensor data secure even against highly sophisticated attacks, while giving users a clear, reliable, and tamper-resistant signal whenever their sensors are fully active.

We also use them to protect the on-screen camera and microphone indicators used in iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max, and iPhone Duo, as well as the camera indicators in MacBook Neo and HomeView, improving security for our users across the board.
This allows each exclave to access only its own memory, providing an additional layer of protection.
This simple but powerful mechanism is applied to both memory isolation and IPC security, enabling us to build a secure system that contains no extraneous authority.
This rearchitecture not only hardened the entire system against certain kernel-level attacks, but also created the foundation for isolating Secure Exclave memory.

When moving from ambient sensing to a full, active sensor use case, such as a conversation with Siri or a FaceTime video session, the system must communicate to the user that it is now sharing broad access to the sensor with the app that has requested it.

extraction.body: We recently introduced HomeView, which can recognize up to six people to deliver a rich and personalized experience. This capability relies on ambient sensing : using the microphone and camera to understand the surrounding environment and recognize an enrolled user’s voice and face. We have always believed features like this must be designed from the ground up to protect user security and privacy, and are now taking these protections even further, with a new security architecture in Apple silicon that’s purpose-built for ambient sensing. This work both benefits our newest features and strengthens the security of features we already ship, such as “Hey Siri” detection. Our goal is to keep ambient sensor data secure even against highly sophisticated attacks, while giving users a clear, reliable, and tamper-resistant signal whenever their sensors are fully active. While ambient sensing relies on processing input from the camera or microphone, it must never record audio or video, nor expose it to the rest of the operating system. Instead, it must reduce the sensor stream to far simpler signals, such as whether a specific sound was detected or whether an enrolled user’s face or voice was recognized, while protecting the raw sensor data during processing and discarding it once complete. Hardwired LED sensor indicator lights are easy to understand and play an important role in privacy and security across our products, but aren’t suitable for ambient sensing use cases, because they would glow continuously. This would defeat the utility of the indicator, and prevent the user from distinguishing background sensing — such as a device listening for a “Hey Siri” invocation — from active audio and video recording. We set out instead to enable ambient sensing to run in a strongly isolated environment with the full power of the main application processor, with a precisely controlled interface into the rest of the system, and with a secure indication mechanism so the user is aware when audio or video data is allowed to leave the isolation boundary. To accomplish this, we have created Secure Exclaves : protected and compartmentalized runtimes used to process camera and microphone data separately from the rest of the system. Isolation features added across many core components of the silicon work in tandem to protect Secure Exclaves and keep them segregated from the rest of the system. Data that is processed and analyzed in a Secure Exclave cannot be accessed by the main operating system, apps, or Apple. We use Secure Exclaves to protect entirely new use cases, like person recognition on HomeView as well as Siri Recap and Live Rewind, as described here . We also use them to protect the on-screen camera and microphone indicators used in iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max, and iPhone Duo, as well as the camera indicators in MacBook Neo and HomeView, improving security for our users across the board. We believe Secure Exclaves are the most advanced architecture for ambient sensing in the industry, defining an ambitious new level of security and privacy for these use cases. To protect ambient sensing, we aimed to build a system that operated in two distinct modes: ambient mode and active mode, for both camera and microphone. In ambient mode, a sensor can respond to particular triggers in the world around it, but only specific metadata may be shared with the rest of the system. In active mode, full sensor data can be released to the main operating system (OS), and a secure indicator reliably informs the user that it’s happening. Meeting this challenge ultimately required building a new, isolated computing environment that could handle the full performance demands of ambient sensing use cases, yet stay cleanly separated from the main OS with three primary requirements: Building a new secure runtime requires a highly secure OS foundation. For this reason, we utilized an Apple-customized version of the L4 microkernel which we originally built for some of our most security-sensitive deployments, including the Secure Enclave Processor (SEP). This microkernel uses capabilities, which are secure resource handles that both identify and authorize access to the underlying resource. This simple but powerful mechanism is applied to both memory isolation and IPC security, enabling us to build a secure system that contains no extraneous authority. The exclaves microkernel, and our approach to formal verification of its correctness, are described in detail later in this post. Secure Exclaves run in a different processor execution context from the main OS, which allows us to employ an independent operating system specially designed to handle high-security, high-performance workloads. But isolation also requires careful handling of all shared resources available to the application processor: most importantly, system memory and communication with coprocessors. Isolating memory for the exclusive use of Secure Exclaves presented a serious engineering challenge: management of the page tables, which organize and protect main device memory, is usually handled by the main OS. We laid the groundwork for isolation in earlier releases, by carving out and rebuilding this subsystem as the Secure Page Table Monitor (SPTM): a standalone component that handles page table and memory logic, and runs at a higher privilege level than the main OS kernel. It doesn’t share data or code with the main OS, and is separately loaded by the boot loader. This rearchitecture not only hardened the entire system against certain kernel-level attacks, but also created the foundation for isolating Secure Exclave memory. SPTM relies on Apple silicon primitives to protect the memory used by exclaves from the rest of the system. It manages every physical page of memory used by the application processor, and enforces that software executing in Secure Exclaves have a separate and isolated view of memory than that seen by the main OS. Microkernel capabilities are used to control memory permissions of every individual exclave. This allows each exclave to access only its own memory, providing an additional layer of protection. Next, Secure Exclaves must account for the other coprocessors and sensors connected to the Apple silicon fabric. Where a coprocessor is essential to secure sensing, such as our Always-On Processor (AOP), a secure compartment within that coprocessor’s operating system handles the processing needed for communication with Secure Exclaves. The coprocessor secure compartment is also built on top of the exclaves microkernel, maintaining security assurance continuity across the application processor and coprocessors. Other resources like sensor memory are protected with specialized memory filters, placed between each resource and the shared fabric, which can only be configured by the SPTM. This propagates the memory isolation property throughout the system. Some of the secure sensing workloads that run in Secure Exclaves need access to high-performance inference hardware to run demanding machine learning models. To enable this, we extended the Apple Neural Engine (ANE) by adding isolated workload queues, like those we use in the SEP. Memory filters protect those queues from being modified or accessed by the main OS, and switching from an isolated to a standard queue flushes any local storage to prevent information leaks. With these changes, we can offer high-performance inference to power intelligent ambient sensing. Altogether, the computational, memory, and peripheral isolation technologies stack together to create an isolated but high-performance execution context. Within this context, we can place a specialized, secure operating system with microphone and camera access, running with the full power of Apple silicon. To handle ambient sensing tasks, Secure Exclaves must be able to exchange small amounts of metadata with the main OS. Traditional inter-process communication (IPC) mechanisms are designed for maximum flexibility, providing open-ended interfaces that can be composed with arbitrary complexity when moving data. For Secure Exclaves, we approached the problem from the opposite angle, and set out to design IPC primitives that could enable tightly restricted, completely predictable communication. To do so, we built a new communication mechanism called Secure IPC, written in Swift for memory safety. It combines an interface description language with a runtime that securely connects the components that are allowed to communicate. All exclaves use Secure IPC to communicate with each other and with the main OS. This design prevents unanticipated crosstalk between components and ensures that only authorized information can flow across IPC boundaries. Each Secure IPC interface from an exclave to the main OS is rigorously audited to ensure that only the minimal metadata needed to run an ambient sensing use case can leave the exclave. Microkernel capabilities are used to control the IPC connections of every exclave. By default, exclaves are unable to communicate or even refer to one another. An exclave may only initiate IPC if it has an explicit capability to an IPC connection. Therefore, Secure Exclaves have complete control over every IPC interface and connection in the system. The combination of the exclaves microkernel and Secure IPC makes Secure Exclaves the most secure runtime Apple has ever created, and we’ve put it at the heart of how we secure ambient sensing. When moving from ambient sensing to a full, active sensor use case, such as a conversation with Siri or a FaceTime video session, the system must communicate to the user that it is now sharing broad access to the sensor with the app that has requested it. We build on our existing visual language to communicate this — either an LED, or an indicator dot drawn on the display — but back it with a novel, high level of security that’s without industry precedent. A specialized exclave, called the Exclave Indicator Controller, is the overall system gatekeeper for sensor data. It only allows data to flow after establishing that the indicator is activated, and has been visible for a sufficient amount of time. Since multiple apps can request audio and video data simultaneously, the Indicator Controller deconflicts these requests and makes sure the appropriate indicator appears. Together with the isolation and controlled interface components of Secure Exclaves, this system provides an incredibly powerful mechanism for securely processing high-sensitivity workloads. To illustrate how these components work together, we describe the person recognition flow using the camera on HomeView — an ambient sensing use case protected by Secure Exclaves. HomeView must passively perform minimal visual processing at all times to detect whether a person is in the field of view, but this must not make camera data available to the broader system. The Secure Exclaves system allows person recognition to occur quickly and accurately, while keeping the ambient visual data protected within exclaves. This means HomeView can recognize who is using it, react to nearby movement, and display content based on whether a user is nearby or far away. At startup, the person recognition exclave loads previously enrolled face and voice recognition models and the identity database from the secure storage exclave (1). Finally, the orchestration service within the person recognition exclave matches the resulting prints against the identity database of enrolled users, and combines the face and voice identification to produce a confidence score. Only this metadata — person identifier, position, and confidence level — is returned to the person recognition daemon running in the main OS (7). The system integrates the outputs so that they are properly reflected in features that depend on user identity, such as Calendar, Messages, Apple Music, or compatible third-party audio and video apps from your iPhone (8). No audio or video data is shared with the operating system as this recognition process is performed. We also describe the “Hey Siri” flow on the latest iPhone models to show how this new architecture can improve security for existing use cases. A phone must passively perform minimal audio processing at all times to detect when a user has said the wake words for Siri. The Secure Exclaves system allows the “Hey Siri” flow to occur quickly and accurately, while keeping the ambient audio protected within exclaves until an active Siri session begins. The flow begins with the Always-On Processor (AOP), a low-power coprocessor that continuously monitors for wake-word utterances (1). If the rough first-pass filter on the AOP detects a potential “Hey Siri,” it wakes up the main processor and passes the audio buffer to the audio exclave (2). This exclave performs an echo cancellation pass to make the audio more intelligible, and then passes the audio to the Siri exclave (3). This section takes a closer look at the underpinnings of Secure Exclaves for those readers who have particular interest in the technical details of the system’s implementation. Microkernels allow large, secure systems to be constructed by minimizing the trusted computing base (TCB), which is the set of code that must be trusted to maintain system security. Unlike traditional kernels, such as XNU or Linux, which handle hardware, networking, and resource management in the kernel, the exclaves microkernel implements only the absolute minimum functionality required to run and isolate application services. While the exclaves microkernel was developed from scratch at Apple, its design is guided by modern microkernel research. It is a capability-based kernel, like seL4 or keyKOS, meaning that system components have no permissions by default. Instead, components may only interact with other components or hardware if explicitly granted a capability to do so. Because the exclaves microkernel has such a small TCB, Apple has been able to incrementally apply formal verification, using mathematical proofs to verify that the kernel's C implementation behaves exactly as defined by a high-level functional specification. This rigorous process has proven highly effective at discovering and eliminating subtle, critical logic bugs in core subsystems that could have otherwise led to kernel compromise: incomplete input validation of syscalls, inconsistent state updates, misaligned reads, and malformed page-table updates. It has also eliminated some classes of C undefined behavior. Formal verification uses mathematical proofs to demonstrate that a system satisfies specific properties that we define. At Apple, we've performed extensive formal verification in silicon development for over 15 years, and in 2019 we began using formal verification to prove classical cryptography, including the hardware Public Key Accelerator (PKA) — the part of Apple silicon that performs elliptic-curve public-key operations. More recently, corecrypto, Apple's cryptographic library, gained implementations of the quantum-secure ML-KEM and ML-DSA algorithms. These implementations have been formally verified to ensure that they are faithful to the FIPS 203 and FIPS 204 specifications. For the exclaves microkernel — the centerpiece in the security of exclave-based systems — we draw on the same internal expertise to formally verify that our C implementation satisfies an abstract functional specification: a precise, mathematical description of what the code should do. This provides a significantly greater degree of assurance than conventional software testing allows; in theory, it gives us strong confidence that our implementation behaves exactly as specified wherever the proof applies. The practical considerations are more complicated. Regardless of how it is applied, formal verification requires a tremendous investment of time and deep expertise. The implementation and its specification must be represented with carefully chosen mathematical formulas. To draw correct conclusions, the formulas must faithfully model the relevant behaviors of both the implementation and the specification, and be structured so as to enable the proof to be written in simple steps. Since the exclaves microkernel is actively developed and frequently changing, our formal verification efforts serve primarily as a tool to discover deep logic problems — for example, incomplete input validation of syscalls, inconsistent state updates, misaligned reads, and malformed page-table updates. As a side effect, we also show the absence of some classes of C undefined behavior for the code we formally verify. While other methods, such as testing and fuzzing, are useful for identifying bugs in the implementation and are often the first line of defense, formal verification has been able to discover subtle but critical problems in many of the kernel's subsystems, with the potential for full kernel compromise — for example, in the recursive algorithm used to free a capability storage object (CNode), in the implementation of sending capabilities over inter-process communication (IPC), and in execution-context (EC) state management when running on a multiprocessor (SMP) system. Thanks to close collaboration between the kernel engineers and the formal verification engineers, many of these issues have been discovered at early stages of development. Because of these constant changes, we do not claim complete coverage of all aspects of the kernel; instead, formal verification is applied gradually and incrementally to different parts. To do this, we rely on Isabelle/HOL with AutoCorres2 to build a mathematical model of the kernel implementation from the C source code, against which we perform our formal verification. Once the root task is destroyed, no remaining part of the system has such broad authority. For example, the root task gives the capability to manage physical memory to the physical memory server but restricts that capability such that memory mapped through it can only be mapped read-only or read-write. On the other hand, the capability to distribute read-execute (but not writable) access to physical memory is given to a code loading server. Every component in the system can request memory from the physical memory server, but only conclave launchers are connected to the code loading server. exclaveOS puts a component architecture on top of the capability model that the exclaves microkernel provides. Communication between these components is handled by Secure IPC. Secure IPC is a system for describing software components and the interfaces they provide, and managing their behavior at runtime. All communication between components, as well as into and out of exclaveOS, is handled by Secure IPC. Component interfaces are described ahead of time in a type-safe description language, allowing RPC data flow around the system to be audited and approved before it’s ever run.

Thanks to close collaboration between the kernel engineers and the formal verification engineers, many of these issues have been discovered at early stages of development. Because of these constant changes, we do not claim complete coverage of all aspects of the kernel; instead, formal verification is applied gradually and incrementally to different parts. To do this, we rely on Isabelle/HOL with AutoCorres2 to build a mathematical model of the kernel implementation from the C source code, against which we perform our formal verification.

Once the root task is destroyed, no remaining part of the system has such broad authority. For example, the root task gives the capability to manage physical memory to the physical memory server but restricts that capability such that memory mapped through it can only be mapped read-only or read-write. On the other hand, the capability to distribute read-execute (but not writable) access to physical memory is given to a code loading server. Every component in the system can request memory from the physical memory server, but only conclave launchers are connected to the code loading server.
exclaveOS puts a component architecture on top of the capability model that the exclaves microkernel provides. Communication between these components is handled by Secure IPC.

Secure IPC is a system for describing software components and the interfaces they provide, and managing their behavior at runtime. All communication between components, as well as into and out of exclaveOS, is handled by Secure IPC. Component interfaces are described ahead of time in a type-safe description language, allowing RPC data flow around the system to be audited and approved before it’s ever run.

extraction.body: IT Home, November 12: Apple has released a technical article today detailing its Secure Enclave security architecture in Apple Silicon chips, explaining how this system prevents raw audio and video data collected by the camera and microphone from being accessed by the operating system, applications, or even Apple itself. Apple's Security Engineering and Architecture (SEAR) team and Core OS team published an article titled "Secure Exclaves and Ambient Sensing" on the Apple Security Research blog on November 12, detailing the design principles, underlying architecture, and real-world applications of Secure Exclaves. Apple states that as devices become increasingly capable of perceiving their environment, cameras and microphones need to continuously process surrounding information. For example, devices must identify whether a user is nearby, detect specific voice commands, and determine if someone is currently using the device. These features require processing sensitive audio and video data, but this does not mean the device must continuously record or store this information. To this end, Apple has introduced Secure Exclaves, which process camera and microphone data in a separate, isolated execution environment. According to Apple, in environmental awareness mode, raw audio and video data are not transmitted to the main operating system, applications, or Apple itself, and are discarded after processing. The system only provides necessary metadata externally, such as whether specific sounds have been detected, whether a registered user has been identified, and the user’s location. Secure Exclaves are built around three key aspects: data isolation, controlled communication interfaces, and secure indication mechanisms. In terms of data isolation, Secure Exclaves operate in a processor execution environment separate from the main operating system and utilize Apple’s custom L4 microkernel. Apple also manages memory access permissions through the Secure Page Table Monitor (SPTM), ensuring that the main operating system kernel cannot read data stored in Secure Exclaves’ dedicated memory. In terms of communication, Apple developed a communication mechanism called Secure IPC, written in Swift, which restricts data exchange between components through predefined interfaces. Each sandbox can access only explicitly authorized resources, and only reviewed, necessary information is passed to the main operating system. For security purposes, Apple has designed a dedicated Exclave Indicator Controller to manage when camera and microphone data may leave the isolated environment. When an application requires full access to sensor data, the system must first ensure that the corresponding indicator light or on-screen prompt is displayed and has remained visible for the required duration before allowing data transmission. Apple also introduced the application of Secure Exclaves on HomeView. The device can recognize up to six registered users via its camera and microphone while determining whether users are near the device. The camera enclave detects faces and generates relevant data, while the microphone enclave processes audio information, which is then inferred through a dedicated neural network engine enclave queue. Ultimately, the system will only pass metadata such as user identity, location, and recognition confidence to the main operating system, not raw images or audio. The operating system can use this information to adjust the display content of features like Calendar, Messages, and Apple Music. IT Home notes that Secure Exclaves are also applied to the camera, microphone, and screen indicators on the iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max, and iPhone Duo, as well as the camera indicators on MacBook Neo and HomeView. Apple used the "Hey Siri" voice wake-up feature on the iPhone 18 Pro as an example to explain how this system works: the device first listens for the wake word using a low-power Always-On Processor (AOP); when a potential "Hey Siri" command is detected, the audio buffer is passed to the Audio Isolation Zone for processing, followed by a second round of recognition by the Siri Isolation Zone. Before confirming the wake word, the main operating system receives only a notification that Siri needs to be awakened, not the audio data. Audio transmission to the Siri service is permitted only after the user enters an active interaction state and the system completes the display of the microphone indicator and security checks. Apple explains that the screen indicator feature is not solely rendered by the operating system. For devices with a screen indicator, a dedicated display isolation zone checks the actual pixels displayed on the screen, including color, shape, duration, and brightness, to ensure the indicator is genuinely visible to users and to prevent malicious software from misleading users by hiding or falsifying the indicator. At the underlying technology level, Apple states that the microkernel of Secure Enclaves uses a capability-based mechanism to manage permissions; system components do not have default access to other components or hardware resources and can only interact after receiving explicit authorization. Apple has also performed formal verification on the microkernel, using mathematical methods to verify that the C language implementation conforms to predefined functional specifications, thereby uncovering low-level logic issues that traditional software testing may miss. However, Apple also emphasized that the current formal verification is being implemented incrementally and does not yet cover all parts of the microkernel.

When an application requires full access to sensor data, the system must first ensure that the corresponding indicator light or on-screen prompt is displayed and has remained visible for the required duration before allowing data transmission.

Apple also introduced the application of Secure Exclaves on HomeView. The device can recognize up to six registered users via its camera and microphone while determining whether users are near the device. The camera enclave detects faces and generates relevant data, while the microphone enclave processes audio information, which is then inferred through a dedicated neural network engine enclave queue.

Ultimately, the system will only pass metadata such as user identity, location, and recognition confidence to the main operating system, not raw images or audio. The operating system can use this information to adjust the display content of features like Calendar, Messages, and Apple Music.

IT Home notes that Secure Exclaves are also applied to the camera, microphone, and screen indicators on the iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max, and iPhone Duo, as well as the camera indicators on MacBook Neo and HomeView.

Apple used the "Hey Siri" voice wake-up feature on the iPhone 18 Pro as an example to explain how this system works: the device first listens for the wake word using a low-power Always-On Processor (AOP); when a potential "Hey Siri" command is detected, the audio buffer is passed to the Audio Isolation Zone for processing, followed by a second round of recognition by the Siri Isolation Zone.

Before confirming the wake word, the main operating system receives only a notification that Siri needs to be awakened, not the audio data. Audio transmission to the Siri service is permitted only after the user enters an active interaction state and the system completes the display of the microphone indicator and security checks.

Apple explains that the screen indicator feature is not solely rendered by the operating system. For devices with a screen indicator, a dedicated display isolation zone checks the actual pixels displayed on the screen, including color, shape, duration, and brightness, to ensure the indicator is genuinely visible to users and to prevent malicious software from misleading users by hiding or falsifying the indicator.

At the underlying technology level, Apple states that the microkernel of Secure Enclaves uses a capability-based mechanism to manage permissions; system components do not have default access to other components or hardware resources and can only interact after receiving explicit authorization.

Apple has also performed formal verification on the microkernel, using mathematical methods to verify that the C language implementation conforms to predefined functional specifications, thereby uncovering low-level logic issues that traditional software testing may miss. However, Apple also emphasized that the current formal verification is being implemented incrementally and does not yet cover all parts of the microkernel.
