extraction.body: We recently introduced HomeView, which can recognize up to six people to deliver a rich and personalized experience. This capability relies on ambient sensing : using the microphone and camera to understand the surrounding environment and recognize an enrolled user’s voice and face. We have always believed features like this must be designed from the ground up to protect user security and privacy, and are now taking these protections even further, with a new security architecture in Apple silicon that’s purpose-built for ambient sensing. This work both benefits our newest features and strengthens the security of features we already ship, such as “Hey Siri” detection. Our goal is to keep ambient sensor data secure even against highly sophisticated attacks, while giving users a clear, reliable, and tamper-resistant signal whenever their sensors are fully active. While ambient sensing relies on processing input from the camera or microphone, it must never record audio or video, nor expose it to the rest of the operating system. Instead, it must reduce the sensor stream to far simpler signals, such as whether a specific sound was detected or whether an enrolled user’s face or voice was recognized, while protecting the raw sensor data during processing and discarding it once complete. Hardwired LED sensor indicator lights are easy to understand and play an important role in privacy and security across our products, but aren’t suitable for ambient sensing use cases, because they would glow continuously. This would defeat the utility of the indicator, and prevent the user from distinguishing background sensing — such as a device listening for a “Hey Siri” invocation — from active audio and video recording. We set out instead to enable ambient sensing to run in a strongly isolated environment with the full power of the main application processor, with a precisely controlled interface into the rest of the system, and with a secure indication mechanism so the user is aware when audio or video data is allowed to leave the isolation boundary. To accomplish this, we have created Secure Exclaves : protected and compartmentalized runtimes used to process camera and microphone data separately from the rest of the system. Isolation features added across many core components of the silicon work in tandem to protect Secure Exclaves and keep them segregated from the rest of the system. Data that is processed and analyzed in a Secure Exclave cannot be accessed by the main operating system, apps, or Apple. We use Secure Exclaves to protect entirely new use cases, like person recognition on HomeView as well as Siri Recap and Live Rewind, as described here . We also use them to protect the on-screen camera and microphone indicators used in iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max, and iPhone Duo, as well as the camera indicators in MacBook Neo and HomeView, improving security for our users across the board. We believe Secure Exclaves are the most advanced architecture for ambient sensing in the industry, defining an ambitious new level of security and privacy for these use cases. To protect ambient sensing, we aimed to build a system that operated in two distinct modes: ambient mode and active mode, for both camera and microphone. In ambient mode, a sensor can respond to particular triggers in the world around it, but only specific metadata may be shared with the rest of the system. In active mode, full sensor data can be released to the main operating system (OS), and a secure indicator reliably informs the user that it’s happening. Meeting this challenge ultimately required building a new, isolated computing environment that could handle the full performance demands of ambient sensing use cases, yet stay cleanly separated from the main OS with three primary requirements: Building a new secure runtime requires a highly secure OS foundation. For this reason, we utilized an Apple-customized version of the L4 microkernel which we originally built for some of our most security-sensitive deployments, including the Secure Enclave Processor (SEP). This microkernel uses capabilities, which are secure resource handles that both identify and authorize access to the underlying resource. This simple but powerful mechanism is applied to both memory isolation and IPC security, enabling us to build a secure system that contains no extraneous authority. The exclaves microkernel, and our approach to formal verification of its correctness, are described in detail later in this post. Secure Exclaves run in a different processor execution context from the main OS, which allows us to employ an independent operating system specially designed to handle high-security, high-performance workloads. But isolation also requires careful handling of all shared resources available to the application processor: most importantly, system memory and communication with coprocessors. Isolating memory for the exclusive use of Secure Exclaves presented a serious engineering challenge: management of the page tables, which organize and protect main device memory, is usually handled by the main OS. We laid the groundwork for isolation in earlier releases, by carving out and rebuilding this subsystem as the Secure Page Table Monitor (SPTM): a standalone component that handles page table and memory logic, and runs at a higher privilege level than the main OS kernel. It doesn’t share data or code with the main OS, and is separately loaded by the boot loader. This rearchitecture not only hardened the entire system against certain kernel-level attacks, but also created the foundation for isolating Secure Exclave memory. SPTM relies on Apple silicon primitives to protect the memory used by exclaves from the rest of the system. It manages every physical page of memory used by the application processor, and enforces that software executing in Secure Exclaves have a separate and isolated view of memory than that seen by the main OS. Microkernel capabilities are used to control memory permissions of every individual exclave. This allows each exclave to access only its own memory, providing an additional layer of protection. Next, Secure Exclaves must account for the other coprocessors and sensors connected to the Apple silicon fabric. Where a coprocessor is essential to secure sensing, such as our Always-On Processor (AOP), a secure compartment within that coprocessor’s operating system handles the processing needed for communication with Secure Exclaves. The coprocessor secure compartment is also built on top of the exclaves microkernel, maintaining security assurance continuity across the application processor and coprocessors. Other resources like sensor memory are protected with specialized memory filters, placed between each resource and the shared fabric, which can only be configured by the SPTM. This propagates the memory isolation property throughout the system. Some of the secure sensing workloads that run in Secure Exclaves need access to high-performance inference hardware to run demanding machine learning models. To enable this, we extended the Apple Neural Engine (ANE) by adding isolated workload queues, like those we use in the SEP. Memory filters protect those queues from being modified or accessed by the main OS, and switching from an isolated to a standard queue flushes any local storage to prevent information leaks. With these changes, we can offer high-performance inference to power intelligent ambient sensing. Altogether, the computational, memory, and peripheral isolation technologies stack together to create an isolated but high-performance execution context. Within this context, we can place a specialized, secure operating system with microphone and camera access, running with the full power of Apple silicon. To handle ambient sensing tasks, Secure Exclaves must be able to exchange small amounts of metadata with the main OS. Traditional inter-process communication (IPC) mechanisms are designed for maximum flexibility, providing open-ended interfaces that can be composed with arbitrary complexity when moving data. For Secure Exclaves, we approached the problem from the opposite angle, and set out to design IPC primitives that could enable tightly restricted, completely predictable communication. To do so, we built a new communication mechanism called Secure IPC, written in Swift for memory safety. It combines an interface description language with a runtime that securely connects the components that are allowed to communicate. All exclaves use Secure IPC to communicate with each other and with the main OS. This design prevents unanticipated crosstalk between components and ensures that only authorized information can flow across IPC boundaries. Each Secure IPC interface from an exclave to the main OS is rigorously audited to ensure that only the minimal metadata needed to run an ambient sensing use case can leave the exclave. Microkernel capabilities are used to control the IPC connections of every exclave. By default, exclaves are unable to communicate or even refer to one another. An exclave may only initiate IPC if it has an explicit capability to an IPC connection. Therefore, Secure Exclaves have complete control over every IPC interface and connection in the system. The combination of the exclaves microkernel and Secure IPC makes Secure Exclaves the most secure runtime Apple has ever created, and we’ve put it at the heart of how we secure ambient sensing. When moving from ambient sensing to a full, active sensor use case, such as a conversation with Siri or a FaceTime video session, the system must communicate to the user that it is now sharing broad access to the sensor with the app that has requested it. We build on our existing visual language to communicate this — either an LED, or an indicator dot drawn on the display — but back it with a novel, high level of security that’s without industry precedent. A specialized exclave, called the Exclave Indicator Controller, is the overall system gatekeeper for sensor data. It only allows data to flow after establishing that the indicator is activated, and has been visible for a sufficient amount of time. Since multiple apps can request audio and video data simultaneously, the Indicator Controller deconflicts these requests and makes sure the appropriate indicator appears. Together with the isolation and controlled interface components of Secure Exclaves, this system provides an incredibly powerful mechanism for securely processing high-sensitivity workloads. To illustrate how these components work together, we describe the person recognition flow using the camera on HomeView — an ambient sensing use case protected by Secure Exclaves. HomeView must passively perform minimal visual processing at all times to detect whether a person is in the field of view, but this must not make camera data available to the broader system. The Secure Exclaves system allows person recognition to occur quickly and accurately, while keeping the ambient visual data protected within exclaves. This means HomeView can recognize who is using it, react to nearby movement, and display content based on whether a user is nearby or far away. At startup, the person recognition exclave loads previously enrolled face and voice recognition models and the identity database from the secure storage exclave (1). Finally, the orchestration service within the person recognition exclave matches the resulting prints against the identity database of enrolled users, and combines the face and voice identification to produce a confidence score. Only this metadata — person identifier, position, and confidence level — is returned to the person recognition daemon running in the main OS (7). The system integrates the outputs so that they are properly reflected in features that depend on user identity, such as Calendar, Messages, Apple Music, or compatible third-party audio and video apps from your iPhone (8). No audio or video data is shared with the operating system as this recognition process is performed. We also describe the “Hey Siri” flow on the latest iPhone models to show how this new architecture can improve security for existing use cases. A phone must passively perform minimal audio processing at all times to detect when a user has said the wake words for Siri. The Secure Exclaves system allows the “Hey Siri” flow to occur quickly and accurately, while keeping the ambient audio protected within exclaves until an active Siri session begins. The flow begins with the Always-On Processor (AOP), a low-power coprocessor that continuously monitors for wake-word utterances (1). If the rough first-pass filter on the AOP detects a potential “Hey Siri,” it wakes up the main processor and passes the audio buffer to the audio exclave (2). This exclave performs an echo cancellation pass to make the audio more intelligible, and then passes the audio to the Siri exclave (3). This section takes a closer look at the underpinnings of Secure Exclaves for those readers who have particular interest in the technical details of the system’s implementation. Microkernels allow large, secure systems to be constructed by minimizing the trusted computing base (TCB), which is the set of code that must be trusted to maintain system security. Unlike traditional kernels, such as XNU or Linux, which handle hardware, networking, and resource management in the kernel, the exclaves microkernel implements only the absolute minimum functionality required to run and isolate application services. While the exclaves microkernel was developed from scratch at Apple, its design is guided by modern microkernel research. It is a capability-based kernel, like seL4 or keyKOS, meaning that system components have no permissions by default. Instead, components may only interact with other components or hardware if explicitly granted a capability to do so. Because the exclaves microkernel has such a small TCB, Apple has been able to incrementally apply formal verification, using mathematical proofs to verify that the kernel's C implementation behaves exactly as defined by a high-level functional specification. This rigorous process has proven highly effective at discovering and eliminating subtle, critical logic bugs in core subsystems that could have otherwise led to kernel compromise: incomplete input validation of syscalls, inconsistent state updates, misaligned reads, and malformed page-table updates. It has also eliminated some classes of C undefined behavior. Formal verification uses mathematical proofs to demonstrate that a system satisfies specific properties that we define. At Apple, we've performed extensive formal verification in silicon development for over 15 years, and in 2019 we began using formal verification to prove classical cryptography, including the hardware Public Key Accelerator (PKA) — the part of Apple silicon that performs elliptic-curve public-key operations. More recently, corecrypto, Apple's cryptographic library, gained implementations of the quantum-secure ML-KEM and ML-DSA algorithms. These implementations have been formally verified to ensure that they are faithful to the FIPS 203 and FIPS 204 specifications. For the exclaves microkernel — the centerpiece in the security of exclave-based systems — we draw on the same internal expertise to formally verify that our C implementation satisfies an abstract functional specification: a precise, mathematical description of what the code should do. This provides a significantly greater degree of assurance than conventional software testing allows; in theory, it gives us strong confidence that our implementation behaves exactly as specified wherever the proof applies. The practical considerations are more complicated. Regardless of how it is applied, formal verification requires a tremendous investment of time and deep expertise. The implementation and its specification must be represented with carefully chosen mathematical formulas. To draw correct conclusions, the formulas must faithfully model the relevant behaviors of both the implementation and the specification, and be structured so as to enable the proof to be written in simple steps. Since the exclaves microkernel is actively developed and frequently changing, our formal verification efforts serve primarily as a tool to discover deep logic problems — for example, incomplete input validation of syscalls, inconsistent state updates, misaligned reads, and malformed page-table updates. As a side effect, we also show the absence of some classes of C undefined behavior for the code we formally verify. While other methods, such as testing and fuzzing, are useful for identifying bugs in the implementation and are often the first line of defense, formal verification has been able to discover subtle but critical problems in many of the kernel's subsystems, with the potential for full kernel compromise — for example, in the recursive algorithm used to free a capability storage object (CNode), in the implementation of sending capabilities over inter-process communication (IPC), and in execution-context (EC) state management when running on a multiprocessor (SMP) system. Thanks to close collaboration between the kernel engineers and the formal verification engineers, many of these issues have been discovered at early stages of development. Because of these constant changes, we do not claim complete coverage of all aspects of the kernel; instead, formal verification is applied gradually and incrementally to different parts. To do this, we rely on Isabelle/HOL with AutoCorres2 to build a mathematical model of the kernel implementation from the C source code, against which we perform our formal verification. Once the root task is destroyed, no remaining part of the system has such broad authority. For example, the root task gives the capability to manage physical memory to the physical memory server but restricts that capability such that memory mapped through it can only be mapped read-only or read-write. On the other hand, the capability to distribute read-execute (but not writable) access to physical memory is given to a code loading server. Every component in the system can request memory from the physical memory server, but only conclave launchers are connected to the code loading server. exclaveOS puts a component architecture on top of the capability model that the exclaves microkernel provides. Communication between these components is handled by Secure IPC. Secure IPC is a system for describing software components and the interfaces they provide, and managing their behavior at runtime. All communication between components, as well as into and out of exclaveOS, is handled by Secure IPC. Component interfaces are described ahead of time in a type-safe description language, allowing RPC data flow around the system to be audited and approved before it’s ever run.

When moving from ambient sensing to a full, active sensor use case, such as a conversation with Siri or a FaceTime video session, the system must communicate to the user that it is now sharing broad access to the sensor with the app that has requested it. We build on our existing visual language to communicate this — either an LED, or an indicator dot drawn on the display — but back it with a novel, high level of security that’s without industry precedent.

A specialized exclave, called the Exclave Indicator Controller, is the overall system gatekeeper for sensor data. It only allows data to flow after establishing that the indicator is activated, and has been visible for a sufficient amount of time. Since multiple apps can request audio and video data simultaneously, the Indicator Controller deconflicts these requests and makes sure the appropriate indicator appears.
Together with the isolation and controlled interface components of Secure Exclaves, this system provides an incredibly powerful mechanism for securely processing high-sensitivity workloads.

To illustrate how these components work together, we describe the person recognition flow using the camera on HomeView — an ambient sensing use case protected by Secure Exclaves. HomeView must passively perform minimal visual processing at all times to detect whether a person is in the field of view, but this must not make camera data available to the broader system. The Secure Exclaves system allows person recognition to occur quickly and accurately, while keeping the ambient visual data protected within exclaves. This means HomeView can recognize who is using it, react to nearby movement, and display content based on whether a user is nearby or far away.
At startup, the person recognition exclave loads previously enrolled face and voice recognition models and the identity database from the secure storage exclave (1).

Finally, the orchestration service within the person recognition exclave matches the resulting prints against the identity database of enrolled users, and combines the face and voice identification to produce a confidence score. Only this metadata — person identifier, position, and confidence level — is returned to the person recognition daemon running in the main OS (7). The system integrates the outputs so that they are properly reflected in features that depend on user identity, such as Calendar, Messages, Apple Music, or compatible third-party audio and video apps from your iPhone (8). No audio or video data is shared with the operating system as this recognition process is performed.

We also describe the “Hey Siri” flow on the latest iPhone models to show how this new architecture can improve security for existing use cases. A phone must passively perform minimal audio processing at all times to detect when a user has said the wake words for Siri. The Secure Exclaves system allows the “Hey Siri” flow to occur quickly and accurately, while keeping the ambient audio protected within exclaves until an active Siri session begins.

The flow begins with the Always-On Processor (AOP), a low-power coprocessor that continuously monitors for wake-word utterances (1). If the rough first-pass filter on the AOP detects a potential “Hey Siri,” it wakes up the main processor and passes the audio buffer to the audio exclave (2). This exclave performs an echo cancellation pass to make the audio more intelligible, and then passes the audio to the Siri exclave (3).
This section takes a closer look at the underpinnings of Secure Exclaves for those readers who have particular interest in the technical details of the system’s implementation.

Microkernels allow large, secure systems to be constructed by minimizing the trusted computing base (TCB), which is the set of code that must be trusted to maintain system security. Unlike traditional kernels, such as XNU or Linux, which handle hardware, networking, and resource management in the kernel, the exclaves microkernel implements only the absolute minimum functionality required to run and isolate application services.

While the exclaves microkernel was developed from scratch at Apple, its design is guided by modern microkernel research. It is a capability-based kernel, like seL4 or keyKOS, meaning that system components have no permissions by default. Instead, components may only interact with other components or hardware if explicitly granted a capability to do so.

Because the exclaves microkernel has such a small TCB, Apple has been able to incrementally apply formal verification, using mathematical proofs to verify that the kernel's C implementation behaves exactly as defined by a high-level functional specification. This rigorous process has proven highly effective at discovering and eliminating subtle, critical logic bugs in core subsystems that could have otherwise led to kernel compromise: incomplete input validation of syscalls, inconsistent state updates, misaligned reads, and malformed page-table updates. It has also eliminated some classes of C undefined behavior.

Formal verification uses mathematical proofs to demonstrate that a system satisfies specific properties that we define. At Apple, we've performed extensive formal verification in silicon development for over 15 years, and in 2019 we began using formal verification to prove classical cryptography, including the hardware Public Key Accelerator (PKA) — the part of Apple silicon that performs elliptic-curve public-key operations. More recently, corecrypto, Apple's cryptographic library, gained implementations of the quantum-secure ML-KEM and ML-DSA algorithms. These implementations have been formally verified to ensure that they are faithful to the FIPS 203 and FIPS 204 specifications.

For the exclaves microkernel — the centerpiece in the security of exclave-based systems — we draw on the same internal expertise to formally verify that our C implementation satisfies an abstract functional specification: a precise, mathematical description of what the code should do. This provides a significantly greater degree of assurance than conventional software testing allows; in theory, it gives us strong confidence that our implementation behaves exactly as specified wherever the proof applies. The practical considerations are more complicated. Regardless of how it is applied, formal verification requires a tremendous investment of time and deep expertise. The implementation and its specification must be represented with carefully chosen mathematical formulas. To draw correct conclusions, the formulas must faithfully model the relevant behaviors of both the implementation and the specification, and be structured so as to enable the proof to be written in simple steps.

Since the exclaves microkernel is actively developed and frequently changing, our formal verification efforts serve primarily as a tool to discover deep logic problems — for example, incomplete input validation of syscalls, inconsistent state updates, misaligned reads, and malformed page-table updates. As a side effect, we also show the absence of some classes of C undefined behavior for the code we formally verify. While other methods, such as testing and fuzzing, are useful for identifying bugs in the implementation and are often the first line of defense, formal verification has been able to discover subtle but critical problems in many of the kernel's subsystems, with the potential for full kernel compromise — for example, in the recursive algorithm used to free a capability storage object (CNode), in the implementation of sending capabilities over inter-process communication (IPC), and in execution-context (EC) state management when running on a multiprocessor (SMP) system. Thanks to close collaboration between the kernel engineers and the formal verification engineers, many of these issues have been discovered at early stages of development. Because of these constant changes, we do not claim complete coverage of all aspects of the kernel; instead, formal verification is applied gradually and incrementally to different parts. To do this, we rely on Isabelle/HOL with AutoCorres2 to build a mathematical model of the kernel implementation from the C source code, against which we perform our formal verification.

Once the root task is destroyed, no remaining part of the system has such broad authority. For example, the root task gives the capability to manage physical memory to the physical memory server but restricts that capability such that memory mapped through it can only be mapped read-only or read-write. On the other hand, the capability to distribute read-execute (but not writable) access to physical memory is given to a code loading server. Every component in the system can request memory from the physical memory server, but only conclave launchers are connected to the code loading server.
exclaveOS puts a component architecture on top of the capability model that the exclaves microkernel provides. Communication between these components is handled by Secure IPC.

Secure IPC is a system for describing software components and the interfaces they provide, and managing their behavior at runtime. All communication between components, as well as into and out of exclaveOS, is handled by Secure IPC. Component interfaces are described ahead of time in a type-safe description language, allowing RPC data flow around the system to be audited and approved before it’s ever run.

Some of the secure sensing workloads that run in Secure Exclaves need access to high-performance inference hardware to run demanding machine learning models.
To enable this, we extended the Apple Neural Engine (ANE) by adding isolated workload queues, like those we use in the SEP.
Memory filters protect those queues from being modified or accessed by the main OS, and switching from an isolated to a standard queue flushes any local storage to prevent information leaks.
Microkernel capabilities are used to control the IPC connections of every exclave.

Next, Secure Exclaves must account for the other coprocessors and sensors connected to the Apple silicon fabric.
The coprocessor secure compartment is also built on top of the exclaves microkernel, maintaining security assurance continuity across the application processor and coprocessors.
This propagates the memory isolation property throughout the system.
Traditional inter-process communication (IPC) mechanisms are designed for maximum flexibility, providing open-ended interfaces that can be composed with arbitrary complexity when moving data.
For Secure Exclaves, we approached the problem from the opposite angle, and set out to design IPC primitives that could enable tightly restricted, completely predictable communication.

Our goal is to keep ambient sensor data secure even against highly sophisticated attacks, while giving users a clear, reliable, and tamper-resistant signal whenever their sensors are fully active.

We also use them to protect the on-screen camera and microphone indicators used in iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max, and iPhone Duo, as well as the camera indicators in MacBook Neo and HomeView, improving security for our users across the board.
This allows each exclave to access only its own memory, providing an additional layer of protection.
This simple but powerful mechanism is applied to both memory isolation and IPC security, enabling us to build a secure system that contains no extraneous authority.
This rearchitecture not only hardened the entire system against certain kernel-level attacks, but also created the foundation for isolating Secure Exclave memory.

sources.title: ‘No family dinners’: AMD boss Lisa Su, 57, is Jensen Huang’s cousin — now she’s on the list to replace him at Nvidia - Yahoo Finance
passages: This article originally appeared on Moneywise.com under the title: 'No family dinners': AMD boss Lisa Su, 57, is Jensen Huang's cousin — now she's on the list to replace him at Nvidia

Jensen Huang is in the middle of a firestorm, as new details emerge about not just one, but two extramarital affairs — one with a suspected Chinese spy, and the latest revelation about an executive who reported to him, which was apparently caught on video.
This week, her name landed on Bloomberg's rundown of possible successors for Huang. .
Su and Huang are first cousins once removed , according to Taiwanese genealogist Jean Wu, who laid out the family tree for CNN.
An Nvidia spokesperson also confirmed the family tie.
AMD reported record third-quarter revenue of $13.4 billion on Nov.
Sales in its data center unit, which makes server processors and AI chips, nearly doubled.
Su said she expects revenue to climb more than 80% in 2027 , above Wall Street's estimate, and analysts at TD Cowen called AMD the leading alternative to Nvidia, Reuters reported.
Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.
Huang worked at AMD as a microprocessor designer before starting Nvidia.
AMD's stock has risen nearly 170-fold on Su's watch, though the company is still a fraction of Nvidia's size.
Su has talked about competing with her relative's company before.
Asked about Huang at a Consumer Technology Association event in 2020 , she called Nvidia a great company, then added : "It is a competitive world, so there's no question that we compete hard.
But it's also a world where you also have to partner with your competitors from time to time."
Nvidia and AMD did not immediately respond to Moneywise's request for comment.
Su joined AMD nearly two decades later and is credited with turning the company around.

passages: It’s almost inconceivable that Nvidia would fire its rock star CEO.
Yet here we are, on the precipice of this happening.
Over at Kalshi, Jensen Huang’s odds of surviving the week are sitting at a lowly 30% .
Even though he built one of the world’s most valuable — and, many would argue, dangerously powerful — companies, the tides have completely turned against him.

He has confessed to an extramarital affair, but as of Wednesday afternoon it isn’t even clear whom he meant: Alice Huang, the Chinese executive suspected by U.S. intelligence of spying for her country, or Kimberly Powell, an Nvidia executive who reports to him and who, five sources told The New York Times in an explosive new report, was also a paramour.
Analysts and former employees have floated him as a possible successor, and Kalshi traders give him a middling shot .
He’s no household name, but the Stanford PhD seems more viable if Huang can can keep that chairman title and push for a successor he can work with.

extraction.body: It’s almost inconceivable that Nvidia would fire its rock star CEO. Yet here we are, on the precipice of this happening. Over at Kalshi, Jensen Huang’s odds of surviving the week are sitting at a lowly 30% . Even though he built one of the world’s most valuable — and, many would argue, dangerously powerful — companies, the tides have completely turned against him. He has confessed to an extramarital affair, but as of Wednesday afternoon it isn’t even clear whom he meant: Alice Huang, the Chinese executive suspected by U.S. intelligence of spying for her country, or Kimberly Powell, an Nvidia executive who reports to him and who, five sources told The New York Times in an explosive new report, was also a paramour. Even if Huang is pushed out as CEO, the board members he has made very rich are unlikely to cut him loose entirely. Barring another shoe dropping, they could keep him on as chairman, a role Nvidia doesn’t currently have. But someone still has to run the company, and there’s no apparent succession plan, which leaves us, like everyone else, to speculate while we wait to see what happens next. While Huang’s 60 direct reports undoubtedly get a closer look, consider this our own parlor game, featuring some obvious and less obvious candidates: Lisa Su . The AMD CEO runs Nvidia’s most credible rival, as well as a distant cousin of Huang. The Information floated her name this week, but why would she leave her job for his? Her company stands to benefit from every day that Nvidia spends distracted by an investigation, congressional briefings, and all the mini dramas that are sure to follow. Her best move might be to send a nice note and keep her current corner office. Eric Schmidt. He was the pick of Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, senior associate dean for leadership studies at the Yale School of Management, who we talked with earlier this week. Schmidt could “parachute in tomorrow and do a very good job,” Sonnenfeld said, and perhaps he could. He ran Google from 2001 to 2011, chaired the National Security Commission on AI from 2018 to 2021, and now runs the rocket company Relativity Space. Chips, software, government, rockets — it’s an impressive range. Then again, Schmidt would bring a lot of baggage when it comes to his own extramarital dalliances . It’s hard to see him clearing the board for that reason. Lip-Bu Tan . Intel’s CEO knows chips, and right now he might welcome a very soft landing. Last month, Intel reported third-quarter revenue up 21% to $16.5 billion, then warned its fourth-quarter results would fall short of Wall Street’s forecasts. The AI boom has caused a memory-chip shortage, pushing up PC prices and cutting PC sales. That’s hurt Intel (PC chips are a big part of its business), and its stock plunged 20% in after-hours trading on the warning, having already slid more than 30% since September. A move to a company that’s eating everyone’s lunch would be a pretty amazing escape hatch. Bret Taylor. The former Salesforce co-CEO and OpenAI board chair now runs the AI startup Sierra, and his resume includes a lot of the biggest brands in Silicon Valley. He co-created Google Maps, served as Facebook’s CTO, and chaired Twitter’s board through its sale to Elon Musk. He then took over as OpenAI’s board chair after the “Blip,” Sam Altman’s firing and fast return. When companies need an unflappable, likable adult in the room, they call Taylor. He probably knows nearly every customer Nvidia has, too. Ian Buck. If the board feels strongly about having a “builder” at the helm, they could do worse than the Nvidia VP who helped develop CUDA, the chip software that has become central to Nvidia’s dominance in AI. Analysts and former employees have floated him as a possible successor, and Kalshi traders give him a middling shot . He’s no household name, but the Stanford PhD seems more viable if Huang can can keep that chairman title and push for a successor he can work with. Someone else down the hall. Andrew Bell, Nvidia’s senior vice president of hardware engineering, arrived 25 years ago as a fresh Cornell grad and has been on an upward trajectory at the company ever since. Like Buck and dozens of other executives who are presumably being scrutinized, he reports directly to Huang. Nvidia CFO Colette Kress is the insider most often named, but analysts say she isn’t necessarily a natural successor as an innovator and visionary, and Bell has the chip pedigree. The wild card? Lori Huang . Nobody has floated her, but hear us out: Jensen met his wife as lab partners at Oregon State, so she has been working with him since before Nvidia existed. After graduating, she worked at Silicon Graphics as a micro chip engineer (making more money than her husband, he has said), then scaled back to raise the couple’s family, and she now co-leads the family trusts. If the board wants continuity, they could do worse than a humbler Huang who is also a brainiac. There’s a reason they say that behind every great man is a great woman (and vice versa). Whatever happens next, we’ll know soon. Get an Early Peek at the Next TechCrunch Disrupt Disrupt, Startup Battlefield, and more will return next year, and you can be at the front of the line. Her best move might be to send a nice note and keep her current corner office.

Eric Schmidt. He was the pick of Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, senior associate dean for leadership studies at the Yale School of Management, who we talked with earlier this week. Schmidt could “parachute in tomorrow and do a very good job,” Sonnenfeld said, and perhaps he could. He ran Google from 2001 to 2011, chaired the National Security Commission on AI from 2018 to 2021, and now runs the rocket company Relativity Space. Chips, software, government, rockets — it’s an impressive range. Then again, Schmidt would bring a lot of baggage when it comes to his own extramarital dalliances . It’s hard to see him clearing the board for that reason.

Lip-Bu Tan . Intel’s CEO knows chips, and right now he might welcome a very soft landing. Last month, Intel reported third-quarter revenue up 21% to $16.5 billion, then warned its fourth-quarter results would fall short of Wall Street’s forecasts. The AI boom has caused a memory-chip shortage, pushing up PC prices and cutting PC sales. That’s hurt Intel (PC chips are a big part of its business), and its stock plunged 20% in after-hours trading on the warning, having already slid more than 30% since September. A move to a company that’s eating everyone’s lunch would be a pretty amazing escape hatch.

Bret Taylor. The former Salesforce co-CEO and OpenAI board chair now runs the AI startup Sierra, and his resume includes a lot of the biggest brands in Silicon Valley. He co-created Google Maps, served as Facebook’s CTO, and chaired Twitter’s board through its sale to Elon Musk. He then took over as OpenAI’s board chair after the “Blip,” Sam Altman’s firing and fast return. When companies need an unflappable, likable adult in the room, they call Taylor. He probably knows nearly every customer Nvidia has, too.

Ian Buck. If the board feels strongly about having a “builder” at the helm, they could do worse than the Nvidia VP who helped develop CUDA, the chip software that has become central to Nvidia’s dominance in AI. Analysts and former employees have floated him as a possible successor, and Kalshi traders give him a middling shot . He’s no household name, but the Stanford PhD seems more viable if Huang can can keep that chairman title and push for a successor he can work with.

Someone else down the hall. Andrew Bell, Nvidia’s senior vice president of hardware engineering, arrived 25 years ago as a fresh Cornell grad and has been on an upward trajectory at the company ever since. Like Buck and dozens of other executives who are presumably being scrutinized, he reports directly to Huang. Nvidia CFO Colette Kress is the insider most often named, but analysts say she isn’t necessarily a natural successor as an innovator and visionary, and Bell has the chip pedigree.

The wild card? Lori Huang . Nobody has floated her, but hear us out: Jensen met his wife as lab partners at Oregon State, so she has been working with him since before Nvidia existed. After graduating, she worked at Silicon Graphics as a micro chip engineer (making more money than her husband, he has said), then scaled back to raise the couple’s family, and she now co-leads the family trusts. If the board wants continuity, they could do worse than a humbler Huang who is also a brainiac. There’s a reason they say that behind every great man is a great woman (and vice versa).
Whatever happens next, we’ll know soon.

extraction.body: It’s almost inconceivable that Nvidia would fire its rock star CEO. Yet here we are, on the precipice of this happening. Over at Kalshi, Jensen Huang’s odds of surviving the week are sitting at a lowly 30% . Even though he built one of the world’s most valuable — and, many would argue, dangerously powerful — companies, the tides have completely turned against him. He has confessed to an extramarital affair, but as of Wednesday afternoon it isn’t even clear whom he meant: Alice Huang, the Chinese executive suspected by U.S. intelligence of spying for her country, or Kimberly Powell, an Nvidia executive who reports to him and who, five sources told The New York Times in an explosive new report, was also a paramour. Even if Huang is pushed out as CEO, the board members he has made very rich are unlikely to cut him loose entirely. Barring another shoe dropping, they could keep him on as chairman, a role Nvidia doesn’t currently have. But someone still has to run the company, and there’s no apparent succession plan, which leaves us, like everyone else, to speculate while we wait to see what happens next. While Huang’s 60 direct reports undoubtedly get a closer look, consider this our own parlor game, featuring some obvious and less obvious candidates: Lisa Su . The AMD CEO runs Nvidia’s most credible rival, as well as a distant cousin of Huang. The Information floated her name this week, but why would she leave her job for his? Her company stands to benefit from every day that Nvidia spends distracted by an investigation, congressional briefings, and all the mini dramas that are sure to follow. Her best move might be to send a nice note and keep her current corner office. Eric Schmidt. He was the pick of Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, senior associate dean for leadership studies at the Yale School of Management, who we talked with earlier this week. Schmidt could “parachute in tomorrow and do a very good job,” Sonnenfeld said, and perhaps he could. He ran Google from 2001 to 2011, chaired the National Security Commission on AI from 2018 to 2021, and now runs the rocket company Relativity Space. Chips, software, government, rockets — it’s an impressive range. Then again, Schmidt would bring a lot of baggage when it comes to his own extramarital dalliances . It’s hard to see him clearing the board for that reason. Lip-Bu Tan . Intel’s CEO knows chips, and right now he might welcome a very soft landing. Last month, Intel reported third-quarter revenue up 21% to $16.5 billion, then warned its fourth-quarter results would fall short of Wall Street’s forecasts. The AI boom has caused a memory-chip shortage, pushing up PC prices and cutting PC sales. That’s hurt Intel (PC chips are a big part of its business), and its stock plunged 20% in after-hours trading on the warning, having already slid more than 30% since September. A move to a company that’s eating everyone’s lunch would be a pretty amazing escape hatch. Bret Taylor. The former Salesforce co-CEO and OpenAI board chair now runs the AI startup Sierra, and his resume includes a lot of the biggest brands in Silicon Valley. He co-created Google Maps, served as Facebook’s CTO, and chaired Twitter’s board through its sale to Elon Musk. He then took over as OpenAI’s board chair after the “Blip,” Sam Altman’s firing and fast return. When companies need an unflappable, likable adult in the room, they call Taylor. He probably knows nearly every customer Nvidia has, too. Ian Buck. If the board feels strongly about having a “builder” at the helm, they could do worse than the Nvidia VP who helped develop CUDA, the chip software that has become central to Nvidia’s dominance in AI. Analysts and former employees have floated him as a possible successor, and Kalshi traders give him a middling shot . He’s no household name, but the Stanford PhD seems more viable if Huang can can keep that chairman title and push for a successor he can work with. Someone else down the hall. Andrew Bell, Nvidia’s senior vice president of hardware engineering, arrived 25 years ago as a fresh Cornell grad and has been on an upward trajectory at the company ever since. Like Buck and dozens of other executives who are presumably being scrutinized, he reports directly to Huang. Nvidia CFO Colette Kress is the insider most often named, but analysts say she isn’t necessarily a natural successor as an innovator and visionary, and Bell has the chip pedigree. The wild card? Lori Huang . Nobody has floated her, but hear us out: Jensen met his wife as lab partners at Oregon State, so she has been working with him since before Nvidia existed. After graduating, she worked at Silicon Graphics as a micro chip engineer (making more money than her husband, he has said), then scaled back to raise the couple’s family, and she now co-leads the family trusts. If the board wants continuity, they could do worse than a humbler Huang who is also a brainiac. There’s a reason they say that behind every great man is a great woman (and vice versa). In a regulatory filing , Nvidia said its board accepted Huang’s resignation on Wednesday. Nvidia said its current chief financial officer and executive vice president, Collete Kress, will take over as interim CEO until the company finds a permanent successor. Kress will continue to serve as the company’s CFO. Nvidia’s shares were down more than 11% in premarket trading on Thursday. Since Friday, the company’s stock has fallen dramatically, resulting in a market cap loss of more than $300 billion. Nvidia’s board has also appointed Harvey Jones, a managing partner of Square Wave Ventures and former CEO of Synopsys, as the company’s first-ever chair of the board of directors. Jones has been on Nvidia’s board since 1993. “Jensen’s contributions to NVIDIA are profound. NVIDIA is one of the most consequential technology companies in the world. The Board and the company thank Jensen for his immeasurable contributions to the company and the industry,” the company said in a statement.
